documents.abstract: Can an agent be in contact with all other agents without being dissolved in them? We give this question a precise topological form. A pairwise-contact foam is a family of regions ("bubbles") of a state space with pairwise disjoint interiors, which represent the preserved individuality of each agent, such that every two regions touch, which represents connection, ideally along a set of positive size. We show that the naive formulation of the condition is degenerate unless the regions are regular closed with nonempty interior, and that point contact is cheap in dimension \( \ge2 \) while contact along arcs is impossible in the plane for more than four disks. We then prove that foams exist for every number \( N\ge2 \) of regions and, in the infinite-dimensional Hilbert space \( \ell^2 \), for countably infinitely many regions covering the whole space: the regions \( D_k=\{x:|x_k|\ge|x_j|\ \forall j\} \) meet pairwise along codimension-one walls \( x_k=\pm x_l \). In dimension three and on orientable surfaces of higher genus the planar obstruction is bypassed as well. Gluing along contact sets leaves every piece intact, which is the formal sense of "union without dissolution". Pairwise contact is strictly weaker than the Wada property, and riddled basins are a degenerate, non-proper case. For empirical use we separate three quantities that are easily confused: the global separation \( d(C_i,C_j) \) of two regions, the switching distance \( d(x,C_j) \) from a given state, and the activation distance to the contact set, together with intervention-specific versions that depend on an actuation model. We replace a single adjacency density by the spectrum of separations, a threshold-free completion scale, and a persistent nerve, with explicit limits on what the nerve proves, dimension-aware null models, and a rule that unsupported regions make a test inconclusive rather than being deleted. We define preservation of an agent's own control pattern so that it includes distinguishability of agents, give a confirmatory test of the composite hypothesis H4 whose unit of analysis is the independent replicate, and outline falsifiable programs in morphospace navigation by bioelectric interventions and in the information topology of human, AI, and biological collectives, including prediction of group fragmentation. No empirical result is claimed. The interpretive layer (cognitive light cone, "noosphere") is kept strictly apart from the mathematical and testable layers.

This paper studies text documents for natural language processing using toolsfrom dynamical systems and topological data analysis. We model a document’sparagraph procession as a discrete semantic trajectory moving around a centralthematic limit cycle Γ in a high-dimensional vocabulary space. Following Majhi,we prove that the Vietoris-Rips homology of the paragraph point cloud near Γ isisomorphic to either 0 or Z under precise density and reach constraints. We also providea geometric proof using the Tubular Neighborhood Theorem, the Borsuk NerveTheorem, and Latschev’s Reconstruction Theorem. The uniform and non-uniformconvergences of a text’s paragraphs to its main theme are rigorously establishedusing Oseledet’s Multiplicative Ergodic Theorem and Pesin’s metric construction.Furthermore, we derive the exponential convergence of the time-evolved persistencediagrams to the geometric profile of Γ via the results on Bottleneck distance for twodistinct temporal-shifted configurations. Finally, we demonstrate that non-essentialwritings and creative noise within a text systematically compress into the dead diagonalsubstrate using 0-persistence exponent formulations. With our results, welist some properties and term a text with these properties as a well-written text.Conversely, any text lacking one or more of these properties may be classified aspoorly written. Generative AI agents can utilize these constraints to automaticallyimprove their own writing quality and objectively evaluate human text.

This chapter outlines the personal and professional foundations of the cognitive behavioural approach developed for occupational health practice. Both occupational health and cognitive behavioural therapy became a vocation for me, providing a stabilising and meaningful thread that supported my movement beyond personal adversity and shaped my progression from nursing into trauma therapy and expert-witness work. The chapter traces a 40-year professional journey alongside the evolution of occupational health, from its earlier focus on industrial injury to its current role as a clinically grounded specialty. It considers how changes in the nature of work, together with increasing recognition of psychological and social influences on health, have reshaped contemporary occupational health practice. My thinking has been strongly influenced by the work of Gordon Waddell, Tom Cox, Cary Cooper and others whose research laid the foundations for biopsychosocial and psychologically informed approaches to work and health. These influences supported my development as both an occupational health practitioner and cognitive behavioural therapist and continue to guide my clinical reasoning. This chapter therefore introduces the values, evidence base and reasoning that underpin the cognitive behavioural approach explored throughout this book.

The growing demand for intelligent and adaptive services is accelerating the transition from conventional communication systems to semantic communication. Task-Oriented Semantic Communication (ToSC) has emerged as an efficient framework that reduces communication cost by transmitting only task-relevant information for downstream processing. This survey reviews the theoretical foundations, system architectures, and enabling technologies of ToSC, providing a taxonomy of design strategies spanning collaborative edge inference, end-to-end optimization, and multi-agent cooperation. Key technologies, including deep learning-based semantic representation and adaptive joint source-channel coding, are discussed. Device heterogeneity and partial observability are examined alongside recent tasks' performance evaluations, such as classification and recognition. The survey also discusses the integration of large-scale multimodal foundation models into semantic encoders for zero-shot task adaptation, continual learning frameworks for on-device semantic processing, cooperative multi-agent reasoning with interpretable information exchange, and cross-layer co-design within AI-native 6G infrastructures, leveraging reconfigurable intelligent surfaces and digital twins. By consolidating existing knowledge and identifying key design trade-offs in latency, accuracy, and bandwidth efficiency, this work aims to serve as both a reference and a roadmap for advancing ToSC toward reliable and resource-efficient communication in 6G and beyond.

As enterprise organizations transition from single-turn large language model (LLM) assistants to autonomous multi-agent execution meshes speaking the Model Context Protocol (MCP) and Agent-to-Agent (A2A) protocol, traditional perimeter-based access controls fail to prevent confused-deputy privilege escalation, batch-array policy bypass, and non-repudiable audit gaps. Building directly upon the foundational Zero Trust Architecture principles established in Durga (2025, DOI: 10.38124/ijsrmt.v4i12.1050) and the multi-agent coordination taxonomies formalized in Durga (2025, DOIs: 10.38124/ijsrmt.v4i11.1049, 10.38124/ijsrmt.v4i10.1048, 10.38124/ijsrmt.v4i9.1047, and 10.5281/zenodo.23723284), this technical report specifies and benchmarks three production enforcement invariants implemented across the OWASP Agent Control Standard (ACS) and the AgentTrust open specification: (1) per-element JSON-RPC 2.0 batch decomposition with deterministic fail-closed semantics; (2) cryptographic monotonic capability attenuation across transitive delegation hops; and (3) RFC 8785 JSON Canonicalization Scheme (JCS) audit receipts mapped to Open Cybersecurity Schema Framework (OCSF v1.3.0) provenance records.

Deploying autonomous AI agents across discrete and process manufacturing environments introduces acute cyber-physical risks when enterprise cloud control planes interact with plant-floor systems across ERP, MES, WMS, and QMS. Extending the self-optimizing factory paradigm formulated in Durga (2025, DOI: 10.38124/ijsrmt.v4i8.1046) and the cloud-native platform architectures established in Durga (2025, DOIs: 10.38124/ijsrmt.v4i7.1045, 10.38124/ijsrmt.v4i6.1044, 10.38124/ijsrmt.v4i5.1043, and 10.5281/zenodo.23723284), this technical report presents deterministic benchmarks for governed industrial agent operations and edge AI model fleets. We evaluate a 4-mode Pre-Release Recovery Reservation Lease with compare-and-swap (CAS) fencing, a cycle-safe transitive rollback DAG across ISA-95 Level 3/4 systems, a hard physical safety firewall isolating Level 0/1 Programmable Logic Controllers (PLCs) and Safety Instrumented Systems (SIS), and a Two-Layer JCS/CBOR Merkle edge model custody protocol achieving sub-100 ms last-known-good (LKG) rollback under intermittent plant connectivity.

AI agents now install packages, call model APIs with their operators' keys and change code in repositories that deploy to production. The network, credentials and write access they need are also how they can leak data, steal a key or change a system nobody approved. Sandboxes contain an agent but leave little evidence of what crossed their boundary; tracing records what happened but contains nothing. We present Tracekit Box, an open-source system (MIT, v0) that does both. Each job runs in its own Firecracker micro-VM with no network card. The only ways out are doors on the host, served over vsock: commands, outbound connections, secrets, model calls and the workspace patch. At every door a Tracekit signer the agent cannot reach decides what passes and signs it into one run per box. Names are resolved on the host; private and cloud-metadata addresses are always refused; secrets never enter the VM, which sees placeholders the host proxy swaps for real values only in one header for bound hosts; and changes come back as a patch applied file by file after the signer decides each file. Box fails closed, and each job ends as a .tkb bundle anyone can verify offline. All 13 end-to-end checks pass on a real KVM runner (the test that runs them takes 28.5 s, including image pull and boot); 15 fuzz targets on the trust boundary produced nine findings, all fixed; and the demo run's 102 signed records verify. Box does not yet run Firecracker's jailer, needs a co-located signer, and records processes inside the VM only where they cross a door.

A dated test protocol, not a pre-registration, for a study of Estonia's policy on identifiers for artificial intelligence (AI) agents. The study traces the move from an agent identifier discussed in June 2026 as an isikukood (the Estonian personal identification code) to a design that keeps the agent from being a person, and the draft act that the Ministry of Economic Affairs and Communications (MKM) sent for inter-ministerial coordination on 08.10.2026 (draft legislation information system, EIS, file 26-1105). It uses explaining-outcome process tracing on its theory-first path. The protocol sets out the rival explanations, the observables that bear on them and how each is tested, the coding design with a human second coder, the collection rules, and the author's interventions in the process, each with its date. documents.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to generate research ideas from scientific literature. Existing systems combine literature retrieval with search, generation, and refinement, making it difficult to determine how the retrieval strategy itself shapes the ideas generated. We isolate this contribution by comparing five retrieval strategies and a No Literature baseline under a shared generation protocol, using 45,000 ideas across 15 machine learning topics and ten open-weight models. Relative to no literature basline, all five retrieval strategies reduce diversity among ideas generated from the same set of papers by $5.6\%$--$17.9\%$, while most increase diversity by $10.2\%$--$18.1\%$ when ideas from different sets are pooled. Effects on idea quality and novelty are modest on average but vary across topics. We further apply a JSD-based attribution method to trace the influence of individual input papers on each idea's motivation, core idea, approach, and validation. In $79.3\%$ of ideas, only one or two distinct papers receive the highest attribution scores across these four parts. These leading sources often recur across ideas generated from the same set of papers, and groups with more varied source attribution contain more diverse ideas ($r=0.70$). These findings motivate various sets of literature and the use of attribution to guide the choice of sources for subsequent ideas.

Abstract Artificial intelligence (AI) is moving from pilot programs into the routine delivery of military mental health care. Predictive models already scan Veterans Health Administration records to flag veterans at high risk of suicide; models trained on Army Study to Assess Risk and Resilience in Servicemembers data can now stratify suicide risk up to a decade after soldiers leave active service, and generative AI models are being positioned to deliver triage, peer support, and low-intensity psychological interventions. The frameworks that govern responsible military AI have not kept up. The Department of Defense Responsible Artificial Intelligence Strategy and Implementation Pathway, NATO’s principles of responsible use, and allied instruments such as the United Kingdom’s JSP 936 provide lifecycle assurance for AI-enabled capability, but none of them makes specific provision for the therapeutic encounter. That omission exposes service members to what this commentary terms a recognition-action gap. Systems trained predominantly on civilian data can transcribe the words of military distress accurately while misreading their clinical meaning: moral injury classified as fear-based trauma, minimized suicidality scored as low risk, routine operational vernacular flagged as threat. The risk is compounded because the boundary between clinical care and occupational capability is porous in the armed forces. The military command exception to the Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act Privacy Rule and command notification under Department of Defense Instruction 6490.08 mean that outputs generated for care could lawfully reach deployability, security clearance, and administrative decisions, with predictable consequences for help-seeking. This commentary proposes behavioral validity, the demonstrated capability to safely manage the behavioral presentations of the population a system will actually serve, as a core governance requirement for mental health AI in defense settings. It specifies 4 conditions of use: clinically supervised pre-fielding assessment, therapeutic firewalling, moral injury and cultural competency, and meaningful human control. Defense health systems should not wait for civilian regulators to notice the gap. They are well placed to define the standard.

documents.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have rapidly become a default source of help for students in science and engineering courses. In foundational engineering mechanics courses such as statics, students routinely use these tools to check answers, work through partial solutions, and ask for explanations. Effective tutoring in this setting requires more than a correct final answer. A model must also confirm correct work when a student doubts it, and identify errors in flawed work. Existing benchmarks evaluate LLMs primarily on final-answer accuracy, so it is unclear whether models that can solve mechanics problems also have the other technical capabilities that tutoring depends on. Here we introduce TrussTutor-Bench, a benchmark of 200 verified two-dimensional truss problems paired with automatically generated student solutions, and use it to evaluate thirteen LLMs on solution accuracy, sycophancy, and error detection. Baseline accuracy ranged from 64.5% to 97.0%. Every model detected nearly all injected errors in synthetic flawed student work (90.4% to 100%), so error detection did not distinguish models under these clean conditions. Sycophancy did. When a student insisted that correct work was wrong, models rejected correct solutions to problems they had themselves solved in 1.6% to 50.0% of cases. These results show that performance varies widely across models: the leading models solve, check, and defend student work nearly perfectly, while others are far less reliable, particularly when a student doubts correct work. TrussTutor-Bench provides a verified, extensible standard for determining which models are technically reliable enough to put in front of students. Follow-up work must now focus on teaching rather than technical capability, drawing on learning science to determine whether LLM help leads students to understand the material or simply to reach the right answer.

documents.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence now drafts travel itineraries that travelers cannot easily verify. Integrating privacy calculus theory with a dual-pathway trust model, this study examines how system attributes shape tourist trust and continued usage, and how technology readiness conditions those links. A two-wave panel (433 Chinese and European travelers), a validation wave (372), and 42 interviews were analyzed using structural equation modeling, importance–performance map analysis, fuzzy-set qualitative comparative analysis, and thematic analysis. Data transparency and content authenticity raised both cognitive and affective trust, and affective trust sustained continued usage most strongly. Technology readiness reversed the expected pattern: readier travelers scrutinized fluent output rather than relying on it, weakening the behavioral effect of trust. Providers should replace generic privacy notices with in-context, verifiable data-use disclosures and checkable citations, and segment interfaces so that ready travelers receive verification tools and less-ready travelers receive reassurance. Regulators can make verifiability, not fluency, the disclosure standard.

Background/Objectives: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) tools are entering clinical documentation ahead of institutional governance, and little is known about whether clinicians who rely on them also check their output, particularly in Central and Eastern Europe. This study characterized regular GenAI use for documentation, verification practices, and exposure to clinically relevant errors among healthcare professionals at a Romanian tertiary center, and identified the attitudes independently associated with regular use. Methods: In a cross-sectional survey of 126 physicians, residents, nurses, and public health specialists (46.0% of 315 invited), regular use was defined as at least weekly use for documentation during the preceding three months. Composites measured AI literacy, trust in output accuracy, perceived confidentiality risk, perceived usefulness, documentation burden, and intention; emotional exhaustion was measured with the Maslach Burnout Inventory. Correlates of regular use were examined with bootstrap-validated multivariable logistic regression, and differences in burden and exhaustion with propensity-score overlap weighting. Results: Regular use was reported by 56 participants (44.4%; 95% confidence interval [CI] 36.1–53.2), mostly with ChatGPT (89.3%) for referral and discharge letters (78.6%) and discharge summaries (69.6%). Users verified a mean of 70.3% (95% CI 65.6–75.0) of outputs line by line, and 36 (64.3%; 95% CI 51.2–75.5) had encountered at least one clinically relevant error. Among users, higher trust was associated with a lower proportion of outputs verified (Spearman ρ = −0.31; p = 0.020). Concern about factual errors was common in both groups (73.2% vs. 77.1%), whereas confidentiality concern, perceived insufficient training, and fear of liability were less frequent among users. Higher trust (adjusted odds ratio [OR] 2.36 per 10 points; 95% CI 1.34–4.15), higher perceived usefulness (OR 1.90; 1.03–3.50), and lower perceived risk (OR 0.49; 0.29–0.83) were independently associated with regular use (optimism-corrected area under the curve 0.905). After overlap weighting, differences in documentation burden (−4.8 points; 95% CI −12.1 to 2.6) and emotional exhaustion (−1.7; −5.9 to 2.5) were not statistically significant but were imprecisely estimated. Conclusions: Regular GenAI use coexisted with incomplete verification and frequent error exposure and was linked to trust and perceived usefulness; AI literacy and training were not independently associated with use once these attitudes were accounted for. Associations with documentation burden and emotional exhaustion were inconclusive. Institutions should treat verification as a distinct, trainable behavior and pair access with explicit confidentiality guidance.

documents.abstract: Skills, as reusable external knowledge, have demonstrated substantial potential to enhance the ability of Large Language Models (LLMs) to solve complex tasks. However, existing skill-augmented generation methods typically rely on separate models for skill retrieval and skill utilization, resulting in disconnected optimization of these two processes. To address this gap, we propose Skill-Uni, a unified reinforcement learning framework that jointly optimizes skill retrieval and utilization. Specifically, we adopt a generative skill retrieval paradigm that enables a single model to both learn how to retrieve relevant skills and leverage them for task solving. To effectively train this unified framework, we introduce a two-stage training strategy consisting of warm-up instruction tuning and GRPO, allowing the model to progressively improve its skill retrieval and utilization capabilities. Extensive experiments on five skill-related benchmarks demonstrate the effectiveness of Skill-Uni, yielding average performance gains of 66.59% and 34.82% over the base Qwen3-4B and LLaMA3.1-8B models, respectively. Besides, Skill-Uni is compatible with various skill retrieval engines, demonstrating its flexibility and generalizability. Additional in-depth analyses also provide insights into the effectiveness of Skill-Uni.

Large Language Models (LLMs) based on Transformer architectures have achieved remarkable performance across artificial intelligence tasks, but their computational cost remains a major bottleneck. Structured sparsification provides a promising approach to reducing this cost. In particular, $\ell_{1,\infty}$ projections can induce column-wise sparsity in model matrices, but existing proximal methods (Prox) typically require $\mathcal{O}(nm\log(nm))$ operations for matrices in $\mathbb{R}^{n\times m}$, limiting their computational and energy efficiency. In this paper, we introduce Two-Stage Clipping (TSC), an efficient structured sparsification operator inspired by bilevel optimization. Rather than solving a bilevel optimization problem in the strict sense, TSC decomposes the computation into two successive stages. First, group-level quantities are projected to allocate the global sparsity budget and identify active groups. Second, the resulting values are used as group-wise clipping thresholds for the matrix coefficients. For square attention matrices ($n \times n$), the complexity of our TSC method is $O(n^2)$, which is linear in the number of matrix coefficients. We establish a theoretical bound on the discrepancy between TSC and the exact proximal projection and show on synthetic data that the additional Euclidean approximation cost remains small in practice. Extensive benchmarks demonstrate substantial runtime improvements over proximal baselines and validate the theoretical norm identities underlying the proposed construction.

Artificial intelligence (AI) is becoming an important technology in health care and is increasingly being explored in hospital pharmacy practice. Hospital pharmacists manage large amounts of medication-related information, including prescriptions, patient medical records, laboratory values, drug interactions, adverse drug reactions, medication histories and inventory data. AI-based technologies can analyse these data rapidly and may assist pharmacists in identifying medication-related problems, improving workflow and supporting clinical decision-making. Recent literature describes applications of AI in prescription screening, medication-error detection, adverse drug event detection, pharmacovigilance, medication reconciliation, dose optimization, clinical decision support, antimicrobial stewardship, inventory management and medication adherence Machine learning, deep learning and natural language processing are among the major technologies used in pharmacy-related AI applications. These technologies can identify patterns in electronic health records and clinical documentation that may be difficult to recognize manually. However, AI should be considered a support tool rather than a complete replacement for pharmacists. Concerns related to data quality, privacy algorithmic bias, explainability, cybersquatting, cost training and clinical validation remain important. Successful implementation therefore requires collaboration between pharmacists, physicians, information technology professionals, hospital administrators and AI developers. The review discusses the major applications, advantages, limitations, ethical considerations and future perspectives of AI in hospital pharmacy practice.

documents.abstract: This study qualitatively inquired into artificial intelligence and the future of audit in Nigeria, specifically investigating whether AI will replace the human auditor. A qualitative phenomenological design was adopted. Twenty-eight (28) participants were purposively selected across Lagos, Abuja, and Port Harcourt, comprising Big 4 and mid-tier audit partners, audit managers/seniors with 10+ years of experience, ICAN/ANAN/FRCN regulators, and audited clients including CFOs and Audit Committee chairs. Data were collected via semi-structured indepth interviews between January and May 2025. Data saturation was achieved at the 23rd interview. Thematic analysis was performed using the Braun and Clarke (2006) framework assisted by NVivo. Results reveal that AI is augmenting, not replacing, human auditors. Four distinct AI implementation levels emerged: Assisted Audit (e.g., IDEA, Excel), Augmented Audit (e.g., Power BI, ACL), Autonomous Testing (e.g., RPA, Machine Learning anomaly detection), and Advisory Assurance (e.g., Generative AI for reporting). AI deployment improved audit efficiency by 60% and increased anomaly detection from 35% to 82%. Key barriers to adoption include technophobia (78%), unstructured client data (72%), tool costs (65%), and a regulatory vacuum regarding AI audit evidence under ISA 500 (60%). The study proposes a Human-AI Collaboration Model (70-30 Model), where AI performs 70% of routine data tasks, and human auditors provide 30% high-level professional judgement, ethics, and skepticism. This represents the first phenomenological study in Nigeria exploring the lived experiences of senior practitioners on the AI replacement debate.

ObjectiveTo describe the experience of pain among people with Parkinson's disease, including its characteristics, psychological effects, and impact on daily life.DesignQualitative descriptive study.SettingCommunity-based study using semi-structured individual interviews.ParticipantsFifteen people with Parkinson's disease (11 women) diagnosed according to the United Kingdom Parkinson's Disease Society Brain Bank criteria and experiencing Parkinson's disease-related pain based on the Parkinson's Disease Pain Classification System.InterventionNot applicable.Main measuresSemi-structured interviews were conducted to explore participants' experiences of pain. Data were analysed using an inductive thematic analysis based on a hybrid approach combining artificial intelligence-powered coding through ChatGPT-4 with manual triangulation.ResultsThree main themes were identified: (1) experiences and perceptions of pain, including the nature and characterization of pain and its relationship with Parkinson's disease; (2) the impact of pain on daily life; and (3) feelings associated with pain, including emotional changes related to pain and its broader psychological impact.ConclusionsPain in people with Parkinson's disease is an interconnected and context-dependent experience extending beyond its physical manifestations. The patient-centred narratives provide contextual insight into how pain interacts with motor and non-motor symptoms, daily functioning, emotional well-being, and participation, supporting individualized and comprehensive approaches to pain assessment and management.

Generative artificial intelligence (GAI) has introduced an important question in education, when AI provides immediate and reliable feedback, do students use it as a learning support tool or gradually rely on it as a substitute for their own cognitive efforts? Drawing on Cognitive Load Theory, Cognitive Offloading Theory, and Metacognitive Monitoring Theory, this study develops a theoretical model to explain the formation process of undergraduate students’ overreliance on GAI feedback. Specifically, this study examines the relationships among perceived cognitive load, cognitive offloading, and overreliance on GAI feedback, while further exploring how metacognitive monitoring levels shape this process. A questionnaire survey was conducted among 600 undergraduate students, and structural equation modeling was performed using AMOS 31.0. The results showed that perceived cognitive load significantly and positively predicted cognitive offloading, which further contributed to students’ overreliance on GAI feedback. Meanwhile, perceived cognitive load also directly predicted overreliance on GAI feedback. Bootstrap analysis further confirmed that cognitive offloading mediated the relationship between perceived cognitive load and overreliance on GAI feedback. In addition, this study established separate structural equation models for students with different levels of metacognitive monitoring and found distinct patterns in the formation of GAI feedback overreliance. Specifically, students with lower metacognitive monitoring were more likely to be influenced by cognitive pressure during learning, showing a more prominent direct relationship between perceived cognitive load and GAI feedback overreliance. This finding suggests that these students tend to rely more directly on GAI feedback when facing higher cognitive demands. In contrast, students with higher metacognitive monitoring demonstrated a more evident cognitive regulation process, in which cognitive offloading played a more important role in linking perceived cognitive load with GAI feedback overreliance. This indicates that these students may actively adjust their cognitive resource allocation when using GAI, although continuous cognitive offloading may still increase their dependence on AI-generated feedback.
topics: Intelligent Tutoring Systems and Adaptive Learning

documents.abstract: Objective: The paper aimed to examine ethical, privacy, and governance challenges in AI-IoT (Artificial Intelligence-based Internet of Things) healthcare environments. Design: A total of 39 peer-reviewed open-access studies were screened and used for a systematic review using the PRISMA (Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses) framework. A multi-stage thematic analysis was used for identifying recurring patterns within the literature and answering the research questions. Results/outcomes: The identified challenges in the AI-IoT healthcare ecosystems, arising from the thematic analysis, are privacy and continuous surveillance, algorithmic bias and lack of explainability, limitations for informed consent, and fragmented governance and accountability. Conclusion: The findings, in sync with STS theory, indicate that challenges in AI-IoT healthcare systems cannot be addressed solely through technological innovations. In response, the study proposed an Integrated Human-Centric Trust Framework to integrate human intervention with technological advancements.

documents.abstract: Supported subnanometer clusters have attracted significant attention in catalysis. Yet, it is challenging to resolve their structural evolution, particularly in the presence of adsorbates. Here, we present an artificial intelligence (AI)-enabled simulation framework that integrates machine learning force field (MLFF) construction, molecular dynamics (MD) simulations, and ML-assisted infrared (IR) and X-ray absorption near-edge structure (XANES) spectra analysis to investigate the restructuring of supported subnanometer clusters. Using Pt10/γ-Al2O3(110) as a model system, we explored the CO-induced restructuring of the cluster under different conditions. The simultaneous machine learning (ML)-spectra elucidate a strong interplay among adsorbate coverage, cluster restructuring, and cluster-support interaction. This work sheds light on the complex dynamics of supported subnanometer clusters that is extendible to other systems.

Here, we developed ViralTensors, an unsupervised artificial intelligence (AI) platform that employs Nonnegative Matrix Factorization (NMF) and Weighted NMF (WNMF) for integration of multidimensional datasets and extraction of interpretable latent features. We demonstrate that ViralTensors extracts biologically relevant host regulatory programs and previously unrecognized associations within complex virus–host interactions from global transcriptomic datasets with virus–host protein interaction data. Systems-level analysis of viruses representing three distinct taxonomic families—Coronaviridae (SARS-CoV-2), Filoviridae (Ebolavirus), and Orthomyxoviridae (Influenza virus)—revealed conserved host pathways and targets associated with diverse cellular functions, including endosomal trafficking, gap junction signaling, and cholesterol biosynthesis. The functional relevance of these predicted host targets was validated in cell-based infection assays using FDA-approved therapeutics to inhibit replication of human coronavirus 229E (HCoV-229E), vaccinia virus (VACV-WR), and Hantaan virus (HTNV), representing viruses with RNA and DNA genomes. Furthermore, quantitative global proteomic analysis of Seoul hantavirus infected human endothelial cells independently supported the relevance of AI-predicted host protein networks to viral replication. Collectively, these findings establish ViralTensors as an analytical framework for identifying conserved host dependencies across taxonomically diverse viruses and demonstrate the potential of targeting shared host cellular programs for the development of broad-spectrum antiviral therapeutics.

Background: The use of artificial intelligence (AI) is rapidly increasing among university students worldwide. However, little is known about how undergraduate medical students in Bangladesh engage with AI tools in their education. Objective: To assess the pattern of using AI and the self-reported knowledge and attitude regarding AI among undergraduate medical students of Dhaka National Medical College (DNMC). Methods: A descriptive cross-sectional study was conducted among 1st, 2nd, 3rd and 5th-year MBBS students of DNMC from December 2025 to July 2026 (4th-year students were excluded). By convenience type of non-probability sampling, 125 medical students completed a structured, self-administered questionnaire distributed as a Google Form through students' WhatsApp number. The questionnaire included sociodemographic data, patterns of AI use, and a 10-item, 5-point Likert scale for assessment of self-reported knowledge and attitudes (range 10 to 50). Data were analysed using descriptive statistics, the chi-square test, independent t-test, and ANOVA; p<0.05 was considered significant. Results: Mean age of 125 students was 21.7±1.7 years, among them 56.0% were female. Almost all respondents (97.6%) were familiar with AI. Most of them (89.6%) were current users, most commonly of ChatGPT (81.2%) and Gemini (32.1%). Majority of them (81.3%) thought that AI would be beneficial to their future career and 74.2% felt it should be taught to all medical students, 41.1% felt confident about replacement of medical specialities. Half of respondents (50.0%) were concerned about AI-generated misinformation, and 79.3% reported at least occasional difficulty verifying AI-generated academic content. The composite knowledge–attitude score (mean 37.2±6.0 of 50) rose significantly with academic year (p=0.023, driven by a 1st- versus 5th-year difference). Gender and current AI-use status were not significantly associated with the score. Conclusion: Most of the undergraduate medical students of DNMC have familiarity with use AIs and positive attitudes of it use for their learning. However, some of them are concerned about the misinformation may be produced by the AIs. Hence, structured AI-literacy training, from the first year of the MBBS curriculum, is a demand of the time. J Dhaka National Med. Coll. Hos. 2026; 32 (02): 60-64
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: Background: Undergraduate healthcare students in India experience heavy academic pressure and exhausting hospital duties, yet rarely consult mental health professionals because of social stigma and fear of losing internal marks. Many students now turn to smartphone artificial intelligence (AI) chatbots late at night for private emotional comfort. This study assessed the prevalence of AI chatbot usage for emotional support, user perception, and emotional reliance among healthcare trainees in rural South India.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: This chapter examines the role of artificial intelligence (AI) as a reflective tool in language teacher education, with a particular focus on its potential to support professional learning during teaching practicums. Drawing on data from pre- and post-practicum group interviews, the study explores the experiences of 12 Vietnamese preservice Teaching English to Speakers of Other Languages (TESOL) teachers, who interacted with AI chatbots over an eight-week teaching practicum at a university in Thailand. The findings reveal that AI chatbots functioned as effective mediating tools, enabling participants to bridge TESOL theories and classroom-based practice. Additionally, the preservice teachers used AI chatbots to navigate cultural differences and to develop pedagogical approaches responsive to Thai classrooms. Most importantly, sustained engagement with AI chatbots throughout the practicum fostered reflective teaching practices among the participants. Based on these findings, the chapter discusses pedagogical implications for integrating AI chatbots to support reflective practice in TESOL teacher education.

Subject. Application of artificial intelligence technologies in the operations of the Chinese internet insurance company ZhongAn – the first professional online insurer in China. Objectives. To conduct a comprehensive assessment of the impact of artificial intelligence technologies on the operational efficiency of the insurance company and to identify factors limiting the full realization of the potential of digital transformation. Methods. The study employed comparative analysis of operational indicators for 2019–2024, trend analysis of the dynamics of investments in research and development, financial analysis of performance indicators, SWOT analysis, and content analysis. Results. It has been established that the automation of the insurance company’s key business processes through artificial intelligence has reached extremely high levels: the underwriting automation rate is 99%, the reduction in claims settlement time is 87.5%, and employee productivity has increased 30‑fold. A paradox of efficiency has been identified: the growth in operational performance is accompanied by a persistently high level of consumer complaints, the opacity (non‑interpretability) of algorithms, risks of homogenization, and a shortage of personnel. A similar phenomenon has also been observed in the Russian insurance market. The hypothesis has been confirmed that technological efficiency alone is not a sufficient condition for sustainable profitability and consumer trust. Conclusions. For Russian insurers, ZhongAn’s experience demonstrates the need for the simultaneous development of technological infrastructure, human capital, and a customer‑oriented culture. The key success factor is the transformation from a technological pioneer into a responsible leader by ensuring the transparency of artificial intelligence systems and striking a balance between innovation and trust.

Fitness-to-work consultations in occupational health are often brief and framed by specific management referral questions. This can limit opportunities to explore beliefs, behaviours and wider psychological and social influences that sustain symptoms and contribute to ongoing work difficulties. This chapter argues that assessments are strengthened when grounded in a clear biopsychosocial framework and supported by the cognitive behavioural approach introduced earlier in the book. It demonstrates how concise biopsychosocial formulation helps practitioners understand how physical health, psychological processes, workplace demands and social factors interact. This enables the identification of modifiable maintaining mechanisms, such as unhelpful interpretations, avoidance patterns or reinforcing organisational practices, that influence functional capacity and return to work. A brief, work-focused method is presented using the ABC model and the 5 Ps formulation, which together form the practical backbone of the cognitive behavioural approach. A case example illustrates how focused enquiry and employee-centred assessment can reveal realistic levers for change and strengthen the clarity and defensibility of fitness-to-work reasoning.

Generative artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly used across the behavioural research lifecycle. It may improve the efficiency and quality of research, but rapid, uncritical adoption carries risks to research integrity: algorithmic bias, ethical concerns around consent, privacy and plagiarism, erosion of researchers’ skills and public trust, and environmental costs. This Open Letter presents Behavioural Research UK’s (BR-UK) statement on using generative AI effectively and responsibly in behavioural research. It was informed by existing guidance and expert consultation. The statement sets out BR-UK’s four key propositions: (1) research ethics and integrity principles must include AI concerns; (2) AI should assist, but not replace, researchers through a human-in-the-loop approach; (3) rigorous evaluation of AI use is essential; and (4) coordinated stakeholder action is needed to move from identifying risks to practical solutions. It then provides recommendations and points to practical tools, such as decision aids and checklists for declaring AI use, for seven stakeholder groups, namely research-generating institutions, funders, publication outlets, behavioural research networks and communities, AI platform and tool providers, individual researchers, and research users. The statement will be reviewed annually until 2028, the duration of BR-UK, as technology and evidence evolve.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI
Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: Abstract Accurate, readily available shaking estimates can improve situational awareness and rapid response efforts following a major earthquake. The spatial distribution of shaking relative to population and infrastructure has major implications for expected fatalities, damage, and disruptions. For large earthquakes, the location, size, and orientation of the causal fault plane (i.e., fault finiteness) play primary roles in determining the distribution of shaking. However, such a description of the causal fault is difficult to establish in the immediate aftermath of a major event, when observations are typically sparse and uncertain. However, during the time window between an event’s detection and the completion of quantitative constraints on the source, tectonic context can provide evidence for the rupture’s likely spatial orientation, thereby improving shaking estimates prior to formal finite-fault inversion results. Here, we propose a new method using tectonic context to describe a constrained, but still uncertain, source to improve early shaking estimates for large earthquakes. We demonstrate its implementation in the U.S. Geological Survey ShakeMap software by applying the proposed method to a catalog of 40 large (Mw>7), impactful global events from 2018 to 2026 and present an analysis of the results. We find that for 18 of the catalog events, the ShakeMap could be automatically constrained based on the seismotectonic context, whereas 14 events would require expert user input to determine whether a constrained approach is appropriate, and 8 events would not benefit from a constrained approach (but could be automatically identified). The results show that using seismotectonic context to constrain the source can substantially improve shaking estimates in the immediate minutes to hours following a major earthquake. We show a detailed comparison of the proposed (constrained) approach to the existing (unconstrained) approach for four earthquakes, each occurring in a distinct tectonic environment, to highlight the advantages and limitations of the method’s application.

Automated red-team auditing of language models is an important way to evaluate safety-relevant behaviors. These audits implicitly search a tree of possible conversation pathways: at each turn an auditor model decides which conversation to continue, and an LLM judge scores the dialogue. We emphasize that this auditing procedure is a Markov decision process, where states are the conversation history, actions are candidate responses, and rewards are judge scores for the target behavior. By adopting this perspective, we introduce two major improvements to auditing. First, we propose adopting beam search for the audit rather than relying on the auditor alone. We then interpret the problem of finding states that are likely to lead to problematic behavior as value estimation. Surprisingly, we show that this value function can be estimated by linear probing from the target model's activations to predict discounted future rewards - a method we term "Value Probes." By using Value Probes as a heuristic in our beam-search audit, we are able to substantially improve auditing success. Across 18 target behaviors and 3 scales of models, our approach raises peak audit scores by roughly 50% compared to (token-matched) standard auditing approaches. Furthermore, we show that Value Probes can be fit using off-policy data from smaller models. We also ablate individual components, and show that our method offers a comparably-performant and more efficient alternative to more expensive language model follow-ups. We hope these methods will improve language model auditing and lead to safer models.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: OBJECTIVE: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly explored for clinical decision support, yet how successive versions of the same model compare on diagnostic tasks remains unclear. This study aimed to quantify version-specific changes in diagnostic performance by directly comparing ChatGPT-4.0 and ChatGPT-5.1 on standardized pure-tone audiogram interpretation. STUDY DESIGN: Comparative diagnostic performance study. SETTING: Controlled experimental study using audiograms generated with simulation software. METHODS: One hundred audiograms, including 20 with intentional masking errors, were generated using AudSim Flex® software and submitted to both model versions through a standardized 7-step diagnostic prompt based on ASHA criteria. Two board-certified otolaryngologists with audiological expertise independently scored each response on a 5-point Likert scale, yielding 1400 evaluations per model. Inter-rater agreement was assessed using quadratic weighted Cohen's kappa, and model comparisons were performed with the Wilcoxon signed-rank test. RESULTS: Inter-rater reliability was acceptable overall (κ = 0.74-0.78), though agreement was lower for degree-of-loss classification with ChatGPT-5.1 (κ = 0.44). ChatGPT-5.1 scored significantly higher than ChatGPT-4.0 on 6 of 7 questions (P < .001), with effect sizes ranging from 0.53 to 0.94. The largest improvement appeared in degree-of-hearing-loss classification (median difference, +1.0 point). Bone conduction threshold identification was the only item without a significant between-version difference (P = .121). Both models performed poorly on audiograms containing masking errors. CONCLUSION: ChatGPT-5.1 demonstrated meaningful improvements over ChatGPT-4.0 in audiogram interpretation, particularly in higher-order diagnostic reasoning tasks. However, both versions struggled with clinically flawed input data. These findings underscore the need for version-specific benchmarking and expert oversight when integrating LLMs into audiological practice.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: Abstract Background FrontierAI laboratories govern deployed systems via model specifications, usage policies, and safety frameworks. These governance documents undergo repeated revisions, yet current practices rarely distinguish substantive normative policy changes from mere editorial clarifications. This produces silent drift: continuous normative modification without clear documentation of changes, reasons for modification, and the institutional authority under which changes were made. The following are examples of an AI API that identifies new drugs and vaccines for a given disease, scaling from a simple “Name that drug!” function to much more advanced models. This paper reviews the revision histories for five publicly available AI governance instruments that are slated for release between 2019 and 2025; OpenAI usage policies and Model Specific, Anthropic Responsible Scaling Policy, the EU Artificial Intelligence Act and the NIST AI Risk Management Framework. This paper identifies the areas where current practices seemed aligned with formal versioning discipline, and it pinpointed the areas where there are persistent implementation gaps. Version number tracking vocabulary is becoming more frequent at the whole document level, while the specific term level is still not being used. The type of AI disruptive technology that incites a substantial shift from a normative route is an exogenous shock. Current changelogs are descriptive, but they are not change classified. Explicit structural rollback mechanisms are not found in any of the examined instruments. Through this analysis, we realize that there are genuine limits of the software-as-a-policy analogy, taking these limitations as hard design constraints for possible AI regulation instead of unconsidered counter-arguments. Implications: AI labs can “self-engineer” a lightweight globally adaptable, versioning approach to formally defined meta-changes, clause granular history logs, design rollback aware implementations, and misclassification preserved as independently audit-bounded events that can be independently audited by regulators/independent auditors and formally accepted by regulators as an independent practice. Does not imply specific compelling AI system substantive policy content.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: This essay, framed within the Science, Technology, and Society (STS) perspective, examines the mandatory registration of mobile phone lines linked to the CURP (Unique Population Registry Code) in Mexico, through an exploration of regulations, judicial rulings, technical documents, and academic literature. It traces the trajectory of three registration initiatives: RENAUT (2009–2012), PANAUT (2021—invalidated by the Supreme Court in 2022), and the current framework established by the Telecommunications and Broadcasting Law and the guidelines from the telecommunications regulatory authority (2025–2026). What data is recorded? Who safeguards it? Who has access to it? Four types of information are identified: the holder’s identity, traffic data, location, and the content of communications. Drawing on concepts such as society, culture, surveillance capitalism, contextual integrity, and technological co-production, the essay argues that this registration is a sociotechnical decision—not a neutral or purely technical act, but a political and social one—that reconfigures power relations by shifting the burden of proving identity onto the users. The result is not the interception of conversations, but rather the linking of existing metadata—already being collected—to the locations of identified individuals. The risk lies not in the state-run database itself, but in the lack of clear rules regarding access, data retention, and transparency. Comparative evidence does not show a reduction in crime; instead, the policy produces unequal, asymmetric effects and encourages practices of evasion. The text concludes by calling for public evaluation and data governance, supported by verifiable controls.

Der Beitrag entwickelt aus den Erfahrungen des Projekts Künstlich Menschlich Intelligent eine soziotechnische Forschungs- und Entwicklungsagenda für die nächste Phase der digitalen und nachhaltigen Transformation (Twin Transformation). Im Zentrum steht die Frage, unter welchen Bedingungen datenbasierte Technologien und insbesondere KI-Agenten und autonome Systeme zu humangerechter Arbeit, Effizienz, organisationaler Wertschöpfung und Nachhaltigkeit beitragen können. Ausgehend von einem Dreiklang aus Wirkung, Gestaltung und Befähigung wird gezeigt, dass die nächste Welle der digitalen Transformation nicht als lineare technische Implementierung verstanden werden kann, sondern als reflexiver Gestaltungsprozess, in dem Mensch, Technik und Organisation gemeinsam unter dem Leitbild der Nachhaltigkeit weiterentwickelt werden. Die Projekterfahrungen und aktuelle Erkenntnisse machen zentrale Ambivalenzen sichtbar: Digitalisierung bedeutet nicht automatisch KI-Readiness; niedrigschwellige KI-Nutzung ersetzt keine organisationale Gestaltungsfähigkeit; und Entlastung durch KI kann zugleich Arbeitsverdichtung, Verantwortungsverschiebung oder De-Skilling erzeugen. Darauf aufbauend formuliert der Beitrag zukünftige Forschungsfelder zu mehrdimensionaler Wirkungsmessung, Mensch-KI-Interaktion, Human-AI Teaming, Ko-Adaption, Partizipation, KI-Governance, Verantwortlichkeit, Aufsicht, Kompetenzentwicklung, Transfer, digitaler Souveränität, Abhängigkeiten und Lock-in-Effekten. Besondere Aufmerksamkeit gilt kleinen und mittleren Unternehmen sowie ressourcenbeschränkten Organisationen, die für nachhaltige KI-Nutzung Orientierungswissen, Methoden, Demonstratoren und intermediäre Transferstrukturen benötigen.
topics: Impact of AI and Big Data on Business and Society

documents.abstract: West Nile virus (WNV) has emerged as a significant public health threat in Greece since 2010. Central Macedonia was the epicentre of the 2010 and 2022 outbreaks, whereas Attica, Eastern Macedonia and Thrace, and Thessaly predominated in other seasons. Climate change and environmental factors are amplifying transmission dynamics, necessitating integrated surveillance approaches. This narrative review synthesizes current evidence on the epidemiology of WNV in Greece, examines the role of climate change in transmission dynamics, and evaluates the implementation of One Health surveillance and early warning systems. It draws on the peer-reviewed literature, official surveillance reports of the National Public Health Organization (EODY) and European surveillance data for 2010–2025. Since 2010, WNV has become seasonally endemic in Greece, with 2184 locally acquired cases, 1547 cases of neuroinvasive disease and 301 deaths recorded during 2010–2025, including major seasons in 2010 (262 cases), 2018 (317), 2022 (286) and 2024 (220). Climate variability, particularly elevated temperatures and altered precipitation patterns, significantly influences Culex vector dynamics and virus transmission. Current surveillance integrates human, animal, avian and entomological monitoring but faces challenges in data harmonization, real-time integration and resource allocation, and public health action is still triggered mainly by human cases. We propose an operational One Health architecture that fuses multimodal data streams in near-real time, applies statistical and artificial intelligence (AI)-based signal detection and probabilistic forecasting, and links predefined alert levels to automated escalation and coordinated surge response. Together with strengthened interdisciplinary collaboration, capacity-building and sustained political commitment, such a system could shift WNV control in Greece from reactive to anticipatory and serve as a model for the Mediterranean region.

The debate over machine consciousness has been dominated by top-down approaches that extract indicator properties from theories of consciousness. Developmental cognitive psychology, which has characterized how self-related capacities are assembled in humans, has been largely absent. We propose the Autobiographical Architecture Model (AAM), a five-layer developmental framework in which embodied affective self-regulation, self-recognition, autobiographical memory, the working self, and narrative self-coherence are linked by asymmetric scaffolding. The first four, in their autonoetic components, are proposed as jointly necessary for autonoetic consciousness in Tulving’s sense, and the fifth is its elaboration into narrative identity. Current large language models show uncontrolled traces at Layers 2 and 4, fluent simulation at Layer 5, and no signature at Layers 1 and 3. AAM is an adequacy constraint on the functional roles a candidate architecture must realize, not a homology thesis. On the evidence to date, the gaps at Layers 1 and 3 are architectural, the gap at Layer 4’s source monitoring is one of training objective and readout, and neither is a matter of scale alone. The sharpest prediction concerns Layer 4. Current systems locate the passage that supports a claim when their context contains one, and AAM predicts that no four-way classification of how a representation arose is trained in or used by default. We state the dependencies component by component, derive predictions for developmental amnesia, autism, and memory ownership, position AAM against indicator-property frameworks and biological naturalism, and specify seven benchmark protocols with controls and a stated falsifier.

Model distillation has become a major concern in the rapidly growing generative AI discourse. In its simplest form, distillation is the phenomenon where smaller firms can use data distilled from transcripts of conversations with powerful proprietary closed-weight models to train their own models, thus achieving reasonably high model quality but at much lower costs. Besides the legitimate safety and security concerns associated with distillation, another major issue is how it can also distort marketplace outcomes. This motivates us to initiate an exploration of the problem from an economic theory lens. We consider a setting with two players: an incumbent and a distilling competitor and characterize how the incumbent's model characteristics drive the incentives around how much the competitor should distill. We also consider the impact of distillation on key market outcomes like user-side surplus and the incumbent's utility. Our key contribution, however, is to study interventions for preventing or limiting distillation attacks. In this context, we study two settings: i) when it is possible, with a certain probability (which grows in the extent of distillation conducted), to detect an attack on the incumbent's model; and ii) when a distillation attack cannot be reliably detected. In the first setting, we show that penalty-based regulations can be very effective in completely deterring distillation, although it can have potentially adverse effects on market competition and user surplus. In the latter setting, we show that the incumbent can use self-distillation as a mitigation strategy. Importantly, the effectiveness of self-distillation depends on how cost-efficiently the incumbent can deploy a new self-distilled model on the market. On the positive side, self-distillation can preserve market competition thus protecting user surplus to some extent.

This perspective article discusses the nature of linguistic computation in cognition vis-à-vis linguistic meaning. In particular, this article explores the computational basis of linguistic meaning from a compositional computability perspective and then shows that linguistic meaning is not computable under certain conditions of compositionality, which requires the dependence of the meaning of a whole expression on the meanings of the parts. In other words, compositionality does not guarantee the computability of linguistic meanings. This is also partly governed by the syntactic underdetermination of linguistic meanings as conceived of within syntactic theories assuming computability of structural operations for compositional mapping. So, syntax, understood in a purely computational sense, does not guarantee computability of semantic composition when understood in the context of a cognitive mechanism of understanding linguistic meaning. The limits of computability of linguistic meaning are then indicated. This is investigated from the vantage point of unification of cognitive and formal aspects of linguistic meaning in brain dynamics. This turns out to have serious consequences for Large Language Models (LLMs)/Generative AI that appear(s) to stumble over linguistically deep or pragmatically rich aspects of meaning. Thus, this article projects insights into the limits of computational basis of linguistic meaning in humans and machines.

Patient attitudes toward AI in gastroenterology are influenced by demographic factors such as age, gender, education, income, and ethnicity. Recognizing these can help tailor engagement and communication strategies to increase trust and acceptance of AI in clinical settings.
