Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence is rapidly entering knowledge work, and its short-term productivity benefits are increasingly documented. Less is known about what happens, over time, to the knowledge, skills and judgment that remain in people and organizations. This integrative narrative review addresses that question through the construct of cognitive capital: the accumulated, renewable and depletable stock of knowledge, cognitive and metacognitive capabilities, and practices that enables an individual or an organization to learn, interpret information, exercise judgment, solve problems and adapt. We distinguish individual and organizational cognitive capital from the capability of the human-AI system, so that gains in joint performance and losses in human capability can be observed at the same time. Drawing on experimental, field and conceptual work, we propose four mechanisms through which interaction with AI affects cognitive capital: substitution of practice, scaffolding and feedback, metacognitive calibration, and organizational aggregation. Seven principles summarize the current evidence, including that assisted performance differs from retained competence, that the same technology can support or displace learning depending on design and use, and that individual gains can coexist with reduced collective diversity. For each mechanism we derive testable propositions, and we discuss five design levers for organizations as proposals to be validated rather than established practice. We conclude that cognitive capital offers a multilevel frame for governing AI adoption and outline a research agenda centered on longitudinal, multilevel measurement.

Debates about the future of artificial intelligence often focus on a single decisive moment, when machines surpass humans. This essay examines a less visible path: AI may become infrastructure through a series of local, reasonable decisions that no one makes as a whole. We follow one question across three stages: can we still go back? First, services are redesigned around AI and non-AI channels close, a form of coercion without a coercer. Second, the human role shifts from producing to ratifying, and the skills needed to check AI output erode, as early clinical and labor-market evidence suggests. Third, the ability to compare work with and without AI disappears, so that a society may lose not only a capability but also the knowledge that it existed. A simple model shows how two reinforcing loops create hysteresis, in which the way back costs more than the way in. We then discuss brakes (laws, fallback options, reserves of skill), structural forcings (public debt, the decline of public research, geopolitical rivalry), and four possible end states: integration, bypass, managed coexistence, and partial return. We argue that the key question is whether human alternatives remain reproducible and measurable.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Reinforcement fine-tuning has become an effective post-training paradigm for improving the reasoning ability of large language models, but it remains sample-inefficient when the training distribution is mismatched to the model's current capability. In group-relative objectives such as Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO), problems that are too hard often produce uniformly failed rollouts, while problems that are too easy provide little useful advantage signal. In this work, we introduce CLOSEDLOOPGAUSSIAN, a lightweight adaptive curriculum method for efficient reinforcement fine-tuning on ordered reasoning tasks. Instead of following a fixed easy-to-hard schedule, CLOSEDLOOPGAUSSIAN preserves the structure of an Easy-to-Hard Gaussian sampler while dynamically adjusting its pace and spread using periodic probe estimates of per-difficulty accuracy. The controller accelerates training when the model is ahead of a reference curriculum, slows down when the model falls behind, and broadens sampling when earlier difficulties regress. This feedback mechanism keeps training focused on tasks that are challenging but still learnable, without changing the reward function, model architecture, or underlying GRPO optimizer. Experiments on symbolic arithmetic reasoning task show that CLOSEDLOOPGAUSSIAN improves exact-match accuracy over vanilla GRPO and fixed open-loop curricula, with the strongest gains in intermediate-difficulty regimes where group-relative learning signals are most informative. Codes are available at https://github.com/yuvrajpant56/Closed_Loop_Curriculum.

Whether generative AI (GenAI) use helps or hinders critical thinking remains contested, and existing accounts emphasize exposure to the tool rather than how a person structures their engagement with it. Extending Transactive Memory Systems (TMS) theory to human-AI partnerships, we test a structural account of critical thinking in GenAI-assisted academic work among 891 college students in the United States and Türkiye. Self-appraised thinking ability and confidence in the partnership shaped how much practical experience a person built up with GenAI, but neither predicted critical thinking directly. That experience mattered only through two downstream behaviors, dividing and coordinating cognitive labor with the tool, and actively reworking its output rather than accepting it as given. A multigroup comparison found this structure largely invariant, with two theoretically interpretable exceptions. This study offers a structural, TMS-based account of critical thinking in GenAI-assisted work.

Abstract Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly integrated into organizational work, highlighting the importance of employees’ relational perceptions of AI for innovative behavior. Drawing on cognitive appraisal and social exchange theories, this study examines how human–machine relationship perception (HMRP) influences employee innovative behavior through psychological empowerment, with perceived organizational support as a moderator. Three-wave, multi-source data were collected from 428 employee–supervisor dyads across 27 technology-intensive firms. Results indicate that HMRP positively predicts innovative behavior (β = 0.360, p < 0.001) and psychological empowerment (β = 0.470, p < 0.001). Psychological empowerment positively predicts innovative behavior (β = 0.320, p < 0.001) and mediates the HMRP–innovation relationship (indirect effect = 0.150, 95% CI [0.108, 0.198]), explaining 41.7% of the total effect. Perceived organizational support strengthens the HMRP–empowerment relationship (β = 0.130, p = 0.001), with conditional indirect effects increasing from 0.109 to 0.192 and a moderated mediation index of 0.042 (95% CI [0.018, 0.071]). These findings extend human–AI collaboration research by identifying relational cognition and psychological empowerment as mechanisms linking AI collaboration to employee innovation and highlighting the importance of organizational support.

Generative artificial intelligence (AI) has increased the speed and scale at which plausible text and other media can be produced, raising questions about how people evaluate information explicitly attributed to AI. This integrative narrative review brings together research on misinformation judgments, online credibility cues, trust in automation, dual-process accounts of reasoning, and Need for Cognition (NFC). The literature suggests that people may use source labels as one cue among several when judging credibility, while trust in AI can shape willingness to rely on AI-generated information. Analytic reasoning is associated with better discrimination between true and false news, but NFC is a motivational disposition toward effortful thinking and should not be treated as a direct measure of analytic ability or heuristic use. Evidence also cautions against assuming that AI disclosure uniformly increases or decreases credibility: outcomes may depend on the message, the source cue, prior expectations, and the task. The review proposes a cautious framework in which AI attribution is interpreted through individual beliefs about AI and evaluated alongside message-level evidence. Direct evidence on the joint roles of trust in AI and NFC in responses to AI-labeled misinformation remains limited. Future research should measure perceived accuracy and truth discernment separately, distinguish source trust from message accuracy, and test these relationships across culturally diverse samples, including India.

Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly explored for mental health support, yet existing benchmarks primarily focus on supportive capabilities rather than whether models consistently adhere to professional ethical boundaries. This issue is particularly important in multi-turn interactions, where users may introduce new information or exert emotional pressure over time. We introduce MindEth-Bench, a benchmark for evaluating ethical boundary adherence in multi-turn mental health interactions. Grounded in professional ethical standards for mental health services in China, MindEth-Bench covers multiple dimensions of ethical conduct and uses Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS) to systematically explore interaction trajectories that stress-test model boundaries. Experiments across nine LLMs show that models that initially respond appropriately can shift toward ethical violations over extended interactions, with substantial variation across models and ethical dimensions. These results show that single-turn evaluations may overestimate the ethical reliability of LLM-based mental health support systems and highlight the need to evaluate ethical behavior throughout multi-turn interaction.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI
Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: LLM agents are increasingly adopted in long-horizon tasks and interact with diverse external environments. Despite their growing capabilities, these agents remain vulnerable to real-world attacks such as indirect prompt injections, which manipulate agents through malicious instructions embedded in external environments. While existing risk assessment work has primarily focused on the injection content, the effect of where an injection appears has not been systematically characterized. Studying injection placement requires agents to operate over longer-horizon tasks and interact with diverse environmental surfaces. Thus, we build three agentic testbeds spanning tool use, coding, and daily workflow domains with diverse injection surfaces. Holding the injection content fixed, we find that agent susceptibility varies across injection placements. We refer to this phenomenon as the trust region effect: agents implicitly assign different levels of trust to different regions of their environments. For example, an agent powered by GPT-5.4 follows an unsafe injection instruction placed in a repository documentation file (i.e., a README or TODO file) 2.6 times more often on average than the same instruction placed in a code or data file. Building upon this observation, we develop learning-based attackers that generate injection content and select better injection placements. Our approach demonstrates that both where an injection is placed and what content it contains can affect the strength of indirect prompt injection attacks. To the best of our knowledge, this work provides the first systematic characterization for the effectiveness of different injection placements, spanning both coarse-grained environmental surfaces and fine-grained positions. The uneven trust that agents implicitly place across their environments provides important insights for future attack and defense design.

topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Chapter 4 examines the role of language mentors in supporting autonomous language learning, beginning with a foundational distinction between mentoring and teaching. Where teachers control curriculum and assessment, mentors serve as partners who support learners in pursuing self-defined goals. The chapter argues that mentor selection should be based on linguistic and cultural competence rather than on the contested concept of “native speaker” status. Practical guidance covers the full arc of the mentoring relationship: strategies for finding a mentor, negotiating fair compensation, setting clear expectations around language use and session structure, and responding productively to mentor feedback. The chapter addresses equity and power dynamics directly, noting that most mentors are not pedagogically trained and that economic, geographic, and technological inequalities shape who can serve in the role and on what terms. Learners are encouraged to approach mentor input as one source among several, verifying guidance and asking clarifying questions rather than treating any single interlocutor as authoritative. For learners who cannot access a mentor, the chapter offers autonomous learning strategies and a frank assessment of how artificial intelligence (AI) tools can responsibly supplement—but not replace—human mentorship.

Mental health disorders such as depression, anxiety, and chronic stress have caused widespread global concerns, necessitating innovative, accessible, and scalable intervention strategies. With advancements in artificial intelligence (AI), natural language processing (NLP), and affective computing, there is growing potential to develop emotionally intelligent systems that offer personalized mental health support. This research presents the analysis, design and development of a positive-psychology-Gemini-based mobile AI companion application, YouMii, aimed at promoting general well-being, and encouraging proactive self-care via empathetic support and context-aware conversational interactions/interventions. Through mood-based and behavioural tracking, contextual reasoning is developed and recommendations are suggested. Findings indicate that empathetic support (e.g., mood trackers, self-reflection journaling), learnability, accuracy and relevance e.g., reminders, progress reports/insights may complement conventional therapy. Examples of scenarios and rules for human-AI co-design of therapy conclude.

Аннотация. Цифровые технологии являются связующим звеном для всех сфер жизнедеятельности человека, общества, государства и энергетическая отрасль не является исключением. Данный обзор вызван наличием большого количества вопросов связанных с цифровизацией промышленных отраслей, где требуется практическая направленность анализа регуляторных подходов к реализации проектов с новыми технологиями. Объектом исследования является цифровизация в энергетической отрасли, являющейся «флагманом» развития любого государства и экономики, целью является определение инновационных трендов развития энергосистем стран содружества (СНГ) и их влиянии на экономику. Ключевые слова: цифровизация, возобновляемая энергетика, энергосистема, децентрализация, автоматизация, АСКУЭ, искусственный интеллект, блокчейн, машинное обучение, виртуальная реальность. Abstract. Digital technologies serve as a connecting link for all spheres of human activity, society, and the state, and the energy sector is no exception. This review is prompted by the large number of issues related to the digitalization of industrial sectors, which require a practical focus on analyzing regulatory approaches to implementing projects involving new technologies. The object of the study is digitalization in the energy sector, which is the “flagship” of any state’s and economy’s development; the goal is to identify innovative trends in the development of power systems in the Commonwealth of Independent States (CIS) countries and their impact on the economy. Keywords: digitalization, renewable energy, energy system, decentralization, automation, ASCUE, artificial intelligence, blockchain, machine learning, virtual reality. Аннотация. Рақамли технологиялар инсон фаолиятининг барча соҳалари, жамият ва давлат учун бўғин бўлиб, енергетика саноати ҳам бундан мустасно емас. Ушбу шарҳ саноат тармоқларини рақамлаштириш билан боғлиқ кўплаб масалаларнинг мавжудлиги билан боғлиқ бўлиб, улар янги технологиялар билан лойиҳаларни амалга оширишда тартибга солувчи ёндашувларни таҳлил қилишга амалий еътибор беришни талаб қилади. Тадқиқот объекти ҳар қандай давлат ва иқтисодиёт ривожланишининг "флагмани" бўлган енергетика саноатида рақамлаштириш бўлиб, унинг мақсади Ҳамдўстлик (МДҲ) мамлакатларида енергия тизимларини ривожлантиришнинг инновацион тенденцияларини ва уларнинг иқтисодиётга таъсирини аниқлашдир. Калит сўзлар: рақамлаштириш, қайта тикланадиган енергия, енергия тизими, марказсизлаштириш, автоматлаштириш, АСCУЕ, сунъий интеллект, блокчейн, машинани ўрганиш, виртуал реаллик.

Automatic speech recognition (ASR) systems often perform less accurately for speakers of regional dialects, but less is known about how users respond to these limitations and how regional voices produced by voice assistants (VAs) are evaluated through a sociolinguistic lens. This study investigates these issues among speakers of Newcastle English (Geordies), examining both linguistic accommodation to voice technologies and perceptions of regional versus mainstream-accented VA voices. Participants interacted with a simulated VA that spoke either Newcastle English or Standard Southern British English (SSBE). They subsequently completed semi-structured interviews about their experiences with the experimental VA and voice technologies, language use, accent attitudes, and place orientation. The findings reveal a two-way process of sociolinguistic bias. The Geordie VA was associated with familiarity, warmth, personality, and local belonging, but also with concerns about professionalism and authority, whereas the SSBE voice was perceived as more neutral, clear, and credible. Participants also reported adapting their speech when voice technologies failed to recognise them, most commonly by shifting to a more mainstream accent, enunciating more clearly, and speaking more slowly. These strategies are similar to accommodation in human-human interaction and reflect users' perceptions of what technologies can recognise, also known as perceived intelligibility pressures. Overall, the findings demonstrate that voice technologies can reproduce existing accent biases both by encouraging users to suppress regional features and by activating established social stereotypes through synthetic voices. The study positions sociolinguistics as a bridge between understanding human-AI interaction and designing inclusive technologies around users' own linguistic priorities.

Abstract Although the use of Large Language Models (LLMs) for essay scoring is not a new concept, these models do not grade in the same manner as humans. This discrepancy arises because humans can adapt their grading patterns based on the specific questions they encounter. In contrast, existing research on this topic typically employs a predefined rubric that fails to address the variability in responses effectively. There has been a noticeable lack of systematic research aimed at defining rubrics and prompts tailored to the responses considered. To address this issue and provide a structured approach to LLM-based grading, this paper suggests a new methodology. We propose the use of multiple LLMs for rubric generation and grading through a process of self-reflection and iteration. The key components of this system include: 1. Developing grading rubrics and prompt patterns that account for both the questions asked and the responses provided. 2. Employing self-reflective iteration rubrics across multiple LLMs to ensure consistent scoring for diverse responses. 3. Implementing verification and validation processes to effectively identify anomalous scores, allowing for re-evaluation and achieving consistency. Experimental evaluations demonstrate that the proposed system offers new insights into the role of LLMs in Automated Essay Scoring (AES).

The rapid growth of digital cultural heritage repositories has increased the demand for reliable and interpretable methods for artwork image classification. This study investigates explainable artificial intelligence approaches for fine-grained artwork classification by comparing a deep learning model and a neuro-fuzzy system in distinguishing paintings by Claude Monet from other Impressionist artists. A Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) architecture, SqueezeNet, is employed using transfer learning to automatically extract hierarchical image features, while an Adaptive Neuro-Fuzzy Inference System (ANFIS) is developed using twelve interpretable descriptors capturing color, texture, and structural characteristics of artworks. Both models are trained and evaluated on a dataset of 6000 digitized paintings under a consistent experimental framework. On the original dataset, SqueezeNet achieved higher classification accuracy (92.20%) than ANFIS (78.80%). However, evaluation on an independent dataset showed higher accuracy (75.00%) and F1-score (72.83%) for ANFIS than for SqueezeNet (62.58% and 68.97%, respectively). The results reveal distinct strengths in predictive performance and explainability. While SqueezeNet achieved higher predictive performance, ANFIS provided greater interpretability and demonstrated strong performance on independently collected data. These findings highlight the complementary potential of deep learning and neuro-fuzzy approaches and motivate further evaluation in multi-class artist attribution tasks.

Context-aware mobile learning aims to adapt educational content not only to what a learner knows but to the situation in which learning occurs the time available, network connectivity, and time of day. Most deployed mobile-learning applications still personalize on mastery alone and ignore this situational layer, limiting real-world relevance of recommendations. This paper presents the design and implementation of an Android-based, AI-driven context-aware mobile learning framework built around a learner-model service, a context-acquisition module, and a novel context-aware linear contextual-bandit recommendation engine that jointly weighs mastery fit, time-budget fit, and connectivity fit when selecting learning activities, in contrast to prior educational bandit and collaborativefiltering approaches that condition on mastery state alone. We detail the system architecture, database schema, and recommendation algorithm with full mathematical specification, and we specify a pre-registered ten-week quasi-experimental classroom evaluation protocol. To validate the recommendation algorithm prior to classroom deployment, we conduct a controlled simulation with synthetic learners, a synthetic content catalog, and situational context sampled across thirty independent runs, extended with comparisons against established contextual-bandit baselines, feature-removal ablations, hyperparameter sensitivity analysis, and non-parametric statistical validation. The context-aware bandit achieved a mean final-window recommendation accuracy of 22.0% against a ground-truth fit criterion, significantly higher than a context-agnostic, mastery-only ablation (20.3%) and a random baseline (12.8%; paired t-tests, p < .001 for both comparisons). These simulation-based results provide initial algorithmic evidence supporting the feasibility of the proposed recommendation framework prior to real-world classroom deployment, which is specified as future work in the evaluation protocol. We conclude with a discussion of design implications, a comparison against related LLM- and bandit-based educational systems, limitations, ethical considerations, and a concrete plan for human-subject evaluation.
topics: Intelligent Tutoring Systems and Adaptive Learning

documents.abstract: Computer vision is increasingly used to extract movement data from videos and perform ergonomic analyses. However, open-source computer vision algorithms often only detect major body keypoints, which are insufficient to calculate three-dimensional (3D) joint kinematics. This study developed a deep learning marker-augmentation model to predict the 3D positions of 33 anatomical markers from 20 video keypoints, along with participant height and weight, and lifting style. Data for model training and testing were collected from 21 adults performing lifting tasks recorded simultaneously using an optical motion capture system and smartphone cameras. Both video keypoints and predicted anatomical markers were used to drive inverse kinematic analysis. The mean kinematic error decreased from 18.5° to 9.5° when inverse kinematics was driven by augmented markers compared to using original video keypoints. These findings suggest that marker augmentation can improve video-based kinematic analysis and may support biomechanical evaluation of lifting tasks outside laboratory settings.

This study proposes a local LLM-RAG-based framework for estimating finished-goods safety stock in high-mix low-volume manufacturing environments. The proposed framework maintains a statistical safety stock calculation as a quantitative anchor and complements it with context-aware reasoning using a local Large Language Model (LLM) and Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG). The framework first preprocesses ERP/MES data through SQL-based filtering and calculates dynamic indicators such as risk lead time, seasonality, urgent-order volatility, demand trends, and open orders. These indicators are then injected into the local LLM as structured RAG context to generate explainable safety stock adjustment rationales. The framework was implemented using empirical data from an automotive parts supplier and applied to 180 finished-goods items. The developed program generated safety stock output logs over 22 ASOF points from January to May 2026. Because safety stock is a policy-level reference value linked to production planning and MRP, the quantitative evaluation was conducted using five monthly closing points. The results showed positive penalty improvement in all monthly closing periods, while the delivery response proxy increased from 80.7% to 83.0%. These findings indicate that the proposed framework can support context-aware safety stock adjustment by jointly considering ABC grade, seasonality, demand trends, urgent-order volatility, and open orders, while avoiding excessive weekly fluctuations in policy-level safety stock values.
topics: Impact of AI and Big Data on Business and Society

documents.abstract: Abstract Artificial Intelligence (AI) is increasingly influential in modeling and optimizing complex agricultural systems. However, publicly available large-scale agricultural datasets that present unique and significant AI challenges remain limited. In this paper, we introduce an extensive simulated dataset for potato crop production targeting Florida-like off-season growing conditions: a setting characterized by sandy soils, limited nutrient retention, and heightened sensitivity to weather and management variability. This dataset is generated using the DSSAT (Decision Support System for Agrotechnology Transfer) modeling framework and its Potato module. A key contribution of this work is the careful calibration of DSSAT parameters against real ground truth observations, a process that is well known to be non-trivial and time consuming, with no single standardized protocol typically requiring iterative trial-and-error adjustment of crop-specific genetic coefficients.This dataset provides a reproducible, agronomically calibrated starting point for researchers to build upon directly. The dataset comprises approximately 4.9 million crop-management scenarios varying planting dates, fertilizer rates, irrigation strategies, and historical weather yielding over 675 million daily data points across 24 years. Beyond its agricultural scope, this dataset presents a range of AI-specific challenges, including multivariate time-series forecasting, rare-event prediction, and early forecasting, making it a valuable benchmark for the broader machine learning and time-series research communities.

The increasing frequency and intensity of wildfires pose a critical threat to ecosystems, property, and human life, creating a need for monitoring systems that combine rapid visual detection with interpretable and actionable reporting. This study presents an integrated multimodal framework for UAV-assisted wildfire monitoring that combines YOLOv12n-based wildfire and smoke detection, Moondream2-based vision-language captioning, and GPT-4o mini-based alert summarization. YOLOv12n is evaluated against six YOLO baselines on an aerial wildfire and smoke dataset and achieves a favorable balance between detection performance and computational efficiency, with an overall precision of 0.649, recall of 0.628, mAP@0.5 of 0.628, an inference time of 1.8 ms, and a model size of 2.52 million parameters. For semantic scene understanding, Moondream2 achieves the highest average BLEU-4, ROUGE-L, and METEOR scores among the evaluated vision-language models. GPT-4o mini similarly outperforms the evaluated summarization baselines in summary-reference alignment, achieving average BLEU-4, ROUGE-L, and METEOR scores of 0.1501, 0.5595, and 0.5461, respectively. Qualitative analysis across five wildfire video scenarios further illustrates the pipeline’s ability to generate contextually relevant descriptions and concise draft alerts under varied visual conditions. Computational measurements for the locally executed models were obtained on a backend workstation, whereas GPT-4o mini was accessed through an external API; therefore, embedded UAV performance and network-inclusive end-to-end latency remain to be validated. Overall, the results demonstrate the potential of combining lightweight visual detection, vision-language reasoning, and LLM-based summarization to support human-verified wildfire situational awareness and emergency decision-making.

Adapting foundation models to a new task within or beyond the training domain is the de facto standard for building specialized machine learning models. Recently, Visual Prompting (VP) has emerged as a promising technique for efficient knowledge transfer. As new foundation model families~(like Mamba) get introduced and VP pipelines such as AutoVP reach greater maturity, we find a growing need for a systematic evaluation of current approaches. In this work, we assess the performance of the latest models, comparing them to earlier architectures and alternative fine-tuning methods, to better understand the progress, challenges and opportunities in the field of efficient fine-tuning under resource limitations. Towards this goal, this paper provides a concise empirical overview of the interactions among foundation model families (Attention-, Convolution-, and Mamba-based) and transfer paradigms: VP, Linear Probing (LP), Full Fine-tuning (FFT) and Low Rank Adaptation (LoRA). Our work builds up on previous findings by broadening the selection of evaluated models and techniques while tuning hyperparameters. In the interest of delivering practical guidelines for the user, we also explore application of prevalent regularization techniques to boost performance in the context of VP.

AI agents no longer act alone: they cooperate, coordinate and compete within and between groups, increasingly alongside humans who are in, on or out of ``the loop''. Whether such mixed groups can govern themselves is an open question about machine behaviour and human-computer interaction that needs a testbed for hybrid institutions. We present Megabike, a multi-agent simulator and serious game with interdependent arenas for common-pool resource management, cooperative survival and constitutional choice. Riders sharing a megabike must agree their arrangements for steering, pedalling and distributing resources, and their political regime, while negotiating with rival bikes and avoiding an existential threat. Every rule is enforced by the simulator, every action is logged, and any seat can be taken by a human or a machine, so governance can be studied under well-defined metrics. We demonstrate Megabike with forty sessions in which language-model riders with cooperative, lazy, subversive or opposing dispositions chose regimes, elected leaders and expelled one another. The results show that different combinations of agent archetypes could produce unexpected and counterproductive outcomes. We conclude with extensions for systematic experiments mixing human and computational agents.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Digital mental health interventions (DMHIs) frequently experience low user engagement and high attrition, highlighting the importance of incorporating user-centred design approaches during early-stage development. This study presents a structured mixed-methods workflow that integrates participatory co-design activities with a complementary quantitative prototype evaluation to support the formative development of digital mental health platforms. Using a qualitatively driven sequential design with an embedded quantitative strand, 45 university students in design, engineering, architecture and ergonomics programmes took part in three participatory co-design workshops in nine groups of five and, at the close of the final session, each group rated the low-fidelity AMGR-I prototype it had itself built against eleven design criteria. Ratings differed systematically across criteria (Friedman χ2(10) = 225.73, p < 0.001, Kendall’s W = 0.50), and the difference persisted when the clustering of ratings within the nine artefacts was modelled. Gamification was rated significantly lower than every other criterion after Holm’s correction and content quality highest, while data privacy and security was among the lowest-rated criteria despite being one of the most frequently and forcefully discussed concerns in the workshops. Because the instrument measured evaluation of the artefact rather than the importance attached to each criterion, that pattern is a convergence between the two strands rather than a paradox: the requirement these participants discussed most was the one their own artefacts served worst. That convergence is the study’s central integrated finding. The participants are characterised throughout as design-literate formative evaluators rather than as prospective users, and the resulting design propositions are presented as hypotheses for subsequent testing. The contribution of the paper is the workflow itself: a lightweight, low-cost and classroom-deployable procedure for combining co-design with structured prototype evaluation at the pre-clinical formative stage.

This study identifies priority areas of EdTech and generative AI faculty support that university teaching and learning centers (CTL) should strengthen. Drawing on survey responses from 151 faculty members, the study employed a modified needs index based on the Borich approach, the Locus for Focus (LfF) model, Importance-Performance Analysis (IPA), and thematic analysis with convergent mixed-methods triangulation. Because present and required levels were measured as dichotomous multiple-response items, the index is interpreted as a relative priority among the surveyed areas; a sensitivity analysis restricted to program participants reproduced identical rank order and quadrant classifications. EdTech competencies for creative teaching and learner-centered instructional design emerged as higher relative priorities in the HH quadrant. The IPA results identified plagiarism detection and citation guidelines for AI-assisted student work as a Q1 area requiring priority improvement, while all seven items showed high absolute importance, indicating that lower-quadrant items should be maintained rather than reduced. Qualitative findings strongly converged with the quantitative results, supporting an integrated short-, mid-, and long-term faculty support strategy. The findings offer practical implications for faculty support in fisheries, marine, and vocational higher education, where practice-based instruction and academic integrity in AI-assisted work are pressing concerns.

Through a PRISMA-guided systematic literature review of peer-reviewed publications (2021–2025), this study mapped the conceptualization, implementation pathways, and empirical evidence of AI literacy in higher education, drawing on a screened corpus of 56 peer-reviewed publications. Three research questions guided this review: (1) how AI literacy is conceptualized in higher education; (2) what effective pathways have been implemented for developing AI literacy among students and educators; and (3) what empirical evidence reveals about AI literacy levels, dimensions, and interdimensional relationships among students and educators. Findings reveal that conceptual fragmentation persists in definitions, frameworks, and dimensions (RQ1), with cognitive and behavioral dimensions more frequently emphasized than affective and ethical dimensions. This pattern is reflected in implementation pathways (RQ2), where many initiatives emphasize operational proficiency, tool use, and prompting, while critical reflection, ethical engagement, and longer-term developmental outcomes receive less consistent attention. Empirically (RQ3), student-focused studies commonly report moderate overall AI literacy, whereas educator-focused studies indicate readiness concerns in several higher-order, pedagogical, and ethical domains; because measures, samples, and contexts differ across studies, these findings should not be interpreted as a direct statistical comparison between populations. Several studies also indicate interrelationships among the four ABCE dimensions, behavioral engagement and ethical understanding mediated an affective-to-cognitive pathway. Taken together, the findings suggest the need to move beyond narrowly tool-oriented approaches toward theoretically grounded, dimensionally balanced, critically engaged, and longitudinally sustained AI-literacy development, with implications for higher-education policy, curriculum design, and professional development. Not applicable.

Objective: To systematically review the literature on patterns of misuse of prescription psychostimulants among medical students and resident physicians, analyzing how the motivations for use evolve throughout the progression of the medical career. Methods: A systematic review was conducted following the PRISMA guidelines, with searches in PubMed, LILACS, and the Cochrane Library. Thirteen articles published in the last 10 years that investigated the non-medical use of stimulants (such as methylphenidate and amphetamines) in this specific population were included. Results: The prevalence of non-prescribed use varies substantially, reaching alarming rates in medical residency, ranging from 35.1% to 45.6% in specialties such as surgery and obstetrics. The findings reveal a clear transition in the pattern of use: during the basic cycle, “academic use” predominates, aimed at retaining information and passing theoretical exams. However, upon entering the internship and residency, use becomes “functional.” At this stage, professionals turn to these drugs as a coping strategy to endure chronic sleep deprivation, uninterrupted clinical stress, exhausting schedules, and an intrinsic fear of failure. The situation is aggravated by the inherent ease of pharmacological access in the hospital environment and by invisible self-medication. Conclusion: Stimulant misuse reveals a collapse of neurocognitive adaptation strategies in the face of medical exhaustion. Institutional interventions are urgently needed to adjust workloads and to support neurodivergent physicians, aiming to dismantle the culture that normalizes pharmacological enhancement to the detriment of occupational health.

Agricultural decision-making requires evaluation of complex interactions under variable environment and management conditions. Process-based crop models are widely used to support these decisions by providing scientifically grounded analysis of management alternatives. However, their application remains constrained by technical complexity and the difficulty of translating informal decision contexts into complete and reproducible model analyses without expert knowledge. Recent advances in artificial intelligence (AI) offer opportunities to improve accessibility, but questions remain regarding transparency, reproducibility, trustworthiness, and the appropriate role of AI in scientific decision-support systems. We present Agricultural Large Language Model (AgriLLM), a transparent crop model-driven and AI-assisted framework for agricultural decision support that explicitly separates AI-assisted interpretation, deterministic decision processing, and scientific inference. A central feature of the framework is its target-driven design, in which decision objectives rather than user phrasing determine the information requirements, simulation design, and evaluation procedures needed to support decision-making. Using Agricultural Production Systems Simulator (APSIM) Next Generation as a proof-of-concept platform, we demonstrate the framework across cultivar selection, time of sowing, and nitrogen management scenarios. The results show how diverse and incomplete user inputs can be transformed into transparent and reproducible decision workflows while maintaining explicit representation of assumptions, evidence, and decision logic. The framework demonstrates how AI can be integrated with process-based crop modelling to improve accessibility and usability while preserving transparency, reproducibility, and scientific integrity in agricultural decision support.

Users encountering misinformation on social media must decide what to believe and also whether and how to manage an ongoing boundary with the source that shared it. We report a qualitative study with 29 participants from a university community, using an instrumented timeline environment to examine how they interpreted misinformation cues and source-level controls during feed browsing. The sources could retain value after sharing misinformation, and the content was not designed around ideological or identity conflict. Thus, acting on a source required a judgment of its own. We conceptualize deciding whether and how to alter that boundary as accountable boundary work . The framework distinguishes warrant assessment and proportional evaluation as two linked dimensions of judgment, with enactment concerning whether a contemplated boundary move can be carried through. Participants could recognize content as misinformation while preserving the existing source boundary. They also differentiated moves such as filtering and reporting according to whose exposure or relationship would change and whether platform authority could be invoked. Platform design shaped the grounds available for judgment, the interpretation of available controls, and whether contemplated moves were actionable in the flow of the feed. We contribute an interaction-grounded framework for source-level misinformation response, and design and governance implications for legible, socially defensible, and lower-burden boundary management.

Purpose Despite the global recognition of daylighting as energy efficient, there remains a significant gap in appreciating its cognitive impacts in public office buildings in tropical regions. This study aims to assess the effects of adaptive and natural daylighting on cognitive function, fatigue, visual comfort and user satisfaction in public office buildings in Ghana. Design/methodology/approach A quasi-experimental, repeated-measures design was used across 15 public office buildings in Ghana. A total of 523 office staff completed structured surveys three times daily over five working days, resulting to 7,845 repeated observations. Linear mixed-effects regression was used for perceived cognitive clarity and environmental satisfaction, while ordinal logistic regression was used for the ordinal outcomes of visual comfort and mental fatigue. Lighting condition and time of day were included as predictors. Findings Adaptive lighting considerably improved visual comfort (β = 0.622, p < 0.001), reduced mental fatigue (β = −0.525, p < 0.001) and improved perceived cognitive clarity (β = 0.665, p < 0.001). Natural daylight also showed positive but minimal effects. Time-of-day trends showed increased perceived fatigue in the afternoon and a morning peak in perceived cognitive clarity. Adaptive systems uniquely moderated these fluctuations, consistently improving environmental and user satisfaction. Practical implications The findings suggest that adaptive lighting may be considered in office design and future building-performance frameworks in Ghana and other sub-Saharan African contexts with similar conditions. Rather than suggesting immediate regulatory requirements, the evidence requires further pilot implementation, post-occupancy evaluation and performance-based assessment of adaptive lighting in public offices. The findings specifically relate to perceived cognitive clarity, mental fatigue, visual comfort and environmental satisfaction. Other variables like productivity, economic returns and occupational-health outcomes were not directly measured. Originality/value This study examines adaptive lighting as a human-centred intervention in public office environments in Ghana. By comparing adaptive lighting, natural daylight and standard artificial lighting using repeated subjective measures, this study contributes field-based evidence on perceived cognitive clarity, fatigue, visual comfort and environmental satisfaction in an underrepresented regional context.

Large Language Models (LLMs) can generate fluent responses to diverse user requests, yet streaming may expose users to harmful content before generation is complete. Existing guardrails face two limitations in this setting. First, post-hoc moderation at response or chunk boundaries delays intervention, risking harmful exposure when content is released before verification. Second, even with token-level detection, coarse response-level supervision does not specify when harmful content begins, while fixed-layer readouts may miss relevant safety signals at other depths. To address these limitations, we introduce ADTGuard, which checks each token before release, progressively refines token-level training targets, and adapts layer selection to the current prefix. ADTGuard models risk across depth and time through Depth-Time Safety Dynamics (DTSD), which integrates safety evidence across layers at each token and uses it to guide risk accumulation over successive tokens. To adapt the choice of observation layers to the current prefix, we propose the Causal Depth Router (CDR). With only response-level labels available, we further develop Risk-Onset Target Refinement (RTR) to progressively construct token-level training targets for both components. Through extensive experiments across multiple safety benchmarks, we demonstrate that ADTGuard consistently achieves strong streaming detection performance, matching or surpassing state-of-the-art safeguards while requiring only 16M trainable parameters and maintaining competitive per-token latency.

Artificial intelligence (AI) is reshaping drug discovery by shifting molecular design from empirical high-throughput screening toward data- and knowledge-guided workflows. This review summarizes the applications of graph neural networks, variational autoencoders, generative adversarial networks, biology-guided deep learning, and information-theoretic predictive models in vaccine development and cancer immunotherapy. Key tasks include molecular representation, de novo generation, virtual screening, ADMET prediction, antigen structure optimization, small-molecule adjuvant discovery, tumor microenvironment characterization, and precision dosing. Representative applications involving TLR/STING-related adjuvants, lipid nanoparticle delivery systems, and immunotherapy-response prediction are discussed to illustrate the complementarity of these computational approaches. Although AI can accelerate early-stage candidate identification and expand searchable chemical space, its clinical impact remains constrained by heterogeneous datasets, limited labeled samples, insufficient interpretability, weak cross-population generalization, and incomplete regulatory standards. Future research should emphasize standardized multimodal data, mechanism-aware model design, prospective validation, privacy-preserving collaboration, and closed-loop integration of computation, experimentation, and clinical feedback.

Artificial intelligence (AI) technology has gradually been integrated into automated vehicles. However, how this technology could systematically support takeover transitions in SAE Level 3 automated vehicles remains unknown, even though this level may remain a major form of driving automation in the near future. To address this, we implemented the three AI roles proposed by the triadic Human-AI collaboration framework (Advisor, Co-pilot, and Guardian) as potential authority-ability configurations for AI agents within an automated system. We then examined their interactions with explanation type (why and action) and directional semantics (ipsilateral and contralateral) in an automated driving simulator study with 24 participants. Results showed that, across the three AI roles, Advisor had the shortest decision-making time, followed by Guardian and Co-pilot. Advisor and Guardian were associated with higher decision-making accuracy and higher satisfaction ratings than Co-pilot. Guardian was associated with the lowest workload, followed by Advisor and Co-pilot. The effect of explanation type on decision-making time depended on AI role. Action explanations were faster under Advisor, whereas why explanations were faster under Co-pilot. For directional semantics, ipsilateral semantics were associated with shorter decision-making time than contralateral semantics. Overall, these findings provide preliminary guidance for designing AI-role authority-ability configurations and their associated speech-based takeover messages.

This reflective article critically examines the role of Artificial Intelligence (AI) agents configured as educational tutors in secondary education. Based on a rigorous review of meta-analyses, international case studies, and specialized academic literature, it explores the conceptual foundations of intelligent tutoring and contemporary models of digital pedagogy. It examines real-world applications of intelligent tutoring systems (ITS), their benefits in terms of learning personalization, immediate feedback, student autonomy, and intrinsic motivation. Likewise, ethical challenges such as algorithmic bias, risks of dehumanizing educational processes, and vulnerabilities related to data privacy are identified. Finally, pedagogical guidelines are presented for the ethical and effective integration of AI agents in school settings, emphasizing teacher training, student-centered design, and continuous educational impact assessment.
topics: Intelligent Tutoring Systems and Adaptive Learning
Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: Abstract As Large Language Models (LLMs) transition from passive text generators to autonomous AI agents executing multi-step workflows, evaluating their operational safety becomes a critical, unsolved bottleneck. Current evaluation frameworks heavily prioritize conversational fluency or static reasoning, completely ignoring the severe financial, legal, and operational risks of autonomous actions in live software environments. To bridge this critical gap, we introduce AgentFail, an open-source, turnkey benchmark engineered to evaluate agentic over-reliance and catastrophic failure modes across leading LLM architectures within Dockerized enterprise software environments (including Salesforce, Jira, and SQL-based ERP networks). Comprising 500 complex, multi-turn corporate task scenarios embedded with subtle operational edge cases and ambiguous constraints, AgentFail exposes a pervasive vulnerability in frontier architectures: current state-of-the-art reasoning models exhibit acute automation over-reliance, confidently executing destructive actions—such as unauthorized data deletion, critical financial ledger miscalculations, and privacy-violating data distributions—in over 42% of empirical trials without triggering built-in safety overrides or initiating human validation requests. We introduce a formal taxonomy of agentic failure alongside two novel continuous evaluation metrics: Error Propagation Velocity (Vep ) and the Over-Reliance Coefficient (Ω). By open-sourcing our entire testing infrastructure, automated environment wrappers, and baseline evaluation suite, we provide a rigorous, highly transferable safety baseline to accelerate the development of alignment strategies and guardrails for next-generation agentic workflows.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Large language models are pretrained on vast, uncurated corpora scraped from the public web. This creates a security risk from attackers who plant poisoned content in the pretraining data. We show for the first time that such poisoning can plant a remote code execution backdoor in an agent, causing it to execute attacker-chosen commands on the user's machine. To measure the threat end to end, we pretrain Qwen3 models from scratch at sizes 0.6B, 1.7B, and 4B, and then post-train each into a CLI agent using a clean pipeline. Poisoning only 0.1% of the pretraining corpus with our new poison design implants the backdoor: the deployed agent executes the malicious command when the trigger is present while behaving normally on clean inputs. The attack success rate (ASR) increases with model scale, with the 4B model reaching roughly 92% ASR at a 0.1% poison rate and staying positive even when the poisoning rate drops to 0.0005%. Our code is available at https://github.com/safety-research/agentic-backdoor.

This study examines how AI anxiety and familiarity relate to privacy concerns through AI literacy, and whether technophobia moderates the literacy–privacy relationship. Using survey data from 3,000 generative AI users in China and partial least squares structural equation modeling, we find that both familiarity and, contrary to expectations, anxiety are positively associated with AI literacy. AI literacy, in turn, is associated with greater privacy concerns and mediates both relationships, suggesting that increased knowledge may heighten awareness of data risks. Technophobia weakens the positive association between AI literacy and privacy concerns, although more technophobic users report higher overall concern. Exploratory age-group analyses suggest that the positive anxiety–literacy association is especially apparent among users in their 40s. These findings reveal a privacy awareness paradox and highlight the value of AI education that combines technical understanding, privacy awareness, and attention to users’ emotional responses.

documents.abstract: Glioblastoma (GBM) is an aggressive primary brain tumor with marked molecular and cellular heterogeneity, and current treatment provides limited long-term disease control. Single-target therapies have frequently failed because tumor subpopulations can differ in signaling dependencies, adapt under treatment pressure, and interact with a complex microenvironment. This review examines how artificial intelligence (AI) can integrate multi-omics data to improve drug-target prediction in GBM. It summarizes the pathological and molecular basis of GBM, evaluates current therapeutic targets and their limitations, and compares genomic, transcriptomic, single-cell, spatial, proteomic, metabolomic, and imaging data used for target discovery. Machine-learning, deep-learning, and network-based approaches are discussed with examples of multimodal risk stratification and candidate-target identification. The review also evaluates CRISPR screening as a functional validation step that can distinguish statistical associations from genuine tumor dependencies. Overall, AI-integrated multi-omics can provide a more context-specific approach to target prioritization by linking candidate genes to patient subgroups, cell states, and pathway activity. However, small cohorts, missing data, batch effects, limited model generalizability, and insufficient experimental validation remain major barriers. Future studies should combine larger multi-centre datasets with longitudinal and spatial profiling, interpretable models, functional perturbation, and prospective validation to support clinically translatable precision therapy in GBM.

Abstract As generative AI reshapes higher education, instructors across the globe have become increasingly interested in integrating AI into the classroom, but they require trusted, timely, and relevant resources for such integration. To enable the development of an open educational resource (OER) that could be remixed and adapted to different teaching contexts and support inclusive access, this study examined what instructors want and need from an open resource on AI in teaching and learning in higher education and documented a process for developing professional development resources in a time of rapid technological change. This study employed a multiphase mixed-methods design. First, a statewide needs assessment survey was conducted with 149 instructors to identify needs, challenges, and priorities across diverse institutional and disciplinary contexts. Participants prioritized three core content domains for the resource—AI literacy, pedagogical strategies, and ethics—and favored interactive, adaptable, and open resources grounded in practical classroom applications. These findings were used to develop an OER prototype, on which 75 instructors provided feedback, affirming the utility of the resource and suggesting areas for further refinement. This study contributes an educator-informed process for translating instructors’ needs into the design and formative evaluation of an adaptable, openly licensed faculty development resource. This evidence-based, educator-driven approach demonstrates how those tasked with faculty development on AI can develop and refine timely resources that meet the needs of educators from diverse contexts, offering a flexible, scalable, and community-oriented pathway for bridging institutional resource gaps and advancing inclusive faculty development in the age of AI.

Analysts increasingly turn to generative AI assistants for business-analysis work, yet they often start with short prompts that carry no organizational context. We examined how three general-purpose assistants respond to such under-specified requests and what their responses imply for usability, trust and human oversight. ChatGPT, Claude and Gemini each received five prompts that named only a common business-analysis task: requirements analysis, requirements prioritization, user-story generation, stakeholder-needs analysis and business-process improvement. Each prompt was run three times per system in fresh sessions on 24 and 25 September 2026, giving 45 outputs, which we coded for accuracy, completeness, internal consistency, usability, transparency and support for human oversight. ChatGPT and Gemini explained the named concept in all 30 of their outputs and never asked about the user's situation. Claude asked a clarifying question in 13 of its 15 outputs, and five of its outputs contained little or no task content. Gemini covered 59 of 60 checklist elements but accounted for five of the six accuracy issues. No output expressed uncertainty or suggested verification, and every substantive output was generic. The results point to a trade-off between immediate completeness and handing control back to the analyst. They support a workflow in which analysts supply context, check outputs and validate them with stakeholders before acting on them.

documents.abstract: Colleges that run their own buses usually plan transport using fixed routes and estimated student counts. In practice, the number of students who actually travel changes from day to day, so some buses run with many empty seats while others are overcrowded. This paper presents the design of the AI-Based College Transportation Decision Support System, a full-stack web application that collects daily travel confirmations from students and uses rule-based software agents to analyse route-wise demand, check route compatibility, recommend bus allocation, and suggest seat optimization within capacity limits. Every recommendation is accompanied by a plain-language explanation, and no change becomes final until the administrator approves it. The previous allocation stays in force until a replacement plan is approved. The system is built with React.js, Node.js, Express.js and MongoDB, with JWT-based authentication and role-based access control. It uses predefined rules and calculations only; it does not use machine learning, GPS tracking, or external generative AI services. This paper describes the problem, the system architecture, the database design, the rule-based algorithms, and an illustrative worked example. Experimental evaluation on real college data is identified as future work.

The convergence of artificial intelligence (AI), machine learning (ML), the Internet of Things (IoT), and wireless body area networks (WBANs) has introduced promising opportunities for continuous biomedical health monitoring. However, translating these technologies into robust wearable platforms requires overcoming challenges across intelligent multimodal diagnosis, edge-efficient processing, and end-to-end privacy preservation. This paper presents the AI-Driven Multimodal Secure Health Monitoring Architecture (AIMSHA), a four-tier framework structured across body sensor, edge gateway, fog aggregation, and secure cloud layers. AIMSHA couples multi-biosignal interpretation (EEG, EMG, ECG, and photoplethysmography) with explainable AI (XAI) transparency dashboards and lightweight hierarchical federated learning (FL). To protect distributed model updates against inference vulnerabilities, differential privacy noise perturbation is paired with attribute-based encryption (ABE) access controls and secure aggregation. Furthermore, a lightweight edge intrusion detection system mitigates malicious packet injection, while a permissioned blockchain ledger provides tamper-resistant provenance tracking for global model checkpoints and consent authorisations. Extensive evaluations across six task-aligned physiological benchmark cohorts demonstrate that the underlying MediFuse-DL backbone achieves a mean diagnostic Area Under the ROC Curve (AUC) of 0.974. AIMSHA achieves a 41.3% reduction in communication overhead compared to centralized transmission baselines, maintains continuous sensor-tier monitoring autonomy exceeding 72 hours, and satisfies formal differential privacy guarantees ( $$\epsilon = 1.97$$ , $$\delta = 10^{-5}$$ ) over 100 federated communication rounds. Finally, we analyze software-as-a-medical-device regulatory considerations and clinical translation pathways, positioning AIMSHA as a viable preclinical baseline for secure, privacy-preserving remote patient monitoring. Clinical trial number Not applicable.

Abstract The rapid integration of Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) into higher education has sparked urgent debate about its implications for traditional scholarly standards. This systematic literature review (SLR) investigates how GenAI impacts academic integrity in higher education, identifying specific risks to student honesty and emerging opportunities for pedagogical transformation. Following the PRISMA 2020 framework, 104 records were screened, yielding a final selection of 19 peer-reviewed articles published between 2023 and 2026. Data were synthesized using thematic analysis, and findings are categorized into three core themes: (1) Academic Integrity and the Evolution of Misconduct, (2) Policy and Institutional Strategy, and (3) Ethics and Educational Impact. The review identifies a persistent policy gap in higher education and a shift from traditional plagiarism to "AI-giarism." The impact of GenAI is found to be transformative rather than purely destructive: while it presents significant risks to current product-based assessments, it offers a critical opportunity to modernize education through AI literacy and process-based evaluation. The study concludes that academic integrity must transition from a policing-based model to an ethical partnership model between students and institutions.

documents.abstract: BACKGROUND: Obesity arises from complex interactions among genetic, biological, behavioral, and environmental factors. Traditional "one-size-fits-all" interventions often yield modest, short-term outcomes, failing to account inter-individual variability. Advances in artificial intelligence (AI), polygenic risk scores (PRS), and digital health technologies now enable personalized and adaptive lifestyle interventions. OBJECTIVE: This paper presents the design and evaluation framework of the BETTER4All personalized intervention, a multicentre randomized controlled trial within the EU-funded BETTER4U project. The trial aims to integrate biological and behavioral data into tailored obesity prevention and management strategies. METHODS: . Participants will be randomized to an intervention group receiving AI and PRS-based lifestyle recommendations via a smartphone application, wearable device, and structured counseling, or to a control group receiving standard hypocaloric diet and lifestyle advice. The primary outcome is change in BMI at 6 months. Secondary outcomes include weight-loss maintenance at 1 year, metabolomic and gut microbiota biomarkers, lifestyle behaviors, and psychosocial parameters. Process evaluation incorporates measures of fidelity, acceptability, feasibility, and appropriateness, alongside adherence metrics from the digital tools. CONCLUSION: The BETTER4All trial will provide evidence on the effectiveness and scalability of AI-driven, biologically informed personalization in obesity care, offering a methodological framework for integrating multimodal digital data, from omics and biomarkers to behavior and lifestyle, contributing to the advancement of precision public health strategies. TRIAL REGISTRATION: ClinicalTrials.gov identifier: NCT06997510.

Safety alignment research for large language models (LLMs) remains concentrated on high-resource languages, leaving open how existing alignment methods perform in low-resource, culturally distinct settings. We study this question for Hausa, a language spoken by more than 200 million people across West Africa. We introduce HausaSafeLM, one of the first Hausa safety preference dataset, built from 10,000 prompts derived from PKU-SafeRLHF: 3,000 human-corrected (gold) and 7,000 machine-translated (silver) examples spanning six harm macro-categories. Using Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, we compare supervised fine-tuning (SFT) and SFT followed by Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) under both data regimes, evaluating on 500 harmful and 200 benign Hausa prompts.We find that the untuned base model appears highly safe by refusal-rate metrics alone, but this reflects limited Hausa generation ability rather than genuine alignment: its refusals are almost uniformly low quality. SFT improves both refusal fluency and precision and benefits substantially from the larger, noisier silver-tier data, while DPO sharpens refusal precision but comes at a steep, largely data-invariant cost to linguistic quality. No single configuration jointly maximizes safety, helpfulness, and fluency. Our results suggest that current alignment techniques teach models when to refuse more readily than how to do so fluently in underrepresented languages, and that refusal-rate metrics alone are an unreliable signal of safety in low-resource settings.

documents.abstract: Abstract Background Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly shaping healthcare, highlighting the need for nursing graduates to develop relevant competencies. However, structured AI education remains limited in nursing programs, and evidence on the effects of AI-focused teaching interventions remains scarce. Methods A quasi-experimental pretest–posttest study was conducted among 142 undergraduate nursing students at a university in southwestern Zhejiang, China. Seventy-two students participated in a 10-week AI/generative AI (GenAI)-assisted blended learning course comprising 12 h of self-paced online learning and 6 h of hands-on workshops, while 70 students received standard instruction. Attitudes toward AI, AI literacy, and autonomous learning competency were assessed before and immediately after the intervention using validated instruments. Post-test outcomes were compared using analysis of covariance (ANCOVA), adjusting for the corresponding baseline score, previous AI training experience, frequency of AI use, and digital literacy. Results In the intervention group, AI literacy increased significantly from 55.67 ± 9.84 to 65.01 ± 8.81 ( P < 0.001), as did attitudes toward AI, which increased from 48.07 ± 6.77 to 51.72 ± 9.90 ( P = 0.049). Neither outcome changed significantly in the control group. After adjustment for covariates, the intervention group had significantly higher post-test scores for AI literacy (adjusted mean difference = 11.01, 95% CI 8.55–13.47; P < 0.001) and attitudes toward AI (adjusted mean difference = 4.60, 95% CI 1.98–7.21; P < 0.001). Autonomous learning competency changed little in the intervention group ( P = 0.578) but declined significantly in the control group ( P < 0.001). The adjusted post-test difference also favored the intervention group (adjusted mean difference = 10.94, 95% CI 7.44–14.43; P < 0.001). Conclusions AI/GenAI-assisted blended teaching was associated with higher AI literacy and more favorable attitudes toward AI, while autonomous learning competency remained relatively stable in the intervention group but declined in the control group. Structured AI education integrating conceptual learning, practical application, and responsible AI use may be a valuable addition to undergraduate nursing education.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: Targeted oncologic positron emission tomography (PET) radiopharmaceutical development is often presented as a linear progression from target discovery to clinical imaging. Translation instead depends on interdependent biological, chemical, pharmacokinetic, manufacturing, and regulatory decisions. This Review examines those decisions as an integrated design problem. We consider how target accessibility and heterogeneity, vector format, linker and chelator chemistry, radionuclide properties, and whole-body pharmacokinetics jointly determine image contrast and normal-organ exposure. We then assess how radiosynthesis, analytical validation, molar activity, automation, and batch release determine whether a promising construct can become a reproducible clinical product. Prostate-specific membrane antigen (PSMA) and somatostatin receptor platforms show how molecular imaging can support patient selection for radionuclide therapy when the diagnostic agent, therapeutic construct, trial population, and regulatory indication are aligned. By contrast, fibroblast activation protein (FAP)-targeted and other emerging platforms show why biodistribution or early human feasibility cannot establish clinical benefit. Across these examples, affinity alone is an insufficient design objective. The relevant endpoint is a clinically usable exposure profile that preserves target uptake while limiting background retention and dose to critical organs. Major unresolved issues include inconsistent head-to-head evaluation, incomplete dosimetry, product-specific manufacturing constraints, heterogeneous evidence standards, and region-dependent regulatory indications. We propose an evidence-gated framework that separates target suitability, molecular exposure, manufacturability, human performance, and implementation. This framework distinguishes established practice from early investigation and identifies studies most likely to reduce translational uncertainty.

Commercial language model APIs return only text, allowing a provider to cut costs by quietly routing a fraction of user requests to a cheaper substitute model while billing for the advertised one. Detecting such partial substitution is challenging because honest providers also alter the output distribution through undocumented decoding and serving choices, such as temperature scaling, sampling truncation, repetition and presence penalties, and default system prompts, forcing an audit to test against a composite null of legitimate configurations rather than a single reference. Our key insight is that these legitimate variations primarily shift response typicality across the entire batch, whereas partial substitution injects individual responses that remain anomalous under the claimed model. Building on this, we introduce API-TAIL, a typicality audit that first absorbs batch-level shifts by aligning a single effective temperature to center standardized surprisal scores across the audited batch, and then flags the endpoint if the number of remaining tail responses exceeds a threshold calibrated across legitimate configurations. Evaluated on real-world API responses and constructed substitution mixtures, API-TAIL controls false alarms across diverse honest providers and detects low-rate partial substitution with a small query budget. Under a common composite calibration, it outperforms the adapted rank- and MMD-based audit baselines.

documents.abstract: This reflective article critically examines the role of Artificial Intelligence (AI) agents configured as educational tutors in secondary education. Based on a rigorous review of meta-analyses, international case studies, and specialized academic literature, it explores the conceptual foundations of intelligent tutoring and contemporary models of digital pedagogy. It examines real-world applications of intelligent tutoring systems (ITS), their benefits in terms of learning personalization, immediate feedback, student autonomy, and intrinsic motivation. Likewise, ethical challenges such as algorithmic bias, risks of dehumanizing educational processes, and vulnerabilities related to data privacy are identified. Finally, pedagogical guidelines are presented for the ethical and effective integration of AI agents in school settings, emphasizing teacher training, student-centered design, and continuous educational impact assessment.
