documents.abstract: Cardiovascular disease (CVD) risk assessment underpins preventive care. Although machine learning models often outperform traditional risk prediction methods, adoption of artificial intelligence (AI)-based clinical decision support (CDS) tools remains limited, especially in resource-constrained settings. This study explored the sociotechnical context of CVD risk assessment in resource-constrained settings and identified potential applications for AI-based CDS. Semi-structured interviews were conducted with 27 Indonesian doctors, including general practitioners and cardiologists. Interviews examined clinical decision-making processes, challenges associated with resource constraints, and potential use cases for AI-based CDS. Data were analyzed using a deductive thematic approach informed by the SEIPS (Systems Engineering Initiative for Patient Safety) framework. Doctors reported managing high patient volumes, relying on paper-based medical records, and making largely subjective decisions due to limited access to confirmatory investigations and specialist support. Acute coronary syndrome resulting from atherosclerosis was identified as the most common and important clinical problem. Participants highlighted atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease (ASCVD) risk assessment as a promising application for AI-based CDS because it uses widely available clinical information and can support preventive care decisions. Implementation of AI-based CDS should be guided by local clinical needs and sociotechnical context. Further research is needed to evaluate effects on clinical decision-making and patient outcomes.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: Earthquake sequences are stochastic on two separated timescales: the seismic waves of any individual earthquake propagate over seconds to minutes, while the earthquakes themselves arrive as a sparse, self-exciting occurrence process, with inter-event intervals from seconds to months. Respecting both scales in one training objective is the open challenge. Foundation models (FMs) for seismic waveforms instead import their learning targets from audio and vision, where every target is computed from a single fixed-length window. Such a window holds one realization of the wave propagation (an earthquake trace), never the occurrence process that decides when earthquakes happen. We develop nine model designs sharing one Mamba encoder-decoder, trained on a fixed corpus of 3M windows, varying the self-supervised objective, quantization bottleneck and mixer; the two key comparisons are architecture-matched, varying the objective alone. Each checkpoint is evaluated frozen on three downstream tasks. Varying the target redistributes downstream skill rather than raising it, and no checkpoint wins everywhere. Adding masking pressure to our strongest classifier re-specializes it rather than making it a generalist: it gains 6.9 points of few-shot P-wave picking precision and loses 9.6 points of few-shot classification accuracy. By the standard imported from language and vision, these models are feature extractors rather than FMs. Controls on capacity, architecture, and domain proximity do not explain why skill moves rather than rises. Against task-specific baselines the advantage is regime-dependent: our checkpoints beat them few-shot on classification and ground-motion prediction, and trail them on full data. We argue the binding constraint is the target, and that settling the question requires a learning target defined across events, the timescale that makes seismicity stochastic in the first place.

Multimodal forgery detection is commonly studied under a static assumption: training attacks are expected to approximate those encountered after deployment. This assumption becomes increasingly fragile as generators, editing systems, and multimodal large language models continually introduce new forgery mechanisms and forensic evidence. We formulate this problem as attack-incremental continual multimodal forgery detection, where the binary real/fake interface remains fixed while emerging attacks must be learned without forgetting previous ones. We introduce Fable-Bench, which organizes attack evolution through complementary joint-modality, text-side, and image-side protocols. We further propose ARISE (Authentic Reference-Informed Stability Enhancement), motivated by the open-ended forged class and the comparatively reusable geometry of authentic content. ARISE fits a real-only Gaussian mixture model to projected authentic replay representations as a compact historical reference. Meanwhile, the proposed Gaussian-Responsibility-Aware Stability Preservation (GRASP) derives a sample-adaptive anisotropic metric that strongly constrains historically stable representation directions while retaining plasticity elsewhere. Our Vulnerability-Aware Replay (VAR) further estimates stage-wise vulnerability from authentic-density degradation, forged-to-authentic boundary confusion, and authentic-mode occupancy drift, then assigns bounded replay emphasis to fragile stages. All adaptive signals are obtained from training-time replay statistics, while inference uses only the original multimodal backbone and binary classification head. Experiments across three attack-evolution protocols and multiple detector architectures demonstrate improved historical retention and final average performance over representative continual-learning baselines.

Chapter Thirteen examines how artificial intelligence (AI) can help your fundraising campaign. AI represents a major opportunity for fundraising in all its aspects – and your campaign will be no exception. For a volunteer-run charity, AI will save time and enable your team to put fundraising applications together more easily, using opportunities not available in the past. But AI does have its limitations and these are explored in this chapter too. Key issues addressed in this chapter: • What does AI mean for fundraising? • The potential of AI • The relationship between AI and traditional fundraising methods • The dangers of AI in grant fundraising – does it answer funders’ questions? • Pitfalls of AI • AI vs humans • The ethical issues of using AI in fundraising .
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Abstract Water leakage threatens the sustainability and resilience of water distribution systems (WDSs) by contributing to treated-water losses, unnecessary energy consumption, service disruption, and deteriorating infrastructure performance. Effective leakage management is therefore essential for resource-efficient and resilient urban water services. This critical review synthesizes statistical and probabilistic data models, classical machine learning, neural and deep learning (DL), physics-informed and hybrid learning, and AI-enabled decision and control for leak detection, localization, prediction, and mitigation. It draws on 41 core comparative studies and 59 contextual sources identified through a transparent and reproducible screening process. Emerging directions include acoustic and multisensor learning, graph neural networks and transformer models, digital twins, physics-informed machine learning (ML), reinforcement learning (RL), and retrieval-augmented large language model decision support, reflecting a transition toward connected and intelligent water infrastructure. A two-axis taxonomy separates analytical method families from leakage-management tasks, while dataset provenance and class-imbalance-aware evaluation guide interpretation of reported performance. No analytical family is uniformly superior: performance depends on sensing modality, leak characteristics, class imbalance, domain shift, uncertainty, and validation design, and often declines from simulation to laboratory or field conditions. Persistent gaps include limited field validation, inconsistent reporting, insufficient imbalance-aware evaluation, incomplete integration with utility information systems, and limited research on emerging generative and agentic artificial intelligence (AI). The resulting decision framework links utility objectives with data, models, metrics, and validation requirements. By connecting leakage analytics with water conservation, operational efficiency, infrastructure resilience, and intelligent decision support, this review supports more sustainable and reliable urban WDSs.

Purpose - This study investigated the relationships of artificial intelligence (AI) utilization and drone patrol implementation with perceived traffic violation reduction in Surabaya, Indonesia. Design/methods/approach – A quantitative explanatory survey was analyzed using multiple linear regression in SPSS 25. The reported analyses contained 77 questionnaire records from personnel associated with the Surabaya City Police Traffic Unit. Findings – AI utilization (B = 0.424, β = 0.450, p < 0.001) and drone patrol implementation (B = 0.280, β = 0.334, p = 0.002) were positively associated with perceived traffic violation reduction. The model was significant, F(2, 74) = 36.065, p < 0.001, with R² = 0.494. Research implications/limitations – The results identify associations among respondents’ assessments, not observed changes in recorded violations. Operational evaluation should combine survey evidence with documented enforcement and road-safety outcomes. Originality/value – The study considers intelligent monitoring and mobile aerial patrols together in a specific urban policing setting while distinguishing perceived benefits from demonstrated causal effectiveness.

Abstract Background As AI becomes integrated into nursing education and clinical practice, students must develop the competence to use, evaluate, and ethically govern AI-generated information. However, the psychological mechanisms linking students’ emotional responses to AI and their AI literacy remain underexplored in vocational nursing contexts. This study aimed to examine the mediating role of artificial intelligence (AI) self-efficacy in the relationship between AI anxiety and AI literacy among higher vocational nursing students. Methods A cross-sectional study was conducted using a convenience sample of 921 nursing students from five higher vocational colleges in Sichuan, China. Participants completed the Chinese Artificial Intelligence Anxiety Scale, the revised Chinese Artificial Intelligence Self-Efficacy Scale, and the Artificial Intelligence Literacy Scale. Structural equation modeling was used to test the mediating hypothesis. Results AI anxiety was negatively correlated with AI self-efficacy (r = − 0.470) and AI literacy (r = − 0.370), while AI self-efficacy was positively correlated with AI literacy (r = 0.392). AI self-efficacy partially mediated the association between AI anxiety and AI literacy, accounting for 42.22% of the total effect (indirect effect β = −0.171, 95% BC CI [− 0.255, − 0.100]). After adjustment for covariates, attitude toward nursing and residence remained independently associated with AI literacy. Conclusions AI literacy among higher vocational nursing students is shaped by psychological (AI anxiety, AI self-efficacy), professional (attitude toward nursing), and educational (residence) factors. AI education should be embedded in competency-based nursing preparation with emphasis on critical evaluation, safe application, professional accountability, and equitable access to structured learning opportunities.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: Abstract Purpose Artificial intelligence (AI) holds strong potential to automate repetitive and data-intensive life cycle assessment (LCA) tasks, thereby reducing costs, enabling scalability, and improving data access. This study critically analyses the integration of AI into LCA from technical, ethical, and organizational perspectives. It aims to evaluate how AI can be implemented across LCA workflow steps to enhance efficiency without compromising effectiveness, inclusivity, and core LCA ethical values such as transparency and scientific integrity. Methods We conducted literature review to identify and characterise the technical approaches of current AI-LCA applications across academic research and commercial tools, complemented by a survey assessing current AI uptake in LCA practice and perceived ethical risks. Ethical risks, like accountability or fairness, were derived from existing AI ethical principles and analysed for their potential conflict with LCA ethical values. Organizational implications including changes in work practices and regional disparities were explored, with attention to role of AI in social LCA. Identified applications were critically assessed against four categories: technical maturity, potential to enhance LCA practices, operational feasibility, and ethical risks, and used to qualitatively derive criticality of ethical risks. Results and discussion Most AI-LCA applications focus on predicting impact scores and estimating missing inventory data. Few are employing generative AI, while it is mainly used by practitioners for auxiliary tasks like literature review and report writing. Despite high automation potential, most applications remain at proof-of-concept stage, lack end-to-end workflow integration, and face operational barriers for inclusivity (coding skills, restricted access) resulting in low adoption. Most critical ethical risks relate to fairness, transparency, accountability and sustainability, driven by black-box models, poor documentation, and representation bias, and threaten all core LCA values. Emerging commercial AI-LCA tools present a high potential to widen AI adoption in LCA, but present higher risks toward sustainability, transparency, safety and security. AI is expected to shift LCA stakeholders’ roles from manual tasks to supervising algorithms and validating outputs, while potentially reinforcing regional disparities due to unequal access to AI tools, data, and expertise. Conclusion AI can significantly enhance LCA efficiency and scalability, but without robust collaborative governance it may undermine methodological rigor and ethical principles. Responsible integration requires need-based adoption, standardized protocols for evaluating AI models in LCA context, human-in-the-loop validation for value choices, transparent documentation, and proactive attention to fairness and inclusivity. These findings provide a foundation for guidance toward effective, inclusive, and responsible use of AI in LCA.

documents.abstract: Films introduce characters incrementally as they progress. We study the problem of identifying principal characters and assigning their names directly from the movie itself, without using external cast lists, actor photographs, or pre-built character banks. We introduce the character naming task: given a name mentioned in dialogue and the associated video context, the model must determine which visible character bears that name. This task is challenging because name resolution often depends on cinematic cues such as shot-reverse-shot structure, self-introduction, direct address, third-party reference, gaze, and temporal continuity. We provide a dataset and annotations for evaluating character naming and first character appearances, develop a video-and-dialogue model for the task, and compare it with proprietary multimodal large language models. We further introduce a progressive framework for building a character bank as the film unfolds. Together, these contributions support online, human-like movie understanding in which character identities are inferred from the film itself.

Purpose: Carpal Tunnel Syndrome (CTS) symptoms are an occupational health concern among office workers who perform repetitive hand and wrist movements during computer-based activities. This study aimed to examine the association between repetitive movement exposure and CTS symptoms among office workers at PT Karya Bintang Mandiri. Materials and Methods: This analytical cross-sectional study involved 164 office workers recruited using purposive sampling. Repetitive movement exposure was assessed using the Occupational Repetitive Actions (OCRA) Checklist, while CTS symptoms were evaluated using the Boston Carpal Tunnel Questionnaire (BCTQ). Descriptive statistics and the Pearson Chi-Square test were used to examine the association between repetitive movement exposure and CTS symptoms. Result: Moderate repetitive movement exposure was observed in 83 participants (50.6%), followed by high exposure in 42 (25.6%) and low exposure in 39 (23.8%). Regarding CTS symptoms, 62 participants (37.8%) reported no symptoms, 68 (41.5%) reported mild symptoms, 32 (19.5%) reported moderate symptoms, and 2 (1.2%) reported severe symptoms. The Pearson Chi-Square test indicated a significant association between repetitive movement exposure and CTS symptom categories, χ²(6) = 35.06, p < 0.001. In a supplementary dichotomized analysis, the prevalence of moderate-to-severe CTS symptoms was 47.6% (20/42) among workers with high exposure and 11.5% (14/122) among workers with low-to-moderate exposure (prevalence ratio [PR] = 4.15; 95% CI: 2.31–7.46). Conclusion: Repetitive movement exposure was associated with CTS symptom categories among office workers at PT Karya Bintang Mandiri. These findings support the importance of ergonomic risk assessment and preventive measures in office environments. Further studies using longitudinal designs and clinical diagnostic assessments are warranted.

Abstract We present ASTRA, an autonomous framework for physics-validated analysis and hypothesis generation in astrophysics without per-step human intervention. It integrates dimensional analysis, structural causal models, Bayesian evidence computation, and multi-wavelength data fusion in a single automated workflow. Five test cases on real observational data recover known results: Herschel filament scaling, Chandra Deep Field South cross-matching, SDSS galaxy correlations, Gaia causal inference, and Bayesian virial model selection. A sixth case runs unsupervised on synthetic galaxy data: the main sequence and mass–metallicity relation are recovered, and the outlier detector, with a false-discovery-rate threshold and no contamination parameter, recovers the blind injected fraction on ten sealed datasets (purity >0.99) and flags nothing on the 3,000-galaxy sample. A knowledge-isolation ablation shows pattern detection and physical validation are invariant to removal of domain knowledge, which affects only interpretation. In a direct comparison, agentic-LLM and pure-ML baselines match the statistical fitting but not the physics-validation stage: they rarely derive the equilibrium benchmark, split evenly on the physical verdict, and adopt a supplied erroneous benchmark in all six trap runs; an astrophysics-specific fine-tuned model completes zero of six runs. On live SDSS DR16 data it flags 197 of 4,999 galaxies at a data-determined threshold, ranked extremes classifiable from withheld spectroscopy. These are recovery validations and capability demonstrations rather than discoveries, with hypothesis generation demonstrated qualitatively.

Reinforcement learning has made Audio Large Language Models (Audio LLMs) better reasoners, but the reward that drives it still comes from outside the model: a final-answer check, a hand-crafted process score, or an external LLM judge that stays fixed while the policy improves. We show that an Audio LLM can supply this reward itself, and can do so recursively: each improved model becomes the critic that trains its successor, so the training signal improves along with the model. We introduce AudioRSI (Recursively Self-Improving Audio Reasoners), a reinforcement learning framework in which a single model plays two roles: as an actor it generates reasoning paths, and as a critic it compares them pairwise, turning its own judgments into a process-level reward. The critic is periodically replaced by the current policy, which closes the recursive loop. Because the critic hears the same recording as the actor, it can reject reasoning that cites acoustic evidence the audio does not contain, rather than reward reasoning that merely sounds plausible. The recursion is what sustains progress: under a frozen external judge, out-of-distribution accuracy plateaus during training, while a critic refreshed from the improving policy keeps it rising. Across four out-of-distribution benchmarks, all disjoint from the AVQA training distribution, AudioRSI outperforms strong baselines including Audio Flamingo 3 and Gemini 2.5 Pro on MMAU test-mini, ranks first on MMSU, achieves a clear lead on the challenging Multi-Audio split of MMAU-Pro, and leads the 7B open-source tier on MMAR among methods without external reward models. With no reward specifying how to reason, AudioRSI also develops structured reasoning behaviors (logical reasoning, perception-aware analysis, and reduced hallucination), corroborated by an external LLM-as-Judge evaluation and a keyword-based behavior analysis.

Medium altitude, long endurance unmanned aerial systems such as Shahed-type strike drones are an unanswered threat in modern conflicts. Conventional air defense systems are too expensive to provide a feasible large-scale solution. Quadcopter interceptors are a cheap, battle-proven alternative, but their extremely limited flight time restricts them to low altitude targets at short range, whereas fixed-wing platforms have the endurance to reach higher altitude targets from longer distances. However, such interceptors are still operated manually. Recent developments in learning-based controllers show potential for automation. In this work, a fixed-wing interceptor is presented that is controlled by a neural network that maps filtered monocular vision observations directly to actuator commands. The policy was trained in a custom Python environment using reinforcement learning and proximal policy optimization. The policy was then deployed on a fixed-wing platform and tested in real interception scenarios. As a baseline, two classical guidance controllers were also developed and tested in simulation. The policy is able to intercept targets both in simulation and in real flight. In simulation, the policy outperforms the classical controllers under most conditions. The interceptor was ultimately successfully validated in real flight by intercepting maneuvering fixed-wing targets. This novel system shows the potential of artificial intelligence for autonomous control of fixed-wing interceptor drones.

Abstract Physical hardware-security evaluation requires both target-specific reasoning and control of laboratory instruments. This study presents a large language model (LLM) agent that links reconnaissance, vulnerability hypotheses, laser fault-injection experiments and reporting through human approval gates. The agent reverse-engineers firmware and instruction behaviour, combines this evidence with documentation and chip imagery, and generates bounded experiments with predefined rules for classifying outcomes. On an ATmega328P microcontroller, agent-derived experiments produced a skipped processor load instruction, acceptance of an incorrect personal identification number (PIN), and the same two-byte Advanced Encryption Standard (AES) encrypted-output difference in 14 trials, with 29 paired fault-free controls. Photon-emission imaging narrowed the physical search region. A second campaign on an Artix-7 field-programmable gate array (FPGA) tested transfer to programmable logic using firmware-binary analysis, optical-to-layout registration and cryptographic-output classification. Recorded agent and operator decisions connect observations to experimental revisions and documented conclusions, demonstrating an autonomous workflow across two hardware architectures.
topics: Physical Unclonable Functions (PUFs) and Hardware Security

documents.abstract: Recommender Systems Engineer Agents (RSE-Agents), which use LLM-based agents to autonomously improve recommendation algorithms, are emerging as a promising paradigm. However, their capabilities and limitations remain poorly understood due to the lack of a unified, standardized evaluation framework and systematic trajectory-level analysis. To address this gap, we introduce AutoRSE, an evaluation framework spanning six representative industrial-grade recommendation tasks, and conduct a large-scale empirical study of three frontier LLMs across three widely used agent harnesses. Our results show that RSE-Agents consistently enhance the performance of backbones on five of the six tasks, with an average relative improvement of 16.1%, indicating that they can already autonomously improve recommendation performance. However, trajectory-level analysis also reveals that current RSE-Agents function primarily as engineering optimizers rather than algorithmic improvers: their gains are largely driven by hyperparameter tuning, training strategies, and model ensembling, while genuine algorithmic innovations are rare. Since the largest gains in recommender systems often stem from algorithmic advances, this behavior underscores a fundamental limitation of current RSE-Agents. To probe this limitation, we perform idea-injection experiments and show that agents equipped with innovative ideas from frontier research or human experts achieve substantially larger improvements than those relying on self-generated ideas. These results suggest that idea generation is a central bottleneck of current RSE-Agents, highlights a key direction for the future recommendation system research. Our implementation is publicly available on GitHub: https://github.com/Ray-Tiann/AutoRSE.

Generative artificial intelligence (Gen-AI) is a form of AI technology that can automatically generate new content, such as text, images, and audio, based on prompts. This study explores the opportunities and structural challenges of using Gen-AI to promote sustainable design in the field of intangible cultural heritage (ICH) from the perspectives of ICH designers and relevant experts. The research employed a variety of methods, including interviews (n= 40), grounded theory, the Delphi method (n = 20), exploratory factor analysis (n = 312), confirmatory factor analysis (n = 324), and expert interviews (n = 10). The study evaluated deep-seated issues arising from Gen-AI’s intervention in ICH design practices, such as cultural subjectivity, knowledge, power relations, and value circulation, through the lenses of Cultural Ecology, Extraction of Intangible Cultural Heritage Genes, Sustainable Communication, Technology Generation, and Human–Machine Collaborative Design. The results suggest that Gen-AI’s empowerment involves a tension between technological generative capabilities and cultural accuracy, as well as systemic-level transformations such as balancing communication efficiency with cultural depth and human–machine collaboration, and re-configuring the designer’s role.

Abstract Background Musculoskeletal disorders (MSDs) are common among construction workers because of physically demanding, repetitive work and heavy lifting. Casual construction workers may face additional challenges to care due to financial insecurity, limited occupational health protections, and the temporary nature of their employment. This study describes the work-related exposures that casual construction workers attributed to their MSD symptoms, and the barriers and facilitators to accessing MSD treatment and care services, in the Kampala Metropolitan Area (KMA), Uganda. Methods A qualitative descriptive study, framed by an interpretivist perspective and a constructionist epistemological position, was conducted among 15 casual construction workers and 10 key informants in KMA. Participants were selected using purposive and snowball sampling. Data were collected through semi-structured in-depth interviews (IDIs) with casual workers and key informant interviews (KIIs) with stakeholders involved in occupational safety and health, labour administration, and construction-site management. Interviews were audio-recorded, transcribed verbatim, and translated where necessary. Data were analyzed thematically using ATLAS.ti 7.5, combining deductive and inductive coding. Reporting follows the COREQ checklist. Results Participants attributed MSD symptoms to heavy lifting, repetitive tasks, prolonged working hours, inadequate rest, poor ergonomics, and limited safety equipment and training. Barriers to accessing care included limited awareness of MSD services and occupational health rights, financial constraints, employment insecurity, inadequate employer support, limited MSD-specific training, complex compensation procedures, weak OSH implementation, and limited access to specialized occupational health services. Workers often delayed care, continued working despite pain, or self-medicated when treatment seemed costly or risked income or job loss. Facilitators included employer support (sick leave, safety programmes, OSH inspections, health assessments, first aid, on-site healthcare, referral linkages, compensation mechanisms, OSH personnel) and social support, but were more consistently available in larger, better-resourced projects. Conclusion Access to MSD care among casual construction workers is shaped by interconnected individual, economic, workplace, and health-system factors. Strengthening worker education, enforcing OSH requirements, improving affordable occupational health services, compensation mechanisms, and workplace support could promote earlier MSD reporting and treatment. Findings reflect 25 participants recruited in one metropolitan area and are not statistically representative.
topics: Occupational Health and Safety in Workplaces

documents.abstract: Software-engineering research relies on benchmarks that evaluate new techniques on a set of problem instances. Unfortunately, manually constructing benchmarks is labor-intensive, as researchers must find suitable instances, prepare execution environments, establish expected outcomes, and validate correctness. This paper presents BenchMeUp, an approach for automatically creating software-engineering benchmarks from natural-language specifications. Given a specification defining the desired instances, data sources, and evaluation procedures, BenchMeUp generates search rules and a construction plan, invokes parallel LLM agents that identify candidate instances and construct executable instances, validates the results in fresh execution environments, and packages the instances behind a unified command-line interface. We evaluate the approach on four tasks: program repair, issue reproduction, compiler autotuning, and fixing static-analysis warnings. Targeting 50 instances per task (200 in total), BenchMeUp constructs 198 instances, of which 196 (99\%) are successfully packaged. Search and construction take 36 minutes and \$0.79 per instance, on average. Evaluating eight existing techniques on the generated benchmarks, we find that 189 of 196 packaged instances (96\%) support end-to-end evaluation, allowing users to study the effectiveness of the techniques. Checking every constructed instance against its source, the specification, and its expected outcome, we find that 180 of 198 (91\%) meet all criteria, compared with 10 of 200 instances delivered by Codex (general-purpose coding agent). Overall, we show that LLM-based agents can automate benchmark construction across diverse software-engineering tasks and produce executable instances that existing techniques can use, while validity beyond execution still needs to be checked.

Abstract The rapid integration of generative AI into creative industries has intensified debates about the future of culturally grounded design practice. This study examines how three production conditions (human-only, AI-assisted, and fully autonomous AI) differentially affect the perceived cultural fidelity, creativity, aesthetics, and commercial viability of textile designs rooted in traditional Anatolian kilim motifs, a question with limited prior empirical evidence in design education. Using a within-subjects design, fifteen undergraduate textile design students produced designs under each condition, using a generative AI platform with substantial commercial reach in the Turkish textile sector for the AI-involved conditions. A panel of ten expert evaluators, five academics and five industry designers, rated 45 designs against a seven-criterion rubric under blind conditions. Cultural fidelity, creativity, originality, and aesthetics differed significantly across conditions (all p < .05). Both human-only and AI-assisted designs preserved cultural fidelity at equivalent levels, and both significantly exceeded fully autonomous AI outputs. Paradoxically, fully autonomous AI outputs received the highest scores for creativity and originality, pointing to a trade-off between perceived novelty and cultural coherence. No significant differences emerged for commercial viability, technical feasibility, or compositional integrity, indicating parity across production methods on industrially relevant dimensions. Academic and industry evaluators converged on cultural fidelity judgements while diverging on more subjective aesthetic criteria. These findings suggest that human involvement acts as a cultural filter that cannot be replicated through textual instruction alone, and that even minimal human intervention, selecting and lightly editing AI-generated variants, is sufficient to preserve culturally identifiable design characteristics. The results have implications for textile design pedagogy, for AI governance in heritage-sensitive industries, and for theorising human–AI co-creation in cultural production contexts.

Students’ learning motivation is an important factor in effective learning, while Islamic Religious Education teachers have a strategic role in fostering motivation through pedagogical, motivational, and exemplary practices. This study aims to describe the planning and implementation of Islamic Religious Education teachers’ efforts to enhance students’ learning motivation and to analyze their outcomes in terms of student engagement, subject comprehension, religious attitudes, and character development. This research employed a qualitative approach with a case study design conducted at MTs Wahid Hasyim Dau Malang. The research subjects and data sources included 2 (two) Islamic Religious Education teachers, and 2 (two) administrative staff, and a class of students. Data were collected through observations, interviews, and documentation, and were analyzed using the Miles, Huberman, and Saldaña model through data condensation, data presentation, and conclusion drawing and verification, with data validity strengthened through cross-checking across sources and techniques. The findings show that teachers enhance learning motivation through systematic instructional planning, including the preparation of teaching modules, engaging learning activities, comprehensive assessment strategies, and adaptation of teaching methods to students’ characteristics. During implementation, teachers create a positive learning atmosphere through educational games, quizzes, discussions, question-and-answer sessions, group work, rewards, contextualization of learning materials, and regular content reviews. These efforts contribute to increased student participation, improved understanding of Islamic Religious Education materials, and the development of religious attitudes and character. The study recommends that teachers maintain varied and adaptive instructional strategies while strengthening students’ intrinsic motivation through meaningful learning experiences, positive reinforcement, role modeling, and collaboration between schools and parents.

Fake news undermines public trust and the integrity of online information ecosystems. Temporally disordered fake news is especially elusive because it rearranges factual events into a false chronology. Individual events may remain factually valid even when their temporal relations are misrepresented. When similar events involving the same entity recur, retrieval may return semantically plausible evidence from the wrong period. Consequently, independent event verification may rely on locally coherent but temporally mismatched evidence and incorrectly validate the article. We call this the \textit{evidence coherence trap}. Because existing benchmarks rarely isolate this setting, we construct ChronoFake, a source-disjoint benchmark of 30,706 articles derived from temporally anchored real events. It distinguishes temporal manipulation from valid narration, including flashbacks. To address this, we propose DelSA, a \underline{D}ocument S\underline{el}ection \underline{S}elf-Updating \underline{A}gent that iteratively refines evidence selection during training and applies a frozen rulebook for one-pass evidence selection at inference. DelSA uses an LLM to characterize candidate evidence, while a verifier-trained reranker balances local relevance against timeline consistency. Finally, the classifier compares the article-implied chronology extracted by the LLM with the evidence-derived chronology to reveal global temporal conflicts. DelSA outperforms existing methods on ChronoFake, while remaining competitive on PolitiFact and GossipCop.

Purpose The post-pandemic recovery of global air transport and rapid developments in artificial intelligence are shifting aviation safety management from reactive accident investigation to proactive risk prediction. To examine how this trend is reflected in recent literature, this study aims to conduct a bibliometric analysis of aviation unsafe event research published between 2020 and 2025. Design/methodology/approach Based on 512 publications retrieved from the Web of Science Core Collection, the authors use Bibliometrix and VOSviewer to construct keyword co-occurrence and co-citation networks. Findings The results show a rapid increase in research output following a temporary decline in 2022, reflecting the field’s resilience and growing attention to post-pandemic safety challenges. Thematic evolution analysis identifies a clear departure from traditional system-level investigations. This field increasingly prioritizes mining valuable information from flight data and unstructured safety reports using machine learning, deep learning and natural language processing. Current studies largely revolve around anomaly detection under complex meteorological conditions, causal inference using Bayesian networks and the application of large language models for safety text analysis. Originality/value These findings suggest that data-driven approaches have established themselves in aviation unsafe event research. Future studies should focus on addressing the interpretability of deep learning models and optimizing human–machine collaboration in safety-critical systems.

Self-supervised foundation models for biomedical imaging are typically trained with non-sequential objectives that encourage invariance between augmented crops or predict missing content within a limited spatial resolution or range. This paradigm can be limiting for biomedical images, where diagnostically relevant structure often depends on relationships across widely different spatial extents and resolutions. We investigate sequential, action-conditioned prediction as an alternative self-supervised pretraining objective for biomedical imaging. As a proof of concept, we adapt seq-JEPA, originally developed for natural images, to 256 × 256 px histopathology images by extending its action space with zoom, and introduce seq-JEPA-dense, which predicts the next representation for every step in the sequence. Under the same per-crop augmentation distribution and with one run per method, seq-JEPA-dense improved tissue classification accuracy in the aggregated linear-probe evaluation from 88.3% to 91.9%, narrowing the gap to SimCLR, which achieved 93.3%. Both sequential variants recover a held-out crop from the preceding crops and the relative action leading to it at roughly twice the chance rate within the same image, indicating that the prediction depends on the action; whether position, zoom, or both drive this remains to be isolated. These results provide proof-of-concept evidence that sequential, action-conditioned self-supervision can be adapted to histopathology by extending its action space with zoom, yielding representations that approach a contrastive baseline, a first step toward its investigation as a self-supervised approach for extended biomedical images such as whole-slide images.
topics: Radiomics and Machine Learning in Medical Imaging

documents.abstract: Three-dimensional (3D) bioprinting has emerged as an enabling technology in regenerative medicine with the potential to redefine the future of orthodontic treatment. By integrating living cells, biomaterials, and bioactive molecules through layer-by-layer fabrication, bioprinting enables the development of patient-specific constructs that closely replicate native craniofacial tissues. In orthodontics, this technology offers potential solutions for challenges such as alveolar bone deficiency, periodontal tissue loss, root resorption, craniofacial defects, and compromised tissue healing following orthodontic interventions. Recent advances in stem cell biology, bioactive hydrogels, tissue engineering, growth factor delivery, and digital manufacturing have expanded the scope of regenerative orthodontics beyond conventional biomechanical tooth movement. The incorporation of artificial intelligence, computer-aided design, cone-beam computed tomography, and additive manufacturing further supports precision treatment planning and customized regenerative therapies. Despite encouraging experimental outcomes, routine clinical implementation remains limited by challenges related to vascularization, scaffold maturation, manufacturing standardization, regulatory approval, long-term safety, and economic feasibility. Continued interdisciplinary collaboration among orthodontists, bioengineers, material scientists, and regulatory authorities is essential to translate laboratory innovations into predictable clinical applications. This article reviews the biological principles, technological advancements, clinical applications, translational challenges, and future perspectives of bioprinting, highlighting current evidence, existing limitations, and research priorities toward clinical translation.

Space infrastructure underpins modern civilisation but remains vulnerable because satellite communications, telemetry, and command systems rely heavily on centralised security architectures. As space becomes increasingly congested, contested, and commercialised, these architectures face growing threats from nation-state adversaries, cybercriminals, and supply chain compromise. This chapter examines blockchain technology as a structural countermeasure, highlighting how decentralisation, immutability, transparency, auditability, and trustless authentication address critical vulnerabilities across ground, space, user, cloud, communication, and supply chain segments. A permissioned consortium blockchain model is proposed to balance resilience, operational confidentiality, and national sovereignty requirements. The chapter explores blockchain-enabled applications including tamper-evident audit trails, decentralised identity and access management, distributed threat detection, smart contract governance, space situational awareness, autonomous satellite operations, and secure inter-satellite communications. It also analyses deployment challenges and future research directions involving post-quantum cryptography, Zero Trust Architecture, AI-enhanced smart contracts, and cislunar blockchain ecosystems for resilient and trustworthy next-generation space cybersecurity frameworks worldwide.
topics: Blockchain Technology in Education and Learning

documents.abstract: Background Occupational noise is a pervasive occupational hazard. While it is a well-established cause of hearing loss, only a few studies have suggested a potential association with cardiovascular diseases, and the evidence remains limited. Furthermore, individual susceptibility varies substantially, and metabolic characteristics, such as body mass index (BMI), may play a modifying role. Objective To systematically examine the effect of BMI modification on occupational noise exposure duration and hypertension risk. Methods A cross-sectional study was conducted among workers at an automobile manufacturing plant. Demographics, occupational history, and medical examinations were collected. Modified Poisson regression models were used to estimate prevalence ratios (PRs). The modifying effect of continuous BMI was evaluated by incorporating an interaction term, with a sensitivity analysis performed using binary BMI classifications. Johnson-Neyman technique was used to determine the point at which the association was no longer statistically significant. Results There were 21.6% of participants with hypertension in this plant. Occupational noise exposure duration was positively associated with the risk of hypertension. The continuous BMI showed a significant negative interaction with noise exposure duration (PR = 0.987, 95% CI [0.979–0.995], P = 0.001). Specifically, at a BMI of 18.5 kg/m 2 , each additional year of noise exposure duration increased hypertension risk by 11.9% (PR = 1.119, 95% CI [1.047–1.196]); at a BMI of 24.0 kg/m 2 , this association was attenuated but remained significant (PR = 1.041, 95% CI [1.008–1.075]); and at a BMI of 28.0 kg/m 2 , no significant association was observed (PR = 0.987, 95% CI [0.956–1.019]). With Johnson–Neyman, the BMI value above which the estimated association was no longer statistically significant was identified at 27.02 kg/m 2 . In sensitivity analysis, treating BMI as a binary variable, the association between noise exposure duration and hypertension risk was attenuated and no longer statistically significant in overweight/obese individuals but remained significant in normal-weight individuals, and the negative interaction between noise exposure duration and BMI remained statistically significant (PR = 0.919, 95% CI [0.863–0.979], P = 0.010). Conclusions The association between occupational noise exposure duration and hypertension risk was modified by BMI in this cross-sectional study of automobile manufacturing workers. The association was more pronounced among normal-weight workers, whereas it was attenuated and no longer statistically significant at higher BMI levels. These findings suggest that BMI may be an important consideration in occupational health surveillance and hypertension risk assessment among noise-exposed workers, warranting further longitudinal investigation.

Near midair collisions (NMACs) remain a complex aviation safety challenge shaped by operational conditions and human factors. Aviation Safety Reporting System (ASRS) narratives provide useful information about communication, visual acquisition, workload, and other event circumstances, but relationships identified from voluntary reports may vary across analytical approaches and over time. This study examined 13,111 NMAC-related ASRS reports from 1988 to 2025 to identify stable report-level associations among operational conditions, encounter proximity, narrative topics, and reported evasive action. Across two Bayesian-network approaches and 500 paired bootstrap samples, traffic-pattern operations/training and tower communication/sequencing were the strongest variables directly associated with reported evasive action. Their recurrence was moderate rather than universal, however, and their inclusion changed under different relationship-selection thresholds. This indicates that the local structure around reported evasive action was sensitive to modeling decisions, even though the two variables consistently ranked as the leading response-adjacent candidates. Additional robustness checks preserved these two response parents in the full-data models while showing changes in the broader network structure. A temporal evaluation produced a different pattern. Models trained on reports from 1988 to 2019 and evaluated on reports from 2020 to 2025 instead identified airspace structure/radar-contact issues and final-approach/base-to-final conflicts as the response-adjacent variables. Because the narrative-topic features were derived from the full corpus, this analysis represents a temporal evaluation conditional on a fixed topic representation, rather than a fully independent validation of the complete modeling pipeline. The changed response parents therefore indicate temporal sensitivity but do not establish nonstationarity. The findings describe associations within voluntary safety reports and should not be interpreted as evidence of causality, collision risk, or operational warning performance. The study contributes a reproducible, systematically stress-tested framework for evaluating Bayesian-network findings in aviation safety narratives. It identifies communication, sequencing, visual acquisition, and traffic-pattern operations as priorities for expert review and prospective measurement while cautioning against treating relationships found in historical narratives as stable operational predictors.

The accelerating integration of brain-inspired artificial intelligence into industrial systems marks a transformative moment for sustainable engineering, directly advancing the United Nations Sustainable Development Goal 9 on Industry, Innovation, and Infrastructure. This chapter provides a rigorous, engineering-oriented examination of how neuroscience principles, including spike-timing-dependent plasticity, predictive coding, hierarchical sensory processing, and lateral inhibition, are being systematically translated into industrial AI architectures with compelling real-world impact. Six interconnected domains are explored: cognitive robotics and human–machine collaboration using ACT-R-grounded spiking neural networks; digital twin-integrated predictive maintenance leveraging liquid state machines and event-driven spike encoding; energy-aware neuromorphic computing for sustainable manufacturing, achieving up to 10,000× power reduction over GPU-based systems; brain-inspired hierarchical decision systems and neuro-symbolic integration for explainable smart factory control; ethical workforce transition frameworks addressing automation’s socioeconomic implications; and six global innovation case studies spanning wind turbine health monitoring, electric vehicle battery assembly, smart city traffic optimization, and predictive water infrastructure management. Collectively, these applications demonstrate that brain-inspired AI is not merely a technical advancement but a principled pathway toward more resilient, equitable, and environmentally sustainable industrial systems aligned with international development goals.

This panel examines the growing convergence of human–AI interaction (HAI) and human–robot interaction (HRI) as intelligent systems become more autonomous, embodied, and embedded in everyday settings such as healthcare, education, homes, and workplaces. Although HAI and HRI have evolved as distinct fields, the panel argues that shared human factors concerns—such as trust, safety, autonomy, teamwork, situation awareness, evaluation, and responsible deployment—now require greater integration across both domains. Drawing on perspectives from leading researchers and doctoral students, the session explores how embodiment, motion, social cues, and system transparency shape human interaction with AI and robots. It also addresses methodological tensions, including laboratory versus field evaluation and short-term versus longitudinal study, while highlighting implications for ethics, training, and design. Overall, the panel aims to identify common challenges, foster cross-disciplinary collaboration, and outline a research roadmap for human-centered intelligent systems that improve performance, well-being, and quality of life across diverse contexts and sectors.

Abstract Under what conditions can a forecasting agent profitably provide liquidity on a prediction market? We derive a decomposition of the optimal market-making spread into a microstructure term and an adverse selection term proportional to the agent's mean absolute estimation error~$\alpha$. The profitability condition $s > 2\varphi\alpha$ depends only on the sign of per-fill profit and holds for any positive fill-rate function. A threshold theorem shows that tolerable calibration error increases with existing market spread---a comparative static suggesting that calibrated agents may add the most value on illiquid long-tail markets that lack human market makers. Monte Carlo simulations across 3{,}000 synthetic markets calibrated to empirical Polymarket parameters ($\kappa = 36$) show win rates near 68--70\% across calibration levels, with mean profit varying by $3.4\times$ (\$5.83 to \$1.72), confirming that calibration quality drives profit magnitude. On the empirical side, the main finding is a calibration gap: five frontier LLMs evaluated on 15 resolved Polymarket questions reveal that market-alignment error (MAD $\leq$ 0.029) underestimates true estimation error ($\alpha$ up to 0.437) by an order of magnitude---a result with implications for any system using market prices as calibration targets. The model omits inventory risk and multi-agent competition, limiting direct deployment conclusions, but the spread decomposition provides a tractable framework for analyzing when AI-agent liquidity provision is viable. JEL Classification: D47 , G14 , G17 , C63

Continual adaptation of large language models (LLMs) to evolving task distributions while mitigating catastrophic forgetting remains an open problem. Existing strategies often struggle to scale or lack a robust mechanism for zero-shot task-to-expert assignment. We introduce CaLLM, a framework that resolves these tensions by combining metric-based meta-learning with modular parameter isolation via lightweight adapters. First, CaLLM projects each input batch into a task-agnostic embedding space to find its nearest prototype. It then routes the batch to the specific adapter specialized for that data distribution. This formulation provides (i)~controllable cross-task interference by design, (ii)~constant computational complexity regardless of task count, (iii)~seamless integration of novel distributions through prototype expansion, and (iv)~regime agnosticism as the local routing decision enables a unified approach to both online and offline settings. Our experiments demonstrate that this routing mechanism discovers semantically coherent task groupings while facilitating constructive interference between similar tasks, and keeping overhead at a minimum. Across diverse and fine-grained continual learning benchmarks, CaLLM consistently outperforms traditional isolation and replay methods, establishing prototype-based modular routing as a principled and scalable approach to lifelong adaptation of LLMs.

Continual learning requires large language models to acquire new knowledge and capabilities while retaining what they have learned. Fine-tuning and replay support acquisition and retention, but deciding whether incoming examples need supervision and which historical examples to revisit remains a challenge. We propose Compatibility-Aware Memory Replay (CAMR), an adaptive framework that jointly controls current-example supervision and historical replay. CAMR combines compatibility checks with a learned memory gate to guide an online policy over three actions: learning incoming examples with general replay, jointly reinforcing compatible related examples, and skipping direct supervision of verified mastered duplicates. The policy learns from acquisition, retention, and training-cost feedback under a bounded per-arrival replay budget. We evaluate CAMR with Qwen3-8B-Base on continual factual updating and cross-task and cross-domain learning. On WikiBigEdit, CAMR consistently leads evaluated methods in Original Match from 3K to 100K facts, reaching 93.66% after just 3K facts and surpassing Full-history Replay (LoRA) after 100K facts. It also achieves the highest final scores on all four selected TRACE tasks and maintains or improves earlier-task performance relative to post-acquisition levels in a sequence spanning financial question answering, mathematical reasoning, code generation, and summarization.

Abstract Objective To evaluate the extent to which large language models (LLMs) reproduce human assessments of the quality of stroke-related information on social media. Background Social media is a major source of health information, yet content quality varies. The reliability of LLMs in evaluating stroke-related social media content against human assessments remains uncertain. Methods This cross-sectional study evaluated 50 TikTok and Instagram videos using human reference scores and three AI models: ChatGPT, Microsoft 365 Copilot, and Claude. Publicly unavailable videos and those featuring songs or lacking transcribable speech were excluded. Spoken audio was transcribed using a free tool, and transcripts were submitted to all three models with an identical standardized prompt. Scores were compared using Mann–Whitney U tests; Spearman’s correlation assessed associations with human ratings, and linear regression quantified explained variance. Results The median human reference score was 37.00 (IQR, 35.00–45.00). All AI models scored significantly lower: ChatGPT, 34.50 (p = 0.001); Microsoft Copilot, 33.50 (p < 0.001); and Claude, 26.00 (p < 0.001). All models correlated significantly with human ratings, with the strongest association for Claude (ρ = 0.593; p < 0.001), followed by ChatGPT (ρ = 0.550; p < 0.001) and Copilot (ρ = 0.396; p = 0.004). Claude explained 32.1% of the variance in human scores (R² = 0.321), compared with 31.4% for ChatGPT and 14.8% for Copilot. Inter-model correlation was strongest between ChatGPT and Copilot (ρ = 0.862; p < 0.001). Conclusions All three LLMs showed significant positive correlations with human ratings but systematically assigned lower scores. Claude showed the strongest correlation, whereas Microsoft Copilot showed the weakest. These findings highlight the limitations of LLMs in reproducing human judgments and the need for further validation before their use as standalone evaluators of social media content.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have made remarkable progress on solving competition-level mathematics, yet their ability to verify natural-language mathematical proofs remains relatively underexplored. This gap is especially pronounced for Olympiad-level proofs, which require meticulous assessment of each claim in a long reasoning chain. Current proof verification thus primarily relies on expert inspection, which is costly to scale. In this paper, we present a systematic study of LLM-based verification in this setting. Specifically, we introduce a human-curated dataset of USAMO 2025 candidate solutions with expert grading, and conduct a broad evaluation of existing LLM verifiers across frontier models. We also propose TROJAN, an iterative self-critique pipeline for generating high-fidelity adversarial proofs at scale. Our comprehensive evaluation covers 20 models spanning seven metrics, two prompt styles, three inference methods, and three prompt templates, showing that state-of-the-art models still leave considerable room for improvement. To narrow this gap, we propose MABGrader, a Multi-Armed Bandit framework that reframes grading as arm selection over the discrete score space. MABGrader outperforms the SOTA ProofGrader by 26.4% in Quadratic Weighted Kappa and reduces grading error by 14%. Code and dataset are available at https://github.com/aziksh-ospanov/TROJAN.

Scientific discovery often begins with an unexpected observation that prompts a new research question. In a world with altered physical laws, can large language models (LLMs) notice unexpected behavior, such as heavier objects falling more slowly, and discover the law through experiments without being told what to investigate? To evaluate this ability, we introduce LongChang, an automated framework that creates simulated worlds with altered physics, where one or more laws differ from ordinary physics. The evaluated LLMs act as explorers, manipulating objects and building tools to investigate their own questions without research tasks or hints about these laws. Separate LLM agents generate and review scenes, review tool designs, and evaluate reports for correctness and experimental support using the altered physical laws and exploration records. These records guide scene evolution for further exploration, allowing the full cycle to run without human intervention. Among 12 LLMs, GPT-6-Astra achieves a discovery rate of 16.7%, while the other 11 score 0%. The exploration records reveal uninvestigated anomalies and only partial identification of the altered physical laws.

Introduction Patients with pulmonary diseases face an elevated risk of osteoporosis. Conventional diagnosis relies on quantitative computed tomography (QCT), which delivers a high radiation dose and requires a dedicated scan. Whether conventional chest CT can be used for osteoporosis screening remains uncertain. Methods A deep learning system was used to measure bone mineral density (BMD) in routine chest CT scans for osteoporosis screening, with QCT as the reference standard. A total of 98 patients who underwent chest and abdominal CT due to medical conditions between August 2024 and March 2025 were analyzed. The BMD of the thoracic vertebrae (T1-T12) was measured, three consecutive vertebral bodies were grouped into averages, and the results were compared with the BMD of the lumbar vertebrae (L1-L3) measured by standard QCT. The differences and agreement between the two BMD measurement methods were compared, and the diagnostic performance for osteoporosis and low bone mass was assessed by receiver operating characteristic curve analysis. Results The cohort included 98 patients (48 female, 50 male; mean age 49.48 ± 14.64 years). AI-measured thoracic vertebrae BMD correlated highly with QCT BMD (r: 0.72-0.92), with the highest correlation observed for T10-T12 (r = 0.98, P < 0.001). All AI-BMD measurements demonstrated high diagnostic performance for osteoporosis and low bone mass. In the osteoporosis analysis,the T10-T12 BMD achieved the highest AUC of 0.998 (95% CI: 0.960-1.000), with an optimal diagnostic threshold of BMD ≤90.86 mg/cm³ (sensitivity 100.0%, specificity 97.6%). In the low-bone-mass analysis, the AUC was 0.990 (95% CI: 0.945-1.000). The volumetric CT dose index for QCT scans was significantly higher than that for chest CT scans (14.63 ± 2.30 vs. 4.13 ± 1.01 mGy, P < 0.001), and the post-processing time for QCT was significantly longer than that for the AI-based measurement (55.76 ± 9.05 vs. 7.50 ± 0.78 s, P < 0.001). Conclusion AI-based BMD measurements from chest CT correlate highly with QCT measurements. AI-derived thoracic BMD from routine chest CT may serve as a potential opportunistic screening-support tool for osteoporosis and low bone mass, but further validation in larger, multicenter, prospective cohorts is required before clinical adoption.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: Cannula detachment during intraocular surgery is an uncommon but potentially blinding complication. When it happens, attention commonly turns to whether the scrub practitioner tightened the connection adequately. This article explains why a well-made connection can still fail under hydraulic load once the junction has been lubricated, why incomplete tightening, where it occurs, is better understood as a foreseeable human factor than as an individual failing, why the cause cannot be established from the outcome alone and what theatre teams can do to reduce the risk and limit the harm.

Abstract Industry 5.0 reframes manufacturing around human-centricity, sustainability, and resilience, and a growing literature has developed intelligent assistance systems human-robot collaboration, AI-driven perception, digital twins, and extended-reality interfaces in pursuit of this aim. Whether this literature accommodates the heterogeneity of the workers it aims to center has not been systematically established. This review analyzes 14,346 Web of Science records (2016–2026, screened from 15,038 raw records across 19 export files, using an empirically validated Advanced Search query) addressing Industry 5.0 manufacturing. Bibliometric analysis confirms a technology-dominant field: robotics/cobots and AI/ML content appear in 51.9% and 26.8% of records respectively, while human-factors and interaction-modality content appear in 11.6% and 10.0%. A purposively verified subsample of 62 records 19 disability-explicit, 8 age-explicit, 4 cognitive/neurodiversity-explicit, and 31 addressing digital literacy or general capability accommodation was identified and hand-checked against the full corpus; despite this real and previously undercounted body of work, capability-diversity terms remain essentially absent from the field's dominant keyword co-occurrence structure (fewer than 3 co-occurrences for any disability-related pair, against 425 for the corpus's leading pair). This indicates a literature that exists but has not been synthesized, is rarely cross-cited, and remains disconnected from the mainstream human-centric Industry 5.0 discourse and its dominant AI-driven technology stack. We propose the Capability-Adaptive Intelligent Assistance Framework for Industry 5.0 (CAIA-5.0), connecting this scattered capability-accommodation literature to current AI-driven assistance mechanisms, with one extension profile-conditioned autonomy allocation explicitly flagged as untested. A six-item research agenda specifies the empirical, technological, and synthesis work required to connect this fragmented literature into a coherent, industrially applicable framework. The review offers manufacturing system designers, human-factors engineers, and policymakers a diagnostic basis and implementation roadmap for inclusive intelligent assistance.
topics: Assistive Technology in Communication and Mobility

documents.abstract: Abstract This case study examines the downfall of Pacific Heights University’s celebrated president, Dr. Samuel Whitaker, whose hidden gambling addiction led to the misappropriation of university funds and plunged the institution into crisis. Through detailed narrative and multi-perspective analysis, the study explores the interplay between personal vulnerability and organizational oversight in higher education. It traces Whitaker’s rise as a turnaround leader, his gradual descent into addiction, the discovery of financial misconduct, and the university’s efforts to restore trust and implement meaningful reforms. By synthesizing the institutional, personal, and societal dimensions of the crisis, the case offers vital lessons on ethical leadership, the necessity of robust controls, and the human factors that can undermine even the most trusted administrators. The narrative concludes with a unified reflection on recovery, accountability, and the enduring importance of vigilance in safeguarding institutional integrity.

PURPOSE: To systematically review all described approaches to cataract surgery in patients unable to lie supine and propose a clinical decision-making framework. CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Conditions precluding supine positioning include kyphosis, orthopnoea, and morbid obesity, which affect a substantial and growing proportion of patients requiring cataract surgery. No standardised guidance exists to direct surgical management in this population, representing a meaningful gap given that cataract surgery is the most cost-effective operation in medicine. METHODS: This systematic review underwent prospective PROSPERO registration (CRD420261288661). In accordance with PRISMA 2020 guidelines, we systematically searched and appraised all described approaches to completed cataract surgery in patients unable to recline for any reason across PubMed, Scopus, and EMBase on August 25th, 2025. Data were extracted regarding technique, equipment required, ergonomic considerations for surgeon and patient, and secondary outcomes including complications or position-specific challenges. Risk of bias was assessed using the Newcastle-Ottawa Quality Assessment Scale for case-control and cohort studies, and the Murad Tool for case series and case reports. RESULTS: Twenty-five studies were included, demonstrating three dominant approaches that have been utilized to perform cataract surgery in patients unable to lie supine: special positioning to facilitate a semi-recumbent position, surgery carried out with the surgeon standing, and positioning so that the surgeon and patient are face-to-face during surgery. There are only a few instances where conventional phacoemulsification has been performed under slit lamp microscopy in seated patients, presenting only limited data evaluating the safety of this practice. CONCLUSIONS: There are three distinct categories of approaching cataract surgery on patients unable to recline, which although still technically challenging, can increase the number of patients eligible to undergo cataract surgery in both developed and developing countries. We present a clinical decision framework proposed to guide approach selection based on mechanism of positional limitation, equipment availability, and case complexity.

This study examined how educational briefings about Artificial Intelligence (AI) hallucinations influence user trust, caution, and willingness to continue using AI systems. We recruited 51 participants through the online platform Prolific for an online questionnaire evaluating AI use and task-focused AI scenarios. After questions about trust and AI, participants read about common inaccuracies in Large Language Models. Participants showed a significant decrease in self-reported trust, indicating increased awareness of AI limitations. Contrary to expectations, perceptions of AI reliability and competence did not predict willingness to reuse AI in academic scenarios. Affective trust played a stronger role than cognitive trust, with perceived emotional support significantly predicting forgiveness of AI errors. Increased caution also predicted greater recalibration of trust, although willingness to continue using AI remained high. These findings suggest that educational interventions can promote calibrated trust in AI without discouraging continued use, highlighting the importance of transparency and context-sensitive design.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Students receive assessment deadlines inside course syllabi, usually as PDFs, and a growing number of tools use large language models (LLMs) to turn these documents into calendars. A common cost-saving design runs cheap rules first and calls the LLM only when the rules appear to fail. We test whether this saves money without losing accuracy. We compare five strategies on 16 public syllabi from eight institutions (151 hand-verified deadlines): regular-expression rules, a general-purpose date library, an LLM given the native PDF, an LLM given text extracted from the PDF, and a rule-first hybrid that calls the LLM only when the rules find fewer than three events. Each LLM strategy was run three times with gemini-3.1-flash-lite. The LLM strategies reached F1 scores of 0.708 (native PDF) and 0.657 (extracted text); the difference was not significant (p = 0.13), and the native-PDF input used fewer tokens with this model. The rule-first hybrid used 57.8% fewer tokens than the text-based LLM but lowered F1 to 0.370, a significant loss (p = 0.002). Rules alone scored 0.186, and 58% of their correctly placed month-day matches carried the wrong year. A sweep of the hybrid's routing threshold shows that every token saved cost accuracy. We release the code, labels, and all predictions.

Human performance often fails not because latent capacity is absent, but because access to high-functioning cognitive states is unstable under fatigue, distraction, overload, and pressure. This hypothesis paper proposes closed-loop cognitive state control—informally, supercognition —as a neuroengineering objective: rapid entry into, stabilization of, and recovery of an individual's highest available task-specific cognitive state. The framework treats cognition as a partially observable dynamical system whose latent states would be inferred from multimodal behavioral, physiological, contextual, and neural signals, and specifies a five-layer architecture comprising multimodal sensing, latent-state inference, predictive transition modeling, closed-loop intervention, and a longitudinal personal neural twin. The proposal is situated against existing closed-loop and neuroadaptive architectures, with an explicit statement of what is and is not new. The state ontology is given as a set of falsifiable assumptions rather than an intuitive taxonomy. Candidate computational implementations are specified for each layer, including hidden semi-Markov and switching state-space models, Bayesian and Kalman filtering, sequence models, hazard models, contextual bandits, model-predictive control, and offline reinforcement learning. The personal neural twin receives an operational specification covering its data requirements, update schedule, calibration and drift-monitoring criteria, and failure modes. Predictive and causal claims are separated, with the evidentiary requirements stated for each. The paper engages directly with the literature that challenges the framework's feasibility, including biomarker reliability, mixed neurofeedback findings, cross-task and cross-subject generalization failure, and the ecological-validity gap in wearable neurotechnology. Operational definitions, application scenarios, a validation protocol with power and diversity requirements, an expanded ethics and governance analysis, and a staged research roadmap are provided. No component of the architecture has been implemented or evaluated here: no simulation, clinical trial, or empirical efficacy claim is presented, and the validation programme described is prospective. The contribution is a falsifiable systems-engineering hypothesis for cognitive-state control.

topics: Intelligent Tutoring Systems and Adaptive Learning

documents.abstract: Claims about the cognitive capabilities of large language models are typically tested by translating behavioral paradigms into text prompts, bypassing the visual interfaces and time pressure through which human participants actually engage with experiments. At the same time, AI agents can now complete online behavioral tasks and produce human-like data, which raises concerns that online datasets in the social and behavioral sciences are increasingly open to contamination. We introduce CogArena, a benchmark of ten experimental paradigms from the social and behavioral sciences. Agents complete the experiments through a standard web browser, working with the same visual stimuli and response interfaces that online participants use. A three-level scoring procedure evaluates whether the agent completed the task, how accurately it performed, and whether its data show the behavioral signatures each paradigm reliably produces in people. Across four multimodal models, each run ten times per task, we find that finishing an experiment and reproducing its signatures are different things. Many sessions did not finish, and those that did reproduced some signatures reliably and others not at all. CogArena provides the tasks, scoring code, and a public leaderboard for new submissions.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents interact with their environments through executable harnesses that govern tool use and feedback. Optimizing a harness for a fixed policy overlooks how its behavior changes during learning, while training a policy under a fixed harness leaves the interface that generates its training experience unchanged. This motivates adapting the harness throughout policy training. We introduce CoHARL, a population-based reinforcement learning framework that co-evolves a shared policy and a population of executable harnesses. The policy learns from rollouts across the population, and a proposer uses its execution traces to revise harness code during training. CoHARL achieves a 27.6% mean resolved rate on SWE-rebench, improving over harness-only search by 6.4 percentage points. Experiments on SWE-bench Verified and Terminal-Bench 2.0 show gains in software engineering and terminal-based tasks. Under matched training budgets, CoHARL also outperforms searching for a harness once before RL and alternating policy updates with revisions to a single active harness.

Abstract Causality extraction—the identification of cause–effect relations in natural language text—has been approached through three successive methodological paradigms: rule-based systems relying on lexical and syntactic cues, deep learning models exploiting neural architectures and pre-trained encoders, and, most recently, large language models (LLMs) applied through prompting or fine-tuning. Each paradigm has been evaluated on different datasets, under different annotation schemes, and with different metrics, making it difficult to determine how far apparent performance differences reflect genuine methodological advantages rather than benchmark artifacts. This study addresses that problem by constructing a unified benchmark for comparative evaluation of rule-based, deep learning, and LLM approaches to causality extraction. We consolidate multiple existing corpora—covering news, biomedical, and safety-incident text—into a harmonized annotation format, re-annotate a stratified subset to ensure consistent treatment of implicit and explicit causal relations, and evaluate representative methods from each paradigm under identical preprocessing, train–test splits, and evaluation protocols. We report span-level precision, recall, and F1, document-level F1, calibration error, inference cost, and annotation efficiency, and we conduct cross-domain transfer experiments to assess generalization. Results are analyzed to disentangle the contributions of architecture, training data, and task formulation, with particular attention to the conditions under which each paradigm retains a comparative advantage. We further examine error profiles across paradigms, identifying whether failures are concentrated in explicit versus implicit relations, local versus distributed constructions, and domain-specific versus general-language contexts.

The rapid integration of generative AI tools into spoken English instruction has produced measurable fluency and accuracy gains, but whether these are evenly distributed across the dimensions of communicative competence remains underexplored.
