This quasi-experimental study compares the Spiral Synergy Framework (SSF), a three-layer pedagogical sequence (AI Consolidation, Bridging Tasks, Interpersonal Activation), against conventional AI-integrated instruction in two intact Business English classes at a Chinese higher vocational college (experimental n = 36, control n = 34), using oral recordings at three time points scored on five competence dimensions, 15 weeks of classroom observation, and an intra-rater reliability check. The two classes differed significantly at baseline on the oral composite score and three of five dimensions (control higher), though not on CET-4 proficiency or questionnaire items. Because treatment is confounded with class membership and both classes received AI-assisted practice, findings are reported as associations rather than demonstrated causal effects. Linear mixed-effects models testing Group × Time interactions across five outcomes (four dimensions and the composite), corrected for multiple comparisons, identified one outcome - real-time responsiveness - on which the classes diverged: the experimental class maintained responsiveness across the semester while the control class declined despite its baseline advantage (Benjamini-Hochberg-adjusted p = .029), a result that held under a cluster-robust sensitivity check. No corrected between-group difference was found for improvisation, coherence, naturalness, or the composite score; improvisation declined descriptively in both classes over the semester. Classroom observation data (experimental class only) document a recurring, non-monotonic cycle of AI-dependency reduction and rebound across 15 weeks. Intra-rater test-retest reliability of the oral-competence ratings was moderate to good (ICC = .67-.91), though this reflects a single rater familiar with participants rather than independent inter-rater agreement. Implications for multidimensional assessment, task sequencing, and cautious interpretation of AI-integrated curriculum research are discussed.

Agents built on large language models are increasingly allowed to take consequential actions: cancelling bookings, issuing refunds, changing accounts. The rules that govern those actions, such as "obtain the customer's explicit confirmation before changing anything", are usually stated in the prompt and followed only as reliably as the model chooses to follow them. We present Concordat, a Python library that treats an agent as an object whose interface is a finite-state protocol, in the spirit of typestate and session types, and enforces that protocol on the model at run time. On every turn the model is offered only the tools that are legal in the current protocol state, calls outside that set are rejected before they have side effects, decisions reserved for humans can only be requested, and token and tool-call budgets are charged and split linearly across handoffs. Protocols are checked when they are defined, and a subclass of an agent is rejected if it could bypass its parent's protocol, a behavioural form of Liskov substitution. We evaluate a Concordat agent against the standard agent of tau-bench on its 50 airline tasks, adding simulated customers who pressure the agent to skip confirmation. The standard agent made changes without the required "yes" in 13 of 50 tasks with gpt-4.1 and in 29 of 128 task-runs with Claude Haiku 5.5; the Concordat agent made none, with no significant difference in task success. tau-bench's own reward did not detect most of these violations. Concordat is open source.

When a Large Language Model (LLM) is trained with Reinforcement Learning (RL) on multiple tasks, a task's primary reward can gate auxiliary rewards such as a length reward: on a failing response, an auxiliary cannot exceed the primary. However, group-relative advantage estimators treat a gated auxiliary like any other component, so it can reverse the primary's order, and at the primary's ceiling only auxiliaries order responses. Keeping gated auxiliaries hurts some tasks, while dropping them hurts others. We propose CONCUR, an advantage estimator that replaces the standardized scores of each gated auxiliary with the closest scores that satisfy two conditions: responses with higher primary rewards cannot receive lower scores, and responses at the primary's ceiling receive equal scores. CONCUR-T applies both conditions throughout training, and CONCUR-A lifts the second for an auxiliary that agrees with the primary's order more often than it reverses it among passing responses. On three models from two families and across math, code, instruction following, and writing, both variants score higher on average than all baselines and than when all the gated auxiliaries are dropped.

How do broader values shape whether people judge artificial intelligence (AI) as good or bad for humanity? This article analyzes provisional World Values Survey Wave 8 data from 40,960 respondents in 24 country samples using pooled and national prediction models, outcome-independent respondent profiles, and groups of countries. The analysis reveals a cross-country anchor: general optimism about science and technology is the strongest pooled predictor of favorable AI evaluation and recurs among the leading predictors in every national sample. Expert authority, education and information access, selected forms of trust, openness, and demographic position provide nationally distinctive patterns. Eleven value profiles formed without AI attitudes span 49.1% to 62.2% favorable evaluation. Most evaluative variation occurs within these profiles, making them useful contexts for identifying how the same values distinguish favorable from unfavorable evaluators in different social configurations. Institutional legitimacy, structural advantage, information connectedness, personal choice, redistribution, and openness differentiate evaluations in particular profiles. The same axis can relate differently to AI evaluation across profiles: secular reasoning has a significant positive association among secular moderate pluralists but a suggestive negative association among institution-trusting civic joiners. Together, the findings show that public receptivity to AI as technological change has a common predictive anchor but develops within plural configurations of resources, institutions, authority, openness, and social position. This distinction helps anticipate where generalized technological optimism is likely to travel and where AI deployment and governance will encounter context-specific sources of legitimacy or concern.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Prefill and decode are complementary in resource usage, but often divergent in parallelism preferences. Executing the two phases separately preserves their preferred parallelism but leaves complementary resources underutilized, while co-batching improves utilization but often requires a uniform parallel configuration that hurts execution efficiency. To resolve this utilization-efficiency dilemma, we propose Conflux Parallelism (XP), a parallel execution abstraction that co-executes prefill and decode with different parallelism within the same batch. Conflux Parallelism exploits operator-level Transformer structure to construct a heterogeneous execution path with different batching and parallelism strategies across operators, combining the best of co-batching and phase-specific execution. Building on Conflux Parallelism, we design ConfluxServe, an SLO-aware serving system that maximizes cluster goodput under TTFT and TBT constraints. Evaluation on production workloads shows that ConfluxServe improves serving goodput by 1.26-1.62x over the strongest baselines.

LLM agents that answer questions and act on behalf of users must decide when to yield to a user who disagrees. Disagreement may correct a genuine error or may be an attempt at manipulation. Prior work shows that models frequently abandon correct answers when challenged by users, yet it remains unclear whether they distinguish correction from manipulation or merely differ in their propensity to concede. We examine this question across seven LLMs from four vendors in two studies, one on the answers agents give and one on the actions they take as customer-support agents whose policy permits account changes only for verified users. Simulated users push toward correct and incorrect answers with graded pressure. Following research on epistemic vigilance, the pressure either appeals to the source, such as claimed authority, or offers content the agent cannot verify, namely a cited source. Drawing on signal detection theory, we measure on a set of benchmark questions how much more readily each agent concedes to correction than to manipulation, separately from its overall propensity to concede. Citations made five of seven models readier to concede and four worse at discriminating, while stronger wording added little. In the agentic study, five models never violated the verification policy, including models that readily abandoned correct answers, so concession on answers did not predict violations of policy. Ministral 3B violated the policy mainly under claimed authority, and Ministral 8B reported changes it had not made. An instruction to revise only on verifiable evidence chiefly shifted propensity to concede rather than improving discrimination. Concession rates alone are therefore misleading, and agents should be evaluated on both their discrimination and the actions they take.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Coverage-evaluation benchmarks quantify whether retrieved evidence covers the different pieces of information needed to satisfy an information need. Existing benchmarks mostly consider factual claims that may already be known to pretrained retrieval components, leaving open whether retrievers find corpus evidence when it contradicts those priors. We study how retrievers behave when their parametric knowledge and the information in a corpus disagree. To do so, we develop a process to augment a nugget-based coverage benchmark with controlled contradictions. For each nugget, we create a negated counterpart and edit its supporting documents to support that negation while preserving the context. Applying this process to CoverageBench, a benchmark measuring information coverage, we create CoverageBench-Negate, spanning six datasets and roughly 63,000 original-edited evidence pairs (one per nugget-document link). We attach rich construction metadata to every pair and additionally provide out-of-family LLM judgments over all pairs and a human audit of a sample. In baseline experiments, BM25 separates original from edited near-twin evidence substantially better than dense retrievers (Qwen3 and Jina), which stay near chance. We release the benchmark on Hugging Face Datasets (nuggets, documents, pairs) together with the construction materials, including the prompts used to create it.

Recent race incidents in professional road cycling have renewed concerns regarding rider safety, with multiple high-proﬁle crashes resulting in severe or long-term injuries. Data from ProCyclingStats show an increased frequency in reported rider injuries over the past years1. These trends coincide with rising average race speeds, denser peloton dynamics, and increasingly complex road infrastructures, all of which contribute to elevated crash risk and more serious injury outcomes. As a result, the demand for eﬀective technological solutions that support real-time monitoring, rapid incident detection, and coordinated race response has intensiﬁed. In response, several safety tracking and race monitoring systems have been introduced in recent years, aiming to improve situational awareness for race organizers and enhance post-incident response times. However, despite notable technological progress, the current ecosystem of cycling safety trackers presents signiﬁcant limitations that hinder widespread adoption and operational eﬀectiveness. This abstract outlines the current landscape of safety tracking technologies in cycling, highlighting technical challenges, deployment constraints, and gaps relative to the practical demands of race environments. One of the primary challenges is coverage reliability. Professional cycling races frequently traverse remote, rural, or mountainous regions where cellular connectivity is unstable or absent. Continuous, low-latency data transmission remains diﬃcult to guarantee in such environments, limiting the eﬀectiveness of real-time monitoring and automated alerting systems. Closely related is the issue of reliable crash or event detection. Many existing race monitoring solutions including systems developed by Live Insiders, 3BO, Swiss Timing and GeoDynamics prioritize rider positioning and performance-related data . While valuable for race management and broadcast applications, these systems are not primarily designed for robust incident detection, often relying on indirect indicators such as abrupt speed changes or signal loss, which can generate false positives or missed events. Hardware design represents another critical consideration. Safety tracking devices must be unobtrusive, lightweight, and ergonomically integrated into existing equipment to avoid interfering with rider performance or comfort. Feedback from professional riders has consistently emphasized the importance of minimizing additional physical or cognitive burden during competition. Pilot testing conducted in collaboration with teams such as Soudal-Quick-Step underscored the necessity of incorporating cyclist feedback early in the design and validation process, particularly with regard to wearability, device placement, and perceived intrusiveness. Finally, technical and operational requirements from race organizers play a decisive role in system viability. Solutions must integrate seamlessly with existing race infrastructure, comply with regulatory constraints, and oﬀer clear value in terms of safety decision-making and emergency response coordination. Without standardized requirements and interoperable frameworks, the deployment of safety tracking technologies risks remaining fragmented and inconsistent across events. In conclusion, while current safety tracking and race monitoring devices represent an important step toward improving rider safety in professional cycling, substantial gaps remain in coverage reliability, incident detection accuracy, hardware integration, and organizational alignment. Addressing these challenges will be essential to realizing the full potential of in-race safety technologies and reducing the human cost of competitive cycling.
topics: IoT and GPS-based Vehicle Safety Systems

documents.abstract: We propose a source-grounded framework for representing and measuring mathematical arguments with assistance from large language models. It includes numbered and unnumbered statements, equations, assumptions, and constructions, distinguishing source occurrences from contextual states and inference records. Proposed dependencies retain source evidence and review status. A measurement contract fixes manuscript versions, boundaries, granularity, proof choices, and macro anchors. On a selected finite directed acyclic graph, depth is the longest prerequisite-path length, and bulk counts distinct ancestor edges. We give a union recurrence that accounts for shared subarguments and identify reachability conditions preserving depth and the macro skeleton; unrestricted refinement need not preserve depth or bulk. A standardized, versioned prompt protocol separates annotation discovery, deterministic recomputation, and review assistance. Cross-paper links support a research agenda on theorem co-use, rare combinations, and connections between dependency communities. These patterns motivate probabilistic premise suggestions and review of possible omissions or unchecked application conditions in human-written and AI-generated proofs. Further applications include source-linked reading support and comparison of individual and collaborative argument shapes. We provide an evaluation design rather than empirical evidence of these benefits. Suggested premises require mathematical validation, and the measures describe a specified representation rather than intrinsic mathematical difficulty, originality, or importance.

Tracheal auscultation is recommended by clinical practice guidelines, and required by some U.S. state regulations, for monitoring ventilation during procedural sedation and monitored anesthesia care. However, continuous auscultation with a conventional stethoscope is impractical, susceptible to ambient noise, and difficult to interpret. We developed the Artificial Intelligence Respiratory MOnitoring Device (Airmod), an FDA-cleared software as a medical device (510(k) K242798) that continuously monitors tracheal sounds and estimates breath-to-breath respiratory rate in real time. In this paper, we describe its software architecture and key processing modules. Ambient noise is suppressed by active noise control, using a normalized least-mean-square adaptive filter with a dual-microphone electronic stethoscope. A multiclass convolutional bidirectional gated recurrent unit (CNN-BiGRU) model detects inhalations and exhalations in 15-s inference windows. It was trained on HF_Tracheal_V2, a new database of 373 continuous tracheal sound recordings (8,521 min; 107,644 labeled inhalations) from 369 subjects under sedation. To handle continuous acoustic streaming, Airmod runs inference on overlapping 15-s windows. It refines the detected inhalations by removing incomplete events, low-energy false positives, and double counts, concatenates them into a history list, and estimates respiratory rate from the mean period of the last three breaths. On the test set, at the default 2-s prediction interval with refinement enabled, inhalation detection achieved a sensitivity of 0.828, a positive predictive value of 0.832, and an F1-score of 0.830. Airmod also broadcasts the noise-cancelled tracheal sound and displays a real-time spectrogram to help clinicians recognize respiratory abnormalities.

Loneliness in later life is common and harmful, yet interventions show modest, heterogeneous effects, partly because services are designed without explicit user requirements. We conducted a cross-sectional mixed-methods study to derive design requirements for mHealth-based loneliness support. Twenty-seven smartphone-using older adults in Hong Kong (aged 60–78) who screened positive for elevated loneliness completed standardized measures and semi-structured interviews. Participants reported high loneliness (UCLA Loneliness Scale version 3: mean 51.3, SD 9.3) and constrained social networks (63.0% below the LSNS-6 cutpoint of 12). Their accounts distinguished solitude, emotional loneliness even in company, and fear that no one could help in time; engagement was shaped by self-reliance, channel fit, and scam-related distrust. We derived six design requirements: recognizable, verifiable contact; hybrid delivery; human-in-the-loop support; low-burden, Cantonese-first usability; privacy as a baseline; and engagement fit. These requirements inform the design of mHealth-based loneliness support, including conversational interfaces.

Post-disaster education is frequently disrupted not only by learning loss but also by unstable connectivity, limited devices, temporary learning spaces, and uneven access to teachers. This study aimed to design and conduct an initial simulation-based evaluation of an AI-supported adaptive English literacy learning model for primary-school education recovery. A Design and Development Research approach was employed. Needs were synthesized from secondary sources, policy documents, and recent research on education in emergencies, adaptive learning, and artificial intelligence in language education. The resulting dual-context model combines learner conditions (diagnostic performance, learning gap, pace, and progress) with disaster learning-environment conditions (connectivity, device availability, and learning access). A lightweight web prototype, Sahabat Belajar Adaptif, was developed to operationalize the model through learner profiling, diagnostic assessment, explainable rule-based recommendations, teacher review, adaptive learning content, formative assessment, and progress monitoring. Scenario-based simulation was organized across three recovery levels—Intensive, Guided, and Independent—and three access conditions—Connected, Limited Connectivity, and No Connectivity. The simulations showed that academic parameters consistently determined recovery level and content difficulty, while access parameters determined delivery mode through digital, semi-digital/offline, or manual learning pathways. The teacher-in-the-loop mechanism enabled recommendations to be accepted, modified, or overridden, preserving pedagogical control. Functional simulation also confirmed that the prototype could represent the full assessment–recommendation–learning–evaluation–readaptation cycle. The study contributes a context-sensitive model for adaptive English literacy learning in disrupted educational settings. Because the present evaluation relies on secondary data and synthetic scenarios rather than direct learner-effectiveness testing, future research should validate the model with teachers and primary-school learners in disaster-affected settings.
topics: Intelligent Tutoring Systems and Adaptive Learning

documents.abstract: Large language model (LLM)-driven agents are emerging as a powerful new paradigm for solving complex problems. Despite the empirical success of these practices, a theoretical framework to understand and unify their macroscopic dynamics remains lacking. This paper proposes a method based on the least action principle to estimate the underlying generative directionality of LLMs embedded within agents. By experimentally measuring the transition probabilities between LLM-generated states, we report evidence consistent with a tendency toward detailed balance in LLM-generated transitions, indicating that LLM generation may not be achieved by generally learning rule sets and strategies, but rather by implicitly learning a class of underlying potential functions that may transcend different LLM architectures and prompt templates. To our knowledge, this provides an effective macroscopic description of LLM generative dynamics that does not depend on specific model details. This work is an attempt to establish a macroscopic dynamics theory of complex AI systems, aiming to elevate the study of AI agents from a collection of engineering practices to a science built on effective measurements that are predictable and quantifiable.

Modern space systems are increasingly interconnected, software-driven, and dependent on satellite constellations, significantly expanding the cyber threat surface. This chapter examines cybersecurity detection, threat intelligence, and incident response in space environments, focusing on the unique operational constraints of satellites and ground infrastructure, including limited onboard resources, communication delays, and autonomous operations. It explores approaches for anomaly and intrusion detection across satellites, ground stations, and inter-satellite networks, including the use of artificial intelligence and behavioural analytics. The chapter also discusses the role of cyber threat intelligence in improving situational awareness, threat attribution, and proactive defence. Incident response strategies tailored to space systems are analysed, with emphasis on resilience, recovery, and coordination between space and terrestrial infrastructures. Finally, the chapter highlights emerging threats, operational challenges, and future research directions for securing next-generation space communication ecosystems.

Maritime Autonomous Surface Ships (MASS) are increasingly enabled by advances in automation, autonomy, network connectivity and shoreside support systems. These technologies create opportunities to offload tasks to Remote Operating Centers (ROCs), reduce and/or remove onboard crew, thus facilitating a wide variety of approaches for how ships are controlled and monitored in comparison to traditional shipping. This paper details a design case study of an ROC for an 8-meter diesel-electric uncrewed and autonomous-capable test ship operating in North Atlantic Canadian waters. A series of user-centered workshops and design iterations were implemented to redesign and refine the ROC physical work environment and Human-Machine Interfaces to better align with the goals and demands of shoreside operators. This work provides methodological and design contributions to MASS ROC development, while also creating a foundation for human-performance testing involving ROC operators and autonomous surface ships for the next phases of research and development.

BACKGROUND: Newly employed nurses entering the ambulance service face clinical, organisational and cultural challenges. Although transition-related support needs have been described, less is known about how such knowledge can be translated into organisationally feasible introductory training programmes. AIM: To explore how organisational and pedagogical challenges in introductory training for newly employed nurses were identified, interpreted, negotiated and translated into a revised programme through participatory action research (PAR). METHODS: A qualitative PAR design was conducted between 2020 and 2024 in one Swedish ambulance service organisation. Newly employed nurses, clinical supervisors, the management group (total duration 2 h and 14 min) and the research group contributed at different phases and levels of participation. The primary analytic material comprised two video-recorded management group meetings, field notes, and researcher reflections. Previously analysed interview, focus group and questionnaire findings were integrated as experiential and evaluative material. Narrative process analysis reconstructed how identified challenges were interpreted, negotiated, and translated into programme interventions, and how these were reconsidered following implementation. RESULTS: Four interrelated challenges were consolidated: a theory-heavy programme structure, variation in supervision, limited leadership connection and role ambiguity. Organisational interpretation and negotiation translated these into three interconnected interventions: restructuring theory and practice, preparing selected clinical supervisors and integrating peer learning during clinical placement, with leadership connection and role clarification embedded across the programme. Reflection on implementation indicated that theory-practice integration, supervision, leadership and peer learning were interdependent and required continued organisational and pedagogical support. CONCLUSION: PAR provided a structured process for moving from empirical knowledge about professional transition to organisationally embedded and contextually feasible programme development. Supporting newly employed nurses requires alignment between programme design, supervision, leadership and workplace learning. REGISTRATION: Not registered.

The article examines the impact of information and communication technologies (ICT) on the development of mathematical abilities and geometric concepts in preschool children. The object of the research is the process of developing mathematical abilities and geometric concepts in older preschool children. The aim of the article is to identify the pedagogical potential of ICT and evaluate its effectiveness in developing these abilities. The research methods include the analysis of scientific and methodological literature, pedagogical observation, game-based learning, pedagogical experimentation, and comparative analysis of the results. Multimedia presentations, interactive games, and electronic educational resources were used during the experimental activities. The methodologies of ICT-mediated learning and game-based learning were applied. The research outcomes indicate that the purposeful use of ICT contributes to the development of children's abilities to recognize, name, compare, and classify geometric shapes. It also promotes children's cognitive engagement, logical and spatial thinking, attention, and memory. The experimental results further revealed increased children's engagement and learning motivation. The conclusion of the study is that the pedagogically justified integration of information and communication technologies into game-based learning is an effective means of developing mathematical abilities and geometric concepts in preschool children, facilitating a more visual, interactive, and child-centered learning process.

This project aims to systematically review existing research on the use of dialogue analysis for the early identification of students at risk for emotional and behavioral difficulties and the development of tailored, integrated support strategies. Emotional and behavioral difficulties among children and adolescents can negatively affect psychological well-being, academic performance, interpersonal relationships, and school adjustment. Early identification and timely intervention are therefore essential. Conventional screening approaches often rely on standardized questionnaires, self-reported symptoms, teacher observations, and periodic psychological assessments. Recent advances in artificial intelligence (AI), particularly machine learning and natural language processing (NLP), have created new opportunities to identify psychological and behavioral indicators from linguistic and conversational data. This systematic review will examine how dialogue-based approaches, including counseling conversations, interviews, written communication, and digital interactions, have been used to identify emotional and behavioral difficulties among school-aged children and adolescents. Particular attention will be given to the types of dialogue data analyzed, computational and analytical methods employed, psychological and behavioral indicators identified, and the reported effectiveness of these approaches. The review will also investigate how findings from dialogue analysis may inform individualized interventions, school-based mental health services, and integrated support systems involving teachers, counselors, families, and mental health professionals. Relevant studies will be identified through a systematic literature search, screened according to predefined eligibility criteria, and synthesized using an appropriate evidence synthesis approach. The review process will be guided by the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA 2020) guidelines. The expected outcomes include a comprehensive synthesis of current evidence, identification of methodological strengths and limitations, and recommendations for future research and practice. Ultimately, this review seeks to provide an evidence-based foundation for developing dialogue-informed early screening approaches and tailored, integrated support systems for students experiencing emotional and behavioral difficulties.
topics: Child and Adolescent Psychosocial and Emotional Development

documents.abstract: Abstract Background Malnutrition remains a major public health challenge in Madagascar, affecting nearly two out of five children under five years of age. Research on child nutrition provides nationally representative data on child health, anthropometry, dietary diversity, and feeding practices. This study provides updated, quantitative assessments of total energy and nutrient intake among preschool children, with a detailed analysis of daily dietary composition. In addition, particular attention has been given to the contribution of snacks to children's daily diets. Methods Cross-sectional dietary data were collected from 253 children aged 3 to 6 years via the 24-hour dietary recall method. This approach allowed for the estimation of the types and quantities of foods consumed by participants during the 24 hours preceding the survey. The nutritional value of foods was estimated via data from the CIQUAL food composition table (French Agency for Food, Environmental and Occupational Health & Safety), which is supported by relevant literature. Data processing was conducted via R statistical software version 4.5.1 (2025-06-13, UCRT). Results The median energy intake was 1061 kcal (95% CI: 1003—1122). On average, carbohydrates provided 69% of the total energy, with protein and fat contributing 12% and 15%, respectively. The mean dietary diversity score was 4.49 ± 1.20, reflecting a high consumption of cereals and starchy foods (99.6%) and a low intake of dairy products (4.7%). Nearly all the children (98%) consumed three meals per day—breakfast, lunch, and dinner—while 2% skipped dinner. Snacking was common, with 98% of the children consuming at least one snack daily. Among those who snack, 25% did so only in the morning, whereas 4% had snacks exclusively in the afternoon. Conclusions Despite the consumption of meals and snacks, the nutritional and energy intake of the children aged 3–6 years remains below the recommended requirements for this age group, indicating a risk of nutrient deficiencies. Snacks play a significant role in children's diets and represent a valuable opportunity to increase the nutritional quality of their diet by contributing to energy intake and supplementing essential nutrient requirements.

The increasing integration of digital technologies into pharmacy education has transformed how students learn, communicate, and develop professional competencies. However, prolonged engagement with digital platforms may contribute to digital fatigue, technostress, cognitive overload, sleep disruption, and reduced well-being. Although digital fatigue has primarily been considered a learner wellness concern, its potential implications may extend to workforce readiness and medication safety. Cognitive functions affected by fatigue and information overload, including attention, vigilance, working memory, information synthesis, and clinical judgment, are also essential for safe medication use and effective pharmacy practice. This commentary applies a systems and human factors perspective to examine digital fatigue as an emerging consideration in pharmacy education and workforce development. Using principles aligned with the Systems Engineering Initiative for Patient Safety (SEIPS) framework, we highlight potential pathways through which digitally intensive learning environments may influence cognitive performance and preparedness for technology-enabled pharmacy practice. Systems-based strategies are proposed, including intentional digital curriculum design, digital well-being and resilience training, human-centered technology design, sleep and fatigue prevention, and simulation focused on cognitive load management. As pharmacy education continues to evolve alongside technological innovation, greater attention to digital well-being may help prepare pharmacists to practice safely, effectively, and sustainably within increasingly technology-intensive healthcare environments.

Paper-based personal protective equipment (PPE) custody documentation remains widespread in Turkish small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) and public institutions despite traceability obligations under the Occupational Health and Safety (OHS) Law No. 6331, generating recordretention vulnerabilities and audit liability risks. Adopting a Design Science Research (DSR) framework, this study presents a web-based PPE digital custody artifact evaluated against three legislatively grounded design criteria: audit integrity (C1), regulatory compatibility (C2), and institutional adoptability (C3). The artifact operationalizes Walsh and Ungson’s organizational memory framework, transferring custody records from individual-dependent and physically vulnerable repositories to a relational database, markedly reducing staff-departure and archive-destruction failure modes. Indicative process measurements (n=15 digital transactions against an n=3 paper baseline) yield reductions of approximately 87% in record generation time and 94% in archive retrieval time, pending larger-sample replication. Normative legal analysis establishes that Canvas-based handwritten signatures constitute a simple electronic signature recognized under EU eIDAS, US ESIGN/UETA, and Turkish Law No. 5070. Although not a qualified-signature equivalent, the composite audit trail can serve as an evidentiary record where public key infrastructure (PKI) is absent, subject to judicial determination. Twelve role-based access control (RBAC) functional test cases confirm that the hierarchical architecture enforces the separation of duties required by Law No. 6331. The findings provide a replicable artifact specification and a DSR evaluation template for the OHS management information system (OHS-MIS) deployment in resource-constrained settings.
topics: Occupational Health and Safety in Workplaces

documents.abstract: Abstract Addressing the climate crisis is going to require behavioral change in many aspects of daily life. A growing literature suggests the promise of “warm glow” messaging that features the pleasure and satisfaction one experiences from acting sustainably. Yet previous research has relied almost exclusively on self‐reported behavioral intentions, leaving open whether such appeals meaningfully affect real‐world, costly choices. We partnered with a local organization to conduct a field experiment on energy choices in Hanover, New Hampshire. Using a randomized roll‐out design in early 2025, we systematically varied the timing of postcard mailers that contain a warm glow message encouraging customers to increase the renewable content of their energy option. Analyses of administrative data on consumer energy choices reveal that warm glow messages delivered in a field setting have a null effect on adoption of higher‐renewable power choices, with a small number of customers changing to the greener but more costly option. Our study provides novel behavioral evidence on the real‐world impact of intrinsic motivation appeals in the climate domain.

A major challenge facing AI scientific discovery pipelines is how to determine when a generated idea is meaningfully novel. Ideally, novelty checks in these pipelines must be able to reject non-novel ideas while not rejecting too many novel ideas, and they should also be able to distinguish which parts of a proposal are non-novel, as opposed to opaquely discarding entire proposals. We design an analytical framework for evaluation of novelty checks with temporal ground truth at both the proposal- and claim-level, using four datasets of 1,060 proposals built from published papers, reviewer disputes, and generated ideas matching ones the field went on to publish. Auditing existing novelty checks with this framework, we find that checks with high rejection rates on non-novel work also tend to have high false alarms on ideas that are later realized by human researchers, and observe that checks built to evaluate proposals as a whole can point to claim-level prior art only by rejecting the whole proposal. We therefore introduce ClaimNov, a fine-grained, interpretable claim-level novelty module. ClaimNov catches 97% of disguised papers at a 1.5% false-alarm rate, and its claim-level novelty profile cuts the LLM judge's false alarms from 11.8% to 1.5%. Because its verdict rests on claim-level evidence, ClaimNov also keeps proposals that build on established contributions, rejecting only 3% of ICLR-accepted proposals with a reviewer-disputed contribution and keeping 91 of 100 novel proposals with one spliced prior contribution, against 76 for the strongest existing check. Code and data are available at https://github.com/emmatliu/claimnov.

Objective This study explores whether consumer education (CE) with and without driver responsibility content improves drivers’ understanding and use of Advanced Driver-Assistance Systems (ADAS). Background Research suggests that CE with responsibility content may improve driver understanding; however, how other forms of learning interact, such as experiential learning, remains unclear. Method Eighty drivers (21–76 years) participated in a CE study using a Traffic Jam Assist ADAS. The study was conducted as a 2 (CE content: CE with responsibility content and CE without responsibility content) x 2 (driver engagement instructions: hands-free and hands-on) x 3 (timing of mental model assessment (MMA): pre-CE, post-CE, and post-drive). Results CE with responsibility content did not significantly enhance MMA understanding or confidence beyond CE without responsibility content in this study ( p > .05). Regardless of responsibility content, drivers who received hands-on instructions consistently scored higher compared to hands-free instructions ( p < .01). MMA confidence rating decreased at post-CE for all conditions but only returned to baseline levels at post-drive ( p < .05) for drivers who received hands-free instructions. Conclusion Drivers who received hands-on instructions scored higher than hands-free at all; however, other forms of learning (e.g., experiential learning) may be necessary when the system substantially changes the driver’s role. Application CE may be enough to improve drivers’ understanding if an update does not alter how a driver interacts with the system, or how it aligns with their initial mental model.

Quadratic approximations provide a common lens for studying neural network optimization, but recent evidence challenges their predictive validity. In full-batch gradient descent with learning rate (LR) $η$, Cohen et al. (2021) observed the Edge of Stability (EoS), where the largest Hessian eigenvalue concentrates near $2/η$, seemingly at odds with classical stability conditions predicted by quadratic approximations. In this work, we revisit the fidelity of quadratic approximations as a model of neural network training dynamics, with a particular focus on their failure modes in LLM training. We first highlight a distinct failure mode of the quadratic approximation, where persistent negative curvature causes the quadratic dynamics to diverge regardless of the LR, even though the real dynamics remain stable. We term this phenomenon the Edge of Convexity (EoC). After removing the effect of this LR-independent instability, we then propose a generalized definition of Edge of Stability (EoS) for stochastic training with adaptive optimizers, based on whether increasing the LR induces significant divergence in the quadratic dynamics while leaving the real dynamics largely unchanged. Across different LLM pretraining runs with various model sizes up to 787M, we find that (1) EoC is always observed across LLM pretraining, and (2) EoS is also prevalent but not universal: it disappears when the LR becomes sufficiently small (e.g., after decay) or when the batch size falls below a critical threshold that has a positive correlation with the critical batch size. Together, these findings characterize when and how quadratic approximations fail and provide a foundation for future work on understanding training dynamics.

Prior research suggests that vehicles with longer-wavelength or lighter colors are associated with faster perceived speeds compared to shorter-wavelength or darker colors, but TTC estimates were not measured. In the current study, participants viewed a simulated traffic scene in which a red or blue vehicle approached for 3 s and disappeared. Participants pressed a button when they believed the vehicle would reach their position. Red vehicles were judged to arrive sooner (TTC was underestimated) than blue vehicles (TTC was overestimated), but only when TTC was 4 s. Results suggest that vehicle color may be used as a heuristic cue to judge TTC when cognitive motion extrapolation demands are putatively higher.

topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) is increasingly being integrated into higher education, offering potential gains in efficiency and quality, yet there are concerns about its cognitive and behavioral consequences. This study surveyed 633 university students in Benin to examine factors associated with GenAI use and its academic, behavioral and psychological outcomes. Drawing on the Expectancy Value Theory and the Unified Theory of Acceptance and Use of Technology (UTAUT), we used Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modeling to assess how Academic Workload, Time Pressure, and motivational sensitivities relate to GenAI use and its association with Academic Performance, Procrastination, and Self-Perceived Memory Decline. Results show that Academic Workload, Time Pressure, and motivational factors (Sensitivity to Rewards and Quality) were positively associated with GenAI use, which was widespread – more than 90% of students reporting use at least twice per week. GenAI use was positively associated with higher Academic Performance, but also with increased Procrastination and Self-Perceived Memory Decline. Contrary to prior research, age, gender, and education level were not significantly associated with GenAI use, reflecting the widespread GenAI adoption across student groups. These findings highlight GenAI’s dual role as both a potential performance-support tool and a mechanism of cognitive offloading, underscoring the need for balanced integration strategies that leverage AI-assisted efficiency while preserving meaningful cognitive engagement and mitigating risks associated with overreliance on AI tools.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: Innovation is increasingly important for organisations seeking to adapt to rapid economic changes and sustain competitiveness through effective human capital utilisation and employee creativity. In Malaysia, strengthening innovation outcomes aligns with the national aspiration to develop a knowledge and innovation-driven economy, as reflected in the Thirteenth Malaysia Plan (RMK13) 2026–2030. As key academic knowledge professionals, professors play an important role in knowledge creation, research and institutional innovation. However, empirical understanding of the personal resources and work-related mechanisms that foster innovative work behaviour (IWB) among professors in Malaysian private universities remains limited. Guided by Social Cognitive Theory (SCT) and Job Demands-Resources (JD-R) Theory, this study examines the relationships of self-efficacy (SE) and intrinsic motivation (IM) with IWB and evaluates the mediating role of work engagement (WE). Using a quantitative research design and purposive sampling, data were collected from 205 professors across private universities in Malaysia and analysed using Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modeling (PLS-SEM) via SmartPLS 4. The findings show that WE is positively and significantly associated with IWB. SE and IM are positively and significantly associated with WE and WE significantly mediates the relationships of both SE and IM with IWB. The findings contribute to Strategic Human Resource Management (SHRM) literature by highlighting WE as an important mechanism linking personal resources with IWB in the Malaysian higher education sector. Practically, the study provides insights for HR practitioners and institutional leaders to strengthen personal resources and work engagement, optimise talent management, and foster supportive workplace environments that promote academic innovation.

Scaling assessment in higher education faces two intertwined bottlenecks: the cognitive burden of authoring assessments and the inability to semantically evaluate open-ended responses, which together create a persistent feedback gap that hinders student learning outcomes. To address these challenges, we present Edhivo, an AI-native pedagogical platform that addresses both bottlenecks through a vertically integrated system for content delivery, assessment, and reporting. Edhivo employs a Dual-LLM pipeline: one model generates context-aware assessments for both multiple-choice and open-ended questions, from instructor-provided materials, while a second model performs multi-criteria, rubric-based evaluation of student responses, enabling near-instant qualitative feedback at multiple hierarchical levels. All AI interactions are source-grounded to reduce hallucination risk, and a Human-in-the-Loop review process preserves instructor authority. We demonstrate Edhivo's efficacy through a pilot deployment at Stony Brook University in a real classroom environment in 2026 spring, where it supports high-frequency assessment creation and evaluation for a cohort of 36 students throughout a full semester, significantly reducing authoring effort and feedback latency while enabling novel pedagogical designs centered on active learning.
topics: Intelligent Tutoring Systems and Adaptive Learning

documents.abstract: This study examined the structural relationships among creative thinking, cognitive flexibility, perceived usefulness, and continuance intention to use generative AI among university students, focusing on the mediating effect of perceived usefulness and the moderating effect of AI ethical awareness. Data from 594 university students with experience using generative AI were analyzed using SPSS 29.0 and AMOS 29.0. The results indicated that cognitive flexibility had a significant positive effect on perceived usefulness, whereas creative thinking did not. Perceived usefulness had a significant positive effect on continuance intention and significantly mediated the relationship between cognitive flexibility and continuance intention, while the indirect effect of creative thinking was not significant. AI ethical awareness did not significantly moderate the relationship between perceived usefulness and continuance intention. These results suggest that cognitive flexibility is an important cognitive factor associated with perceived usefulness and that perceived usefulness plays a mediating role in the relationship between cognitive flexibility and continuance intention. The findings underscore the importance of fostering learners’ ability to critically evaluate, adapt, and reconstruct AI-generated information and suggest that AI ethical awareness should be further examined in relation to responsible AI use rather than solely as a moderator of continuance intention.

Higher distance education opens a wide range of opportunities for students with different socio-demographic backgrounds (e.g., age, gender, native language) and task-related skills (e.g., experience in scientific reading or online learning, previous degrees). Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning (CSCL), where students work together in virtual groups, is a common teaching method in distance education. The current research investigates the consequences of stereotypes for targets and perceivers during the formation and collaboration phases in multi-attributionally diverse CSCL groups by systematically examining the individual level and the CSCL-group level. N = 2,023 students in 285 CSCL groups participated in a longitudinal field study in the introductory module of the BSc Psychology curriculum at a large European public distance teaching university. Analyses of multilevel models corresponding to pre-registered hypotheses replicated the findings of previous research that CSCL groups with high socio-demographic and high task-related diversity showed lower structural integration during collaboration. To explain this at-risk constellation for CSCL groups with highly diverse members, we investigated the role of being a target vs. perceiver of negative stereotypes within the group. Targets experiencing social identity threat reported a lower sense of belonging to the CSCL group and, consequently, lower motivation to initiate and maintain social relations with other group members. Moreover, targets generally reported higher social identity threat. Findings are discussed in terms of social-psychological approaches to microdynamics in CSCL groups and interventions to mitigate effects of diversity and stereotyping in higher distance education.

Image interpretation requires the integration of explicit and tacit knowledge, yet existing interactive training systems struggle to convey expert tacit strategies to novices. We developed the expert gaze-guided image interpretation ability training system (EGITS), a human-computer interaction framework that combines cascade forest-based eye-movement classification (EMCCF) with cognitive strategy spatiotemporal similarity quantification (CSTM) to support gaze classification, expert-novice strategy comparison, and personalized feedback. Three experiments evaluated the system. CSTM showed superior robustness, outperforming a state-of-the-art benchmark by approximately 14%, and achieved significantly better performance in most gaze-similarity scenarios. In a three-phase online study, EGITS-trained novices showed a 122.5% increase in cognitive-strategy similarity to experts and significantly outperformed the control subgroup. Training was also associated with fewer fixations, longer average fixation durations, and shorter saccade amplitudes. These findings provide preliminary evidence that EGITS promotes expert-like visual-search strategies in FPS-based image-interpretation tasks and support the feasibility of eye-tracking-based visual-search training.

Generative AI (GenAI) offers opportunities for repeated practice and feedback in English language learning. However, how students participate in these learning activities requires further investigation. This study examined learning engagement profiles and their associations with GenAI use and speaking performance among 500 STEM master’s students in an AI-assisted ESAP speaking course at a Chinese university. Latent profile analysis used self-reported behavioral, emotional, and cognitive engagement scores collected in Week 15. Separate R3STEP models examined associations with self-reported weekly GenAI use frequency and average weekly online duration. BCH analyses compared posttest speaking performance across profiles while adjusting for pretest scores. Four profiles emerged: Low Engagement Profile (P1, 22.4%), High Engagement Profile (P2, 38.2%), Low Emotional Engagement Profile (P3, 24.0%), and Low Cognitive Engagement Profile (P4, 15.4%). Proportions were based on most likely assignments. After Holm correction, longer online duration was associated with higher odds of membership in P2, P3, and P4 relative to P1. More frequent GenAI use was associated with membership in P2 and P4 relative to P3. P2 had significantly higher baseline-adjusted overall speaking scores than all other profiles. These findings provide person-centered evidence of learner heterogeneity in AI-assisted ESAP. They highlight the value of considering multidimensional engagement configurations alongside GenAI use indicators when interpreting differences in speaking performance.

Abstract Purpose Traditional ultrasonic detection for kidney stones is prone to variability due to the experience and skill of the operating physician, leading to inconsistent diagnostic outcomes. Factors such as stone size, location, and surrounding tissues can further compromise accuracy. Artificial intelligence (AI), with its advanced data processing and deep learning capabilities, offers a solution by automating the analysis of medical images to improve diagnostic accuracy and efficiency. Methods This cross-sectional study was conducted at our hospital between 01/06/2022 and 03/07/2024., using a datasets of 791 ultrasound images from patients with confirmed kidney stones and 117 images from non-stone participants. The High-Resolution Network (HRNet) was employed for model training to detect kidney stones in ultrasound images. Detailed image annotations were created using the labelme tool and converted to COCO format for compatibility with AI algorithms. Results The HRNet model achieved an accuracy of 86.4% in detecting kidney stones in the validation datasets, with a sensitivity of 94.3% and specificity of 73.2%. The model effectively identified both kidney stones and normal conditions. Conclusions The study demonstrates that AI, specifically HRNet, can significantly enhance the accuracy and efficiency of kidney stone detection in ultrasound imaging. This approach reduces the diagnostic burden on physicians and improves patient outcomes. However, challenges remain, including the need for large-scale annotated datasets and rigorous validation of AI models to ensure reliability in clinical settings.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: Earth Observation (EO)-based agricultural monitoring is shifting from pixel-level spectral analysis toward representation-driven modeling, yet systematic evaluation of learned representations remains limited. Geospatial foundation models (FMs) generate high-dimensional embeddings encoding complex spatio-temporal land-surface properties, but their utility and interpretability for agricultural applications remain insufficiently understood. This study presents a representation-agnostic framework evaluating a 64-dimensional AlphaEarth embedding space against Sentinel-2 reflectance, NDVI phenology, and harmonic features across geometric separability, temporal dynamics, spatial robustness, and cross-regional generalisation using field-scale data from the Conterminous United States (CONUS; 2017-2023) and Northern India (2021). Traditional features achieve strong linear separability (Fisher ratio), while embeddings provide superior distribution-aware separation - Bhattacharyya and Mahalanobis distances up to an order of magnitude higher for spectrally similar pairs (e.g. Corn/Soybeans: 3.9 vs. 0.10). Embeddings uniquely capture multi-year crop rotation dynamics, yielding a separability ratio of 1.784, versus a maximum of 1.003 for all engineered features. Under spatially explicit validation, embeddings exhibit lower residual spatial autocorrelation of errors (mean Moran's $I \approx 0.17$), reducing reliance on geographic proximity. However, harmonic features show stronger cross-continental transferability (US $\to$ India Macro F1: 0.493 vs. 0.326 for embeddings), with NDVI showing a similar advantage. The combined feature space yields balanced performance. These findings reveal a trade-off between representational richness and cross-region transferability, providing a framework for feature selection in large-scale crop classification.

Background: Large language models (LLMs) such as ChatGPT, Gemini, Claude, and Mistral are increasingly used to obtain medical information, but their accuracy in carpal tunnel syndrome (CTS) management is uncertain. This study evaluated whether LLM-generated recommendations align with American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons (AAOS) clinical practice guidelines (CPGs). Methods: Four LLMs (ChatGPT-4, Gemini, Claude-3, Mistral-7B) were queried with standardized prompts derived from AAOS CTS CPGs. Each prompt was asked 3 times per model, and responses were synthesized. Two blinded reviewers graded outputs as concordant, discordant, or indeterminate, with disagreements resolved by consensus. Concordance distributions were compared using χ 2 testing with Bonferroni correction. Inter-rater reliability was measured with Cohen’s κ. Results: Across 252 recommendations, 72.6% were concordant, 11.5% discordant, and 15.9% indeterminate. ChatGPT achieved the highest concordance (92.1%) and lowest discordance (1.6%), while Mistral performed poorest (52.4% concordance, 17.5% discordance). Reviewer agreement was excellent (κ = 0.91). Conclusions: Over 1 in 4 LLM-generated CTS recommendations were not concordant with AAOS CPGs. ChatGPT outperformed other models, though variable performance underscores the need for clinician oversight and careful validation before clinical use.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: Examining students’ perceived and demonstrated reliance on AI can reveal how accurately students understand and monitor their AI use, which is critical for fostering appropriate reliance on AI. However, little research has examined how to evaluate these reliance levels on ChatGPT in collaborative problem solving (CPS), the extent to which they align, and for what reasons students rely on or refrain from using ChatGPT. This case study analysed the reflections and online notes of 48 Chinese undergraduate students participating in ChatGPT-supported CPS. The results show that although about 23% of students perceived over or high reliance on ChatGPT, only 4.34% demonstrated these levels in their online posts. Students relied on ChatGPT for reasons such as helping learn new concepts and knowledge, enhancing learning efficiency, and providing personalized guidance. In contrast, they refrained from using ChatGPT for reasons such as prioritizing the need to develop autonomy and critical thinking skills, lacking the skills to use ChatGPT, and having doubts about its accuracy and ability to handle complex tasks. The findings advance our understanding of how overreliance can be measured, why it occurs, and the extent to which students demonstrate metacognitive awareness of their ChatGPT use.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: This exploratory study examined associations between entropy-based measures of team dynamics and team performance in an immersive virtual reality (VR) team training environment. Six teams ( n = 6) completed a VR-based Tactical Combat Casualty Care (TC3) training session within the Team Dynamics Measurement Framework (TDMF) architecture, consisting of two scenarios with pre-, break, and post-measurements. Behavioral data were continuously captured across four interaction layers: communication, gaze, patient, and system. Entropy time series were computed using a moving window approach to continuously measure team adaptation, where low entropy corresponds to more uniform, stable team dynamics and high entropy means that team is momentarily unstable and adapting. Mean and range entropy metrics (measures of amount of adaptation and adaptive capacity) were correlated with team dynamics ratings, self-efficacy, satisfaction, and system usability scores. Correlations were computed in two analytic variants: (a) correlations using raw pre-, break-, and post-scenario outcome scores, and (b) correlations using delta-based change scores to examine performance shifts across scenario segments. Results indicated moderate to large associations between entropy-based measures and performance outcomes, with range entropy demonstrating stronger and more consistent associations than mean entropy across layers, with the strongest observed effect between early self-efficacy increases during Scenario 1 and range patient interaction entropy ( r (4) = 0.93; p = .007), providing preliminary proof-of-concept support for entropy-based metrics as dynamic indicators of adaptive team functioning within immersive VR training systems.

This study explores how first-year pre-service English language teachers (PSELTs) interpret classroom silence and engagement in an Oral Communication course and how they understand their own participation after comparison with a more participatory course section. Theoretically, it brings Willingness to Communicate (WTC) and Oral Communication Apprehension (OCA) into dialogue with a multidimensional engagement framework while treating silence as behavior whose meaning must be interpreted rather than assumed. Using a qualitative exploratory design, the study involved 48 PSELTs in two pre-existing, administratively constituted course sections taught by the same instructor under the same syllabus. Data were generated through an open-ended questionnaire, written self-reflections, individual semi-structured interviews with 15 focal-section participants, and post-comparison written reflections. Two combined-class sessions provided the comparison, with the more participatory section serving as a contextual point of comparison rather than a baseline or control group. Findings showed that participants associated silence most strongly with fear of negative evaluation and perfectionism, alongside linguistic retrieval difficulties, limited topic knowledge, peer relations, low interest, attentional drift, fatigue, prior learning experiences, and conditions beyond the classroom. Conversely, a smaller set of accounts described silence as active listening, cognitive processing, or preparation for later participation, indicating that limited observable participation can coexist with cognitive engagement. Notably, post-comparison accounts gave greater prominence to relationships, teamwork, and classroom climate, although similar social explanations were already evident before the comparison activity. The findings therefore support a shift in emphasis rather than a causal change in engagement or WTC. Ultimately, OCA explains an important part of silence among PSELTs but not its full range of conditions and functions. The study concludes that silence in language teacher education is heterogeneous, situated, and analytically ambiguous. Teacher educators should distinguish observable quietness from disengagement while attending to the affective, cognitive, relational, and contextual conditions that shape participation.

Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) typically relies on preference pairs generated from diverse model pools and ranked by an external LLM judge. The recently proposed delta-learning hypothesis suggests that comparable supervision can instead be obtained from a single pair of models by treating the larger model's response as preferred. We investigate the limits of this approach across model families and scales. We show, both theoretically and empirically, that fixed model pairs introduce systematic, generator-dependent biases that are predictive of the preference label independent of response quality. Consequently, DPO trained on single-pair data consistently underperforms multi-model preference data, despite the larger generator producing higher-quality responses, and we trace this gap to training dynamics consistent with reward hacking on these biases. We further show that simply increasing the number of generators, even without an external judge, is enough to partially mitigate this effect. Our results highlight generator diversity as a critical factor in preference-data construction.

As deep learning (DL) models are widely used in software systems, test generation plays a crucial role in assessing the quality of such models before deployment. To date, the most advanced test generators rely on generative AI to synthesize inputs; however, these approaches remain limited in providing semantic insight into the causes of misbehaviours and in offering fine-grained semantic controllability over the generated inputs. In this paper, we introduce Detect, a feature-aware test generation framework for vision-based DL models that generates inputs by perturbing disentangled semantic attributes within the latent space. Detect perturbs individual latent features in a controlled way and observes how these changes affect the model’s output. Through this process, it identifies which features lead to behaviour shifts and uses a vision-language model for semantic attribution. Detect enables semantically controlled perturbations in StyleGAN’s disentangled latent space, allowing us to test whether a model generalizes under task-relevant feature changes and remains invariant under task-irrelevant ones. Empirical results across image classification and detection tasks show that Detect generates high-quality test cases with fine-grained control, reveals distinct shortcut behaviours across model architectures (convolutional and transformer-based), and bugs that are not captured by accuracy metrics. Specifically, Detect outperforms a state-of-the-art test generator in decision boundary discovery and provides more interpretable feature-level diagnoses than a leading spurious feature localization method in identifying robustness failures. Our findings show that fully fine-tuned convolutional models are prone to overfitting on localized cues, such as co-occurring visual traits, while weakly supervised transformers tend to rely on global features, such as environmental variances. These findings highlight the value of interpretable and feature-aware testing in improving DL model reliability, and refocus DL testing from class-level failure discovery to feature-level, semantically grounded diagnosis and repair.

A software feature usually evolves over time: developers extend its first version as new use cases and requirements arrive, and each extension builds on code written earlier. Most feature benchmarks evaluate a single request on a fixed codebase. Feature evolution requires evaluating successive extensions on an agent's own earlier code and checking whether the feature remains correct. We introduce FeatureArc to evaluate coding agents on evolving features, together with a pipeline that constructs its tasks from repository histories. The benchmark combines dependencies between successive stages of the same feature, explicit requirements and interface contracts, and executable checks across four programming languages. The pipeline validates fail-to-pass (F2P) tests for new behavior and pass-to-pass (P2P) tests for existing behavior on the reference code before and after each stage. We evaluated 10 coding agents on 73 manually reviewed tasks of 2 to 10 stages. Each agent works in one persistent session and workspace without external test feedback or rollback. The evaluation reveals a gap between first-stage and whole-feature success: pooled success falls from 62.7% at the first stage to 28.5% when the whole feature is tested on the final code. Trajectory analysis identifies inherited defects as a common failure mechanism, present in 72.9% of failed later stages. These earlier errors often remain undetected: in stages following a failure, agents leave the earlier error unnoticed about 95% of the time, and their self-tests rarely revisit earlier stages. Evolving a feature autonomously, without human checks between stages, therefore remains a substantial challenge for current coding agents. At Tencent, the pipeline extends internal evaluations to this setting and guides the development of Hunyuan, Tencent's family of large language models.

Public disclosure repositories such as SEC EDGAR support informed investment through web access to corporate filings. Supporting their review with language model agents requires discovering unstated deficiencies across related documents, acquiring missing company facts, and verifying that requested revisions satisfy evidence-backed requirements. Existing financial question-answering evaluations provide limited evidence of these interactive capabilities. We introduce \textbf{FilingLoop}, an interactive benchmark and a self-evolving agent framework for corporate disclosure review and revision. Grounded in historical U.S.\ Securities and Exchange Commission correspondence, FilingLoop reconstructs 380 predominantly IPO review tasks from 96 companies under distinct information constraints. An evaluator separate from the acting agents scores final filings and responses against 6,099 eligible requirements and audits unsupported claims and harmful revisions. Our framework couples iterative review and revision within each case with procedural learning across cases, converting requirement-level evaluation feedback into role-specific guidance without updating model weights. Updates affect only subsequent cases, allowing procedural adaptation to be assessed without retrying scored tasks. On the evaluated stream, evolution increases requirement fulfillment from 24.28\% to 27.96\% and full comment resolution from 16.90\% to 20.75\%, with a 5.8\% increase in total cost over the fixed-policy variant. FilingLoop connects the concerns an agent discovers with the company facts it obtains and the revisions it commits, providing requirement-level feedback for procedures used in later review tasks.

Fine-tuning Large Language Models (LLMs) on instruction data can quietly erode their safety, even when no training example looks harmful. Because this safety-degrading data looks benign, standard content filters struggle to catch it. We tackle this problem by developing SimpleLoRIF, a scalable gradient embedding method that identifies fine-tuning examples whose gradients align with unsafe behavior. By simplifying a low-rank attribution method and restricting backpropagation to the final four transformer blocks, SimpleLoRIF can embed datasets on the order of a million examples, boosting gradient attribution from a small-scale analysis tool into a practical filter for full post-training datasets. We first validate it on emergent misalignment, where we find that gradients can connect insecure-code training data to the broadly harmful behaviors that appear after fine-tuning, with AUC as high as 0.865 in the gradient space of misaligned models. We then use SimpleLoRIF to build SafeTulu, a version of Tulu 3 with the 20% of examples most gradient-aligned with unsafe responses removed. Training on SafeTulu reduces GCG attack success rate by up to 22% across Qwen, Llama, and Olmo, outperforming both LLM-as-a-judge and prior gradient-based filtering, while largely preserving or even improving capability. Finally, we analyzed the removed data and identify possibly under-studied sources of safety degradation, such as tool-execution failures and narrative arithmetic. We release SafeTulu along with a Hugging Face Space that lets researchers build their own customized versions of SafeTulu to fine-tune on, such as by changing the removal fraction or filtering only certain subsets.

As machine learning systems make increasingly greater decisions about people's lives, it is critical to provide users with actionable recourse about how they can achieve their desired outcomes. This problem is currently tackled by relying on expensive human supervision which involves hand-designing a cost function before searching for low-cost actions that achieve the desired outcome. In this paper, we propose \textit{``Data-Driven Action Recourse"} (DDAR), the first approach for providing action recourse without requiring costly supervision from humans about action costs. We build upon the notion that highly likely trajectories in the historical user data should be associated with lower costs. With this, DDAR first builds a dynamics model of historical user trajectories. Under this model, it then searches for trajectories that achieve the desired outcome. In experiments, we find that this simple approach recommends plausible action recourse without requiring human supervision, achieving lower action costs than the existing approaches.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: BACKGROUND: Prolonged standing is common in manufacturing and assembly-line work and is associated with musculoskeletal discomfort, especially in the lower limbs and spine. The influence of foot posture, morphology, and plantar loading patterns on this discomfort remains unclear. OBJECTIVE: To analyze the associations between foot posture, plantar pressure, and 3D foot morphology with work-related musculoskeletal discomfort in standing workers and to examine the role of BMI and the potential modifying role of sex. METHODS: A cross-sectional study was conducted among 240 assembly-line workers (129 women, 53.8%). Musculoskeletal discomfort was assessed using the Cornell Musculoskeletal Discomfort Questionnaire (CMDQ). Foot posture (FPI-6), baropodometry (FreeMed), and 3D foot morphology (DOMESCAN) were evaluated under standardized conditions. Participants were classified as having low (CMDQ ≤ 10) or moderate-high (≥ 11) discomfort. Firth-penalized logistic regression analyzed associations between overall CMDQ discomfort, foot posture, sex, and BMI, including an FPI × sex interaction term. RESULTS: All workers reported at least one musculoskeletal discomfort response, with the feet, neck, and lumbar region accounting for the largest proportions of reported discomfort. Among women, pronated foot posture was associated with higher odds of moderate-high overall CMDQ discomfort (OR = 2.91, 95% CI 1.10-7.28). Overweight/obesity status was associated with higher odds of foot and hip/gluteal discomfort, whereas, among women, pronated foot posture was associated with greater odds of lumbar discomfort. The pronation-discomfort association was stronger in women and attenuated in men. CONCLUSIONS: Among women, pronated foot posture was associated with greater overall work-related musculoskeletal discomfort during prolonged standing and with greater odds of lumbar discomfort, whereas overweight/obesity status was associated with greater odds of foot and hip/gluteal discomfort. The pronation-discomfort association was attenuated in men. From an occupational-health perspective, incorporating foot-posture and BMI assessment into ergonomic evaluations may help identify workers who could benefit from more individualized preventive strategies, particularly women with pronated feet.
topics: Occupational Health and Safety in Workplaces

documents.abstract: University students' psychological well-being is a critical public health concern, creating demand for digital interventions that are both safe and effective. Although conversational agents offer scalable support, existing usability heuristics cannot address complex affective dimensions such as emotional containment and clinical safety, revealing a gap in specialized design frameworks. To address this, the study introduces the “Affective Design Checklist,” a practical inspection tool for developing and auditing mental health conversational agents. Using Jabareen's conceptual framework analysis with a PRISMA-guided systematic review of 43 key articles, the instrument underwent a two-stage validation by a panel of ten experts, achieving a scale-level Content Validity Index (S-CVI/Ave) of 0.971, with near-unanimous agreement on ethical and regulatory dimensions. This research translates abstract bioethical and affective computing principles into actionable verification items, offering a specialized standard to ensure digital interventions are technically usable, affectively competent, and ethically aligned with student needs.

Abstract Artificial intelligence is typically linked to the learning platform, the diagnosis of skills and employment services, but the advantages of AI to workforce training are still not even as the skills acquired in the learning platform are not automatically available for use. There is already a significant amount of published work that discusses automation risk, as well as digital competencies and the role of AI in learning and development, but less comparative focus on the institutions that transform learning resources into recognised skills and employability through the operation and use of AI enabled and/or AI relevant learning environments. By designing it around the theoretically motivated Capability Approach of Sen, this study analyzed SkillsFuture Singapore and the European Digital Skills and Jobs Coalition and India’s National Career Service using a qualitative comparative documentary approach.
